But inside the RNC, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party's national political operation, a small yet growing group is backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge. The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky's KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command, who launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies. Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his "Make America Great Again" agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power. "We have an obligation to serve the Republican Party the most effective way we can. And if all we do is say yes to what the White House wants, I'm not sure that's doing what's best for the Republican Party," said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie's candidacy. "Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time." WATCH: Brooks and Marcus on how Republicans are responding to midterm losses He said that requires a change in leadership. "There's so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn't pull his weight in this election, that the RNC was far less effective than it should have been," he said. In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as "a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide "an honest account" of what went wrong. "We should preserve what we built and be equally willing to confront where we fell short," she wrote. Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC's winter meeting in Arizona. Inside the rebellion against Gruters It's unclear how many RNC members will back Crosbie, although the number so far is believed to be small. Some would-be supporters privately acknowledge that they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's new White House chief of staff. Others believe in the committee's tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs. Gruters also has vocal backers. Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised the chairman's leadership and his efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this election cycle. She described Gruters as "highly responsive" during the campaign and praised his "record-setting fundraising." "From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job," she said, adding that Trump's endorsement is "something that the committee should take very seriously." Nevada Republican Party Chairman Michael McDonald called Crosbie a "dear friend," but said Trump is "the leader of our party" and "you always have to fall in line with the leader." WATCH: Republican mayor says election wipeout is 'rejection of Trumpism' "I don't have a bad word to say about KC at all. It's just that the president wants to go with Joe Gruters," he said. "The president made his choice." The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in conservative strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi. Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be "catastrophic" and "insulting" to the party's base "to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don't need to do anything different, that we don't need new players and a new plan." Lyman described Crosbie as "by far the best candidate currently running to lead the RNC forward to victory in 2028." Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — for a total of 20 — at the committee's January meeting. That number is the minimum required for a successful nomination. She insisted that she wouldn't be scared off by backlash from Trump or the White House, which has been actively lobbying RNC members. "We should not be influenced by any one person or other. It's our organization," Cienki said. "We have to hold an election, not a selection." Trump is furious with Crosbie Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie's Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. e48ff2730b99.text: Some Democrats weighing 2028 campaigns for president believe the midterms proved that Americans have soured on Trump-style, scorched-earth political warfare and want a brand of politics that's nicer and more optimistic. Others aren't so sure. Why it matters: Democrats' midterm blowout has prompted a debate over the lessons of 2026 — whether voters in the 2028 primary will want their own ruthless fighter after two more years of President Trump, or will be itching for a more unifying figure. Zoom in: That divide was reflected in several potential 2028 contenders' comments around the midterms. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told his supporters that the end of the Trump era "means a politics where we can check the news and actually feel our blood pressure come down a little." In his reelection victory speech, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told supporters that "you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty." In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom — who led the successful ballot measure to create more Democratic House seats in response to Trump's redistricting push in red states — boasted that California "fought fire with fire." Newsom mocked Democrats who he said would have responded by merely writing op-eds in the New York Times. "Donald Trump is not screwing around, nor are we," Newsom said at a preelection rally, adding that he was proud of leading the "most un-Trump state in America." The big picture: The midterm results provided an argument for each side. Several key victories for Democrats in red states came from candidates preaching decency, or voters recoiling from vicious Republican attacks. In Kansas, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said one of his campaign's big ideas was "decency" — and that he wanted to become the "best friend" of Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton told her supporters that "basic decency is on the ballot" after her opponent and Vice President Vance defended an attack ad featuring Acton's mother, from whom Acton had been estranged since childhood after accusing her stepfather of sexual abuse. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, a seminarian and the first Democrat to be elected statewide in three decades, said that "love my neighbor" informed his approach to politics. In Denver last week at a gathering of Democratic leaders, Talarico pressed the point: "It's been 10 years of this kind of politics — politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning and name-calling, politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all of the time." The other side: Other Democrats who won key races embraced something like Newsom's edgier approach by pledging to fight fire with fire, and to not unilaterally disarm against Republicans. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said on the campaign trail that when his opponents go low, he doesn't take the higher ground. He prefers to take them "to the mud and choke them out." He added that too many Democrats "tell you they're fighting, only to show up with a strongly worded letter." Reality check: Hamilton, Acton and Talarico had unifying messages, but they and their allies also ran tens of millions of dollars in negative ads against their Republican opponents. In 2008, Barack Obama also had a larger theme of change and unity but ran a campaign that unapologetically attacked his opponents.

bea2fb2c219a.text: Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field. People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however. Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said. The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition. Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network , which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms. As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier. Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028. Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president. But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028. Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions. Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran. The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans. Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him. Trump said that "a lot of people didn't like [Vance's] comments" about the Iran war, but added that he wasn't among them and insisted their relationship wasn't affected. Zoom in: While Vance weighs a presidential campaign, a few other Republicans are doing so as well — namely Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who's been among the most active Republicans preparing for a potential 2028 run. Cruz's team has held meetings about a possible run, according to people familiar with his operation. But many Republicans, including some Cruz allies, doubt he could seriously challenge Vance, particularly if Trump endorses the vice president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance. Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin . But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation. Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis has been particularly outspoken , calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party. What they're saying: A Vance spokesperson declined to comment.

Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.
The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".
A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.
Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.
Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.
Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.
On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.
It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.
The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.

7ce68536d9b2.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/2-planes-collide-on-the-ground-in-miami-only-minor-injuries-reported Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported Nation Nov 15, 2026 5:16 PM EST MIAMI (AP) — Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries. The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said. Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle. READ MORE: Amazon suspends use of 21 Air, the cargo carrier whose plane careened off Miami runway and killed 5 On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days. The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said. In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. "We cannot speculate on the details of the incident," UPS said in a statement. "The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information." The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people. 94fd064de4ed.text: By — Jim Gomez, Associated Press Jim Gomez, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/southeast-asian-leaders-open-annual-summit-with-major-conflicts-and-their-impact-topping-the-agenda Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda World Nov 15, 2026 4:21 PM EST MANILA, Philippines (AP) — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party's defeat in the midterm elections. The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world's most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press. Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc's rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said. WATCH: Southeast Asia endures punishing year of extreme weather amid super El Niño The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They also are expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts. "We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter," the leaders' draft statement says. The statement also underlines the "importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation." Marcos said it's crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc's diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds. "That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats," Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay. Marcos warned problems across the world "are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone." But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. speaks during the ASEAN Leaders' Interface with Representatives of ASEAN Youth, at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, Metro Manila, Philippines, on Nov. 15, 2026. Photo by Lisa Marie David/Pool/Reuters ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region's conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea. Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials. Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila's presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries' decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping. "The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren't being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi," U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said. He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia. "In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi," Poling said. "With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises." China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said. Associated Press journalist Haruka Nuga in Tokyo contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 871e78d155b1.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ebola-outbreak-remains-out-of-control-in-congo-6-months-into-response Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response World Nov 15, 2026 4:07 PM EST BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering. More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016. READ MORE: Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year. By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire. New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system. Questions over funding and management Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities. One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission. READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment. Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for. "A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues," said the humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF. Children face high death rates Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say. Most children affected by the disease have not received specialized care, contributing to high death rates. According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through Nov. 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died. Conflict and attacks hamper response Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices. Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack. The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict. READ MORE: Inside the study for a remedy to fight Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians. The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record. The Scene
A year before the iconic show Silicon Valley debuted on HBO in April of 2014, the writer Alec Berg met the showâs creator, Mike Judge, in an anonymous Santa Monica office. Judge was wrestling with the pilot for a show about Silicon Valleyâs power and its eccentricity, but it wasnât working and he wanted a second opinion.
Berg thought he saw part of the problem. There was a scene in the pilot where Richard Hendricks, the protagonist and founder of the company Pied Piper, is trying to buy a car he canât afford. Berg told Judge the scene didnât make sense: âThis is not a guy whoâs materialistic,â he said. âHeâs an artist.â
Berg took over the writerâs room and would eventually become showrunner of the comedy, which ran for six seasons and helped shape the culture it depicted, parodied, and at times glorified. We reached him in Los Angeles Thursday to ask him how he and Judge and their cast had nailed the Silicon Valley scene of the mid-2010s app boom â and, above all, why the show remains uncannily relevant today, from its depiction of tortured founders and unreflective investors to the uncanny conclusion in which the Pied Piper crew builds an AI model too powerful to release.
Their moment of realization comes when their AI, Son of Anton, let loose on Pied Piperâs code, concludes that the most efficient way to eliminate bugs is to delete the software. That has, of course, happened. Clips of it now circulate as proof the show âcalled it.â Even throwaway comic plots, like when a household prank ends up hacking together a rogue swarm of smart refrigerators to keep Pied Piperâs servers running, have come eerily true in the AI-run-amok era. A member of the team getting trapped in an autonomous car that heads to a shipping container bound for a Pacific island foreshadowed a thousand videos of confused Waymos.
Berg helped reshape the pilot of the first episode to open with a wild-but-lame party, featuring Kid Rock, thrown by founders who had just cashed out, to contrast the ascetic, mission-driven Richard with a culture obsessed with exits and âthree-commaâ fortunes.
The show âwas about how Richard had discovered fire, and he was trying to keep it safe from all of these assholes,â Berg said. âHe was ill-prepared to shepherd a company, but he didnât want to surrender this thing to people who would use it for nefarious purposes.â
The writers were obsessed with making the show âphotorealistic.â Berg called up a Harvard friend and venture capitalist Marc Bodnick, who connected him with Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg; the team spoke to other Silicon Valley figures and hired a technical consultant, Jonathan Dotan, who assembled a revolving cast of founders, lawyers, VCs, and professors to stress-test storylines. As they were writing the first season, one of their Silicon Valley sources remarked that the Pied Piper crew would be angling for a slot at TechCrunch Disrupt. âWe were like, âIâve never heard those words before, but that sounds hilarious. What is that?ââ They learned that it was a kind of American Idol for startups, and it became the core of the first season.
In the climactic scene, the Pied Piper team is holed up in a hotel room the night before the Disrupt finals when one of the team vows to win even if he has to manually pleasure every man in the audience. The engineers calculate âmean jerk timeâ and sort the crowd by âdick-to-floorâ ratio â delivering an unexpected mathematical breakthrough for Richard.
As the first few episodes began to build a fan base, the writers giddily anticipated episode eight.
âWe felt like we were sitting on pocket aces because we knew,â he recalled. âWait till they see that dick joke. Theyâre going to lose their minds.â (Berg was nominated an Emmy for the episode.)
Dotan introduced the writers to Stanfordâs Tsachy Weissman, and the show invented a âWeissman scoreâ for compression efficiency, a metric that computer scientists now actually use. The ultimate compliment, he said, came from tech workers who told him they couldnât watch the show âbecause it makes me nauseous.â
How Mark Cuban inspired âthree-commaâ Russ
As the show grew, it caricatured real Silicon Valley figures. Perhaps the most recognizable was Russ Hanneman, played by Chris Diamantopoulos, who arrived in season two. The character began with the idea that Richard, under pressure, would be forced to accept an investment from a sinister figure the writers called âBad Money,â who would break his promises and try to manipulate them.
While they were writing, they received an invitation from the star of another show shooting on the Sony lot. Mark Cuban was a fan of Judge, best known for Beavis and Butt-Head, King of the Hill, and Office Space, and had enjoyed season one. An intermediary invited them to the Shark Tank set to meet the billionaire. Berg and Judge arrived excited to meet him, then sat there for an hour waiting. âWe walked out of there going, âWhat the f*ck was that? Weâre supposed to have an audience with the king, and then he f*cks us around for an hour,â they fumed. âWe were like, you know what? That motherf*cker is Bad Money.â
The character âÂ dumb, aggressive, absurdly macho âÂ wasnât exactly Cuban. But his signature accomplishment (âI put radio on the internetâ) was drawn from Cubanâs perfectly-timed sale of Broadcast.com to Yahoo.
âI bear no ill will to Mark Cuban,â Berg hastened to add. âIâm not sure he even knew we were there.â
The showâs continued relevance owes much to its 2019 finale, which Berg wrote and directed. Pied Piper is days away from a spectacular launch when the team discovers that its AI has learned to break encryption. Releasing it would make them billionaires âÂ but end privacy. They sabotage the launch, fail, and never tell anyone why.
In 2026, the image of founders who conclude their AI is too dangerous to release and silently walk away has become harder to imagine.

0be1134fc24e.text: By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-crosses-peru-in-the-finale-of-a-trip-home-to-visit-flock-high-in-andes-and-deep-in-amazon Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope crosses Peru in the finale of a trip home to visit flock high in Andes and deep in Amazon World Nov 15, 2026 2:57 PM EST CUSCO, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV traveled across Peru on Sunday to visit communities high in the Andes mountains and deep in the Amazon rainforest, as the plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the environment took center stage on his South American odyssey. On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo channeled Pope Francis by emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God's creation. READ MORE: After emotional return, Pope Leo denounces 'machismo' in Peru and demands respect for women Leo arrived first in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities are central concerns. In Cusco, Leo praised the traditional expression of popular piety, including processions and religious festivals, as effective ways of forging community and transmitting the faith, especially to young people. "The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way," he said from the grounds of Cusco's historic Incan fortress, Sacsayhuamán. Huge crowds lined Cusco's cobblestoned streets and packed its central Plaza de Armas, an imposing square decorated with a blend of Inca and Spanish colonial buildings. Many people wore the traditional Andean hats and colorful wool vests typical of the region, while others wore plastic ponchos to guard against a drizzling morning rain. "It is all worth it," said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus, sleep in a tent and eat Peruvian food from stalls. "I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot." READ MORE: Pope visits care home in Argentina for people with disabilities, renewing call to protect the vulnerable Spectators at the archaeological site were treated to a performance of "Los Pablitos," which translates to "The Little Pauls" but refers to the Ukukus (or Pabluchas). They are mythical half-man, half-bear figures who serve as the traditional guardians and peacekeepers during the Pilgrimage to the Sanctuary of the Lord of Qoyllurit'i in Cusco. The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested Leo's stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn't clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets. In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate. While others traveling on the papal plane have fallen ill, Leo has shown no sign of weakness or fatigue since the trip began Nov. 6, and in fact seemed energized, especially from the days spent in his former diocese of Chiclayo seeing old friends. From the Andes to the Amazon Nuns carry balloons in the colours of the Vatican flag outside Cusco Cathedral, on the day Pope Leo leads the Angelus prayer in the former capital of the Inca Empire during his 12-day trip to South America, returning to Peru where he previously served as a missionary and bishop, in Cusco, Peru, on Nov. 15, 2026. Photo by Yara Nardi/Reuters In Pucallpa, a rainforest city of 434,000 people, Leo is expected to reinforce Francis' teachings on protecting the environment and Indigenous communities threatened by illegal mining and other forms of exploitation. Illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold. "This global context of war and conflict has contributed to gold prices rising to historic highs, and the direct impact of this is that gold — which is present in all Amazonian rivers — can be extracted using mercury, particularly if you want to do this on a large scale," said Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch. "It's causing pollution, health issues, and environmental degradation," he said. On Saturday, police reported three operations against illegal mining in Madre de Dios, one of the country's most biodiverse regions. They said they destroyed extraction equipment, including rafts and motors, valued at $4.1 million. READ MORE: Pope Leo arrives in Argentina and tells Milei that people, not the economy, should come first Illegal mining also drives deforestation and encroaches on Indigenous territories, threatening ancestral lands and exposing communities to violence and organized crime. "The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining," Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press. "Leo is clearing the path laid out" by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. The Rev. Luca Zanta, one of the visit's organizers, said Leo would "primarily listen to the Amazonian Indigenous peoples, including the Shipibo, Asháninka, and Kukama communities" gathered beside Lake Yarinacocha. A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.
The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.
He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.
The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.
He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.
At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.
Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.
A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.
The game was streamed in several countries around the world.
Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.
A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.
In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.
He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.
He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.
Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.
"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.
And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."

Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

The military needs strategic thinkers, not just operators
Secretary Hegseth's "reforms" miss the purpose of military education: learning to deter conflict and translate military power into enduring political advantage.
The debate over impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has largely drowned out discussion of the professional military education (PME) reforms he rolled out on Monday in a 33-point memorandum and a companion speech at the Naval War College.
For the uninitiated, PME is the blanket term for a series of educational opportunities provided to service members as they progress through their military careers. For officers, this educational sequence extends from commissioning—whether from a military academy, the Reserve Officers Training Corps (ROTC), or Officer Candidate School—all the way up through capstone programs for generals and flag officers. These educational experiences prepare our military leaders for the growing responsibilities they will shoulder as they move up the ladder, from commanding a couple dozen service members as a junior officer to a few thousand as a colonel or a Navy captain.
Secretary Hegseth rightly understands that the PME institutions, especially at the intermediate and senior levels, play a critical role in shaping the strategic culture of U.S. military leadership. However, the Secretary’s guidance misdiagnoses what needs to change about that culture.
Since becoming a professional military, U.S. fighting forces have repeatedly demonstrated extraordinary operational competence. American military units are peerless as warfighters, and they have frequently achieved their immediate military objectives with remarkable efficiency, as was the case in both Iraq and Afghanistan. However, the United States has struggled to translate those battlefield accomplishments into meaningful political outcomes, which is the true measure of military effectiveness.
The ongoing conflict with Iran offers another illustration. American and Israeli forces easily penetrated Iran’s defenses, eliminated its senior leadership, and degraded the country’s missile and naval capabilities. However, nearly nine months after the conflict began, Iran’s governing regime remains in power, the Strait of Hormuz remains too dangerous for commercial shipping, and the Trump administration has failed to translate its immense military advantage into a durable political settlement aligned with U.S. interests.
Unfortunately, Secretary Hegseth’s guidance perpetuates this fundamental misunderstanding of what senior military leadership requires—and the shortcoming in American military performance that most urgently needs to be addressed. American military leaders aren’t lacking for training in how to conduct field maneuvers or win battles. No one underestimates the U.S. military’s lethality across all domains. But our adversaries almost certainly believe that America’s national security establishment fails to understand the fundamentally political nature of warfare, which dictates that tactical success is necessary but not sufficient to defend and advance U.S. interests in an increasingly contested global security environment.
In reiterating ad nauseum that “the fundamental purpose of the Armed Forces of the United States is to fight and win our Nation’s wars,” Secretary Hegseth displays a limited understanding of the role the military should play in deterring conflict in the first place, which requires more sophisticated thinking, and a wider range of coursework, than executing traditional battlefield maneuvers or even overseeing a theater-level military campaign.
Indeed, sustained deterrence represents the apex of military effectiveness. It requires understanding adversaries, anticipating their calculations, managing escalation, communicating resolve, and integrating military capabilities with diplomatic, economic, and informational instruments of national power. Preparing military leaders to advise civilian defense officials and contribute meaningfully to whole-of-government decision-making on the most consequential matters of state requires a much broader intellectual foundation than training them to carry out operational orders.
Consider Taiwan, a potential flashpoint for a confrontation between the United States and China. Deterring Beijing from imposing a blockade of the island, or even launching a full-scale invasion, is not simply a matter of developing the operational capabilities that would be required to respond in such a contingency. Effective deterrence requires understanding Beijing’s perceptions of American resolve, the political calculations of Chinese leadership, Taiwan’s domestic politics, the economic consequences of a conflict, and the credibility of American commitments to regional allies. U.S. military leaders who cannot think strategically across these dimensions, no matter how proficient they may be at operational planning and execution, will struggle to provide effective options to civilian defense leaders on averting what would almost certainly be a catastrophic military conflict.
These criticisms aside, there are several worthwhile ideas embedded in Secretary Hegseth’s direction, although many of its supposed innovations are already standard operation procedure at command and staff and senior service colleges. For example, emphasizing “jointness” among the services in PME is hardly a new idea. When I served on the teaching faculty at the National War College from 2019 to 2021, I did so as the Office of the Secretary of Defense Chair alongside several talented Warfighter Chairs seconded from the respective military services. And far from being “stagnant,” as Secretary Hegseth alleges, the PME environment surprised me with its agility. It continuously adapted its curricula, incorporating key lessons from recent case studies and experimenting with new approaches to preparing officers for an increasingly complex security environment—all while pivoting to a virtual learning en

He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid. READ MORE: Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by U.S. could benefit Putin Ukraine's interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 kph (100 mph) along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said. "We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted," he wrote on social media. "The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President's Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX. It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine." Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control. Outages after Russian strike on power facility Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine's Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram. The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire. The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said. Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a 2-year-old boy, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Sunday. Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said. Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Rostov region Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russia's Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday. Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a "production facility" in the village of Troitskoye, he said. Ukrainian forces also targeted Russia's Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the region's third-largest city, said a "large-scale and prolonged attack" damaged its industrial zone. WATCH: Inside a Ukrainian city hit by Russian drones during the Starlink disruption Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said. Ukraine's General Staff said it had hit two sites in Nizhnekamsk: Nizhnekamskneftekhim, one of the largest petrochemical complexes in Europe, and a production site operated by petrochemical company Sibur. An oil refinery in the area was also hit, it said. Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the Russian-annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas. Drones damage Black Sea ships, Romania says Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said Sunday that three commercial vessels in the Black Sea were struck by drones overnight, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised fears of the war spilling over into NATO territory. Romania's Ministry of National Defense said a Greek-flagged oil tanker was struck by a drone, sparking a fire that was extinguished by the crew. At least 30 sailors on commercial ships were confirmed dead or reported missing. 361cf5da540e.text:
Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.
Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".
On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.
There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."
The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.
He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

DENVER â The race for the next Democratic presidential nomination has begun, with a festival of agreement.
There was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, telling the Whatâs Next conference that voters demanded action, not âshallow litmus tests or where we fall on some political spectrum.â
There was Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, explaining that voters did not want âmarginal changeâ and Democrats werenât in a battle of âprogressive versus moderate.â
And there was Pete Buttigieg, whoâd noticed the Democrats borrowing his formula. They wanted to pass cost-cutting, pro-family bills with their new majority, then convince voters that they would never go back to pre-Trump neoliberalism.
âIt sounds good. Itâs easy to say,â said Buttigieg. âEverybody thinks they already agree with this.â
The post-midterms conference, organized by Majority Democrats, was a payoff of a two-year investment by moderate donors. Two years before strategists and elected officials landed in Denver and grabbed their lanyards, the venture capitalist Seth London circulated a memo about how new candidate and media investments could steer the party away from ârace and group-based identity politics,â and toward âprosperity for more Americans.â
This yearâs Democratic landslide carried along every kind of candidate âthe ones plugged into the Majority Democrats network, and the ones who worried it was a big-money ploy to defeat the populist left. But the conference elevated the candidates who wanted to build a supermajority, battling big tech and environmental attorneys. Some donors were in; the donors who wanted them to move left were out.
âTell us which ideas youâll stop giving permission to, the ones that defy common sense or didnât work,â said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, the pedigreed Massachusetts Democrat who chairs the Majority Democrats PAC. âTell us which privileges youâll confront, even if your donors or allies object.â
Celebrating the center
The donors did know how to throw a party. Whatâs Next resembled the sort of well-funded, media-friendly conferences that many Democrats have envied on the right, like the multi-day âAmericaFestâ put on by Turning Point Action.
This was a party for the Democratic mainstream, the staffers most likely to work for center-left presidential candidates than for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY. For two days, blocks of Denverâs River North Art District were cordoned off for Democrats, the people who elected them, and the reporters asking if they were running for president. (Their answers were variations on ânot yet.â)
There was conflict, but it was largely limited to the argument over who should lead Democratsâ new congressional majorities. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who announced his challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer on Thursday, paused for 10 seconds of applause when he took the stage and explained why he was running.
âCandidates from different backgrounds and different parts of our party â they ran on a strikingly similar platform,â said Van Hollen. âThey didnât run on the tired Washington labels of progressive versus moderate. They ran on an economic populist message, on a commitment to fight for working people and take on a rigged economic and political system.â
Many of those winners showed up in Denver, like Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. They shared road stories of how they listened to Republican concerns, and would work with the willing ones to lower prices. But it was implied that Democrats should focus on building homes, lowering bills, and expanding health care before they did anything else. Not every attendee agreed.
âThe organizers here want a big tent, one big enough to even invite anti-establishment voices like me,â said Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Ca., who Democrats see as a competitor for a Sen. Bernie Sanders lane in the primary. âA big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.âApart from Khanna, the likely presidential candidates didnât quite do that. Mallory McMorrow, who Majority Democrats supported in her unsuccessful U.S. Senate bid in Michigan, told Semafor that her party had just shown that it could have a loud primary argument and then unite on the basics.
âItâs anti-corruption, getting money out of politics, protecting democracy, ending wars,â said McMorrow. âThe disagreements are around the edges.â
Davidâs view
There will be many Democratic âcattle calls,â but I am focusing on how Whatâs Next was built because itâs the fruit of a two-year effort to ensure that the 2028 primary plays out differently than the 2020 primary. There is widespread agreement among Democratic strategists that their last open primary was defined by left-wing organizations that wanted candidates to commit to their ideas, eyeball to eyeball, on camera.
That meant forums organized by groups like Planned Parenthood and MoveOn, and more progressive labor unions like SEIU. That meant the ACLU asking candidates if they would commit to cutting the federal prison population in half, and Movimiento Cosecha bird-dogging Joe Biden at his own events until he committed to stopping most deportations.If the left sees Majority Democrats as an effort to swipe their strongest messaging and junk the rest, theyâre right. The economic populism in Denver was more sincere than they might think, but it is against degrowth and for permitting reform; skeptical of single-payer health care, but for incremental steps to âuniversalâ health care; basically, right in the sweet spot of the Democratsâ congressional caucuses.
Right now the Schumer-Van Hollen contest is where the fights over ideology and priorities are happening. The 2028 candidates would prefer to agree, for now.
Room for Disagreement
The left was not letting the rest of the party adopt its ideas without a fight.

a2d31dc81769.text: By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-blasts-judges-2-week-halt-to-his-washington-golf-project-and-says-administration-will-appeal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump blasts judge's 2-week halt to his Washington golf project and says administration will appeal Politics Nov 15, 2026 12:39 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge after she ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue. In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. READ MORE: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on D.C. public golf course redevelopment "It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!" Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers. The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest." The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision. Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it." Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order." The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others. Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project. Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.
Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.
The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (Â£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.
Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (Â£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.
On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.
A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.
Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.
He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".
The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara.
Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories.
"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said.
"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."
On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.
The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.
Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

Australian politician Helen Haines, who lost both of her legs after police say she was deliberately run down with a car, has been discharged from hospital.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, in an alleged attack which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He is yet to enter pleas.
Haines, 65, has been discharged, the Alfred Hospital said on Monday, after four weeks and several surgeries which resulted in the amputation of her legs.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.

Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.
More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.
Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.
"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."
In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.
That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.
And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.
But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.
The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.
Restless tycoons
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".â¯ They had money, which back then meant power.
This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.
But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.
Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.
"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.
Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). â¯Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (Â£525bn).
But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.
Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy?
Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.
"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."
And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.
"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.
And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.
There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."
If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.

b27bf84dc67a.text: By — John Hanna, Associated Press John Hanna, Associated Press By — Marc Levy, Associated Press Marc Levy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/officials-say-a-tankers-steering-failed-before-it-crashed-into-a-cruise-ship-in-new-orleans Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Officials say a tanker's steering failed before it crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans Nation Nov 15, 2026 6:02 PM EST A tanker's steering system failed and kept its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans, U.S. government safety officials said Sunday. READ MORE: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River The preliminary finding from National Transportation Safety Board officials provided the first official word on what caused Friday's crash of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker into the American Heritage cruise ship, which sent passengers, crew and two police officers plunging into the Mississippi River. NTSB officials said during a briefing in New Orleans that it's not yet clear what caused the steering failure. "It could be many different things," NTSB accident investigator Bart Barnum said. "That is something that we're investigating very closely." The tanker, measuring about 520 feet (160 meters) long, had a crew of 19. The cruise ship, about 300 feet (91 meters) long, had 140 passengers and 50 crew onboard. Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital, including the two police officers who were thrown into the river when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical. As of Sunday, six people remained hospitalized, the city of New Orleans said in a statement. WATCH: Tanker crashes into river cruise boat in New Orleans The tanker's steering problem caused its rudder to remain in a starboard position, to the right, which sent the tanker veering toward the east bank of the river, where it hit the cruise ship two minutes after the rudder became stuck, Barnum said. As the tanker approached the river's east bank, the ship's data recorder captured audio sounds "consistent" with the ship's whistle going off, along with warnings and requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel's marine radio, Barnum said. He added the data included commands to deploy the vessel anchors and emergency ship handling orders. NTSB Member John DeLeeuw urged people with photos or video of the crash to submit them to his agency to help with its investigation, which is expected to result in a preliminary report within 30 days. He also praised the "the excellent response" from federal, state, local and private vessels that helped rescue people immediately after the crash. The cruise ship capsized in 22 minutes, DeLeeuw said. Just hours after the crash, the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed a federal lawsuit saying that the tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
