The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a steering failure, officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision.
It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.
The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".
The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.
Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.
"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.
The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.
A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.
Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.
Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.
The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships.
Canada said it would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine.
"Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement.
It said that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer."
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it said in a statement.
"The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments."
Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the ban.
It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in its events.
The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine and along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships.
Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo.
On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating.
It is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport.
This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March.
The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.
In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable".
However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria.
While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.
Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.

The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

Five EU countries are expected to announce the creation of a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, according to diplomatic sources, part of a broader push to boost deportations and curb irregular migration.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a "return hub" located in the landlocked east-central African country's capital Kigali.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of such hubs outside of the bloc.
It is understood the scheme would only apply to asylum seekers who had exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the EU, unlike a scrapped 2022 British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed.
Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually scrapped by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
In August, Rwanda confirmed it had begun "preliminary discussions" with several European states.
The Rwanda hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency.
The EU countries reportedly expressed hope that a centre would be running in 2027. The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they are redeploying troops to defend the country's interim capital, Aden, following weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Southern Armed Forces said it was withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.
Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the key shipping route which the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis. The Iran-backed fighters said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
It said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area" with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured territory overlooking it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital, Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The timing of Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World this week, which brings together global business and political leaders at the intersection of technology and geopolitics, could not feel more urgent. When we came up with the name of the California convening this spring, the phrase was meant to represent a broad sense that AI and geopolitics were on a collision course. Policymakers and CEOs were starting to come to terms with the pressing need to talk to one another. Then, here in the US, they spent a long bitter summer campaigning for and against each other.
Thirteen days ago, that collision course became a head-on collision. The US is preparing to inaugurate a new Congress deeply skeptical of the tech industry and its leaders, and âÂ perhaps more consequential âÂ new governors from Texas to Ohio who have pledged to stop data center construction.
Similar sentiments are rising in Europe,Â but much of the rest of the world is rushing to get in on the action, and eager to pick up data-center investments forced out of North America. And now Washington is facing questions about how it managed the interactions between its main geostrategic rival, China, and one of the worldâs most valuable companies, Nvidia, and what, if any, involvement it had in the undoing of the CEO atop an American chip champion.
There are, of course, far more than two sides to this story: Silicon Valley is divided on the fundamental questions of how fast to develop new technology, on open- versus closed-weight models, on the role of startups and hyperscalers, and on the correct place for regulation. Washington, too, is balancing the promise of AI against the impact it could have on citizens. And senior officials from Singapore to South Africa bring their own pressing agendas.
You can join us live here for conversations with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, and dozens of other CEOs and world leaders.
We donât have all the answers, but you can be sure weâll be asking the right questions.

South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.
Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.
Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.
South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.
Police say they responded to reports of a shooting â outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.
Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.
"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.
The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.
They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.
Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.
"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.
It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.
Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.
In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.
Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.
In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.
Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.
According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.
Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

eedd9d202c15.text: There's new evidence that double-digit health cost increases were hitting employers well before the forecasts of big spikes for 2027 — forcing big changes in workplace coverage for millions of Americans. Why it matters: The findings offer a higher-resolution view of how much health spending is putting a drag on the labor market and increasing affordability concerns for the approximately 160 million Americans who get coverage through work. They also show how factors like surprise billing disputes, more cancer diagnoses and expensive specialty drugs are combining to exert cost pressure, with no immediate relief in sight. Driving the news: A new Gallagher benefits survey of more than 3,700 firms found 36% of the companies reported premium increases of 10% or more during their most recent renewal. Pharmacy costs account for a quarter or more of some companies' total health spending. Cancer care is the No. 1 cost driver for about 7 in 10 firms. The survey, fielded from January to March, also found employers are trying to avoid saddling workers with a disproportionate share of rising costs while struggling to balance the quality of care with their financial risk. "The last two renewal cycles have been unlike anything we've ever seen before," said Robby White, Gallagher's U.S. benefits business line leader. "It's unsustainable, obviously. Every additional dollar that an employer spends on health care, they can't spend on their employees." Between the lines: The 2027 coverage year was already shaping up to be painful for many employers. Projections are showing premium spikes due to rising demand for health services, more chronic disease and increased use of drugs like GLP-1s. In fact, double-digit premium increases for both the 2026 and 2027 plan years suggest there are more underlying causes, according to benefits experts. One leading factor is chronic disease: More people are being diagnosed with cancer at a younger age, and advanced treatments and related care can result in $10,000 a month in expenses or claims. Drug costs also are surging — and not just because of demand for GLP-1s. The high cost of specialty drugs for chronic or rare conditions is prompting companies to scrutinize the way formularies are designed and how well pharmacy benefit managers administer their benefits. White said another big cost driver is the No Surprises Act, which shielded consumers from large, unexpected medical bills but also created an expensive arbitration process. The arbitration has added administrative costs and is giving providers big payouts, which add millions in costs for large employers that self-fund their health plans. That's an assessment shared by big health insurers, which say the surprise billing law is creating unintended financial consequences. "The [independent dispute resolution] process has now become a top-three single driver of health care cost increases for employers," Aetna president Steve Nelson told Axios, adding the company wants to work with Congress to overhaul the system. The big picture: In a volatile health market, more employers are self-insuring and directly paying medical claims to have greater visibility and control over health costs, the Gallagher survey finds. As workers get tired of high deductibles, some employers are testing copay-only plans, which vary out-of-pocket costs by medical service and steer workers to providers deemed to be providing the most value. Part of this involves more digital tools to help patients decide. They're also re-evaluating their relationships with pharmacy benefit managers in response to rising drug costs, leading to what White says is a "huge shift" away from the big three PBMs — CVS Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts. On GLP-1s, Gallagher says the question isn't whether the drugs are effective, but whether coverage is financially sustainable. More companies are exploring direct-to-consumer sales through outside vendors and giving employees debit cards or defined subsidies. What we're watching: Benefits experts are waiting to see how much congressionally mandated changes to PBMs' business practices bring down drug prices and improve transparency. They're also watching the growing number of worker lawsuits against plan sponsors, alleging they breached their fiduciary duty by failing to negotiate reasonable prescription drug prices or keep fees reasonable. Caitlin Owens contributed to this story .

Samir Serhan had an unenviable start at the helm of Acwa, one of the worldâs top clean energy developers: The day before saw the first fusillades of the war in Iran.
Acwa, which is part-owned by Saudi Arabiaâs Public Investment Fund, operates power and desalination plants across the Gulf, and Serhan quickly understood they could become targets. Sure enough, some of the companyâs assets were damaged in the war, although for security reasons it hasnât disclosed exactly what was hit. Acwaâs net income rose 0.6% in the first nine months of the year compared to the same period last year, but was held back as the war slowed its pipeline of new projects and raised its shipping costs in the region ten-fold.
But Serhan remains defiant: âYou take the cards youâre dealt and make the best out of it,â he said in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in TÃ¼rkiye. Acwa operates nearly 100 gigawatts of gas and renewable power projects in more than a dozen countries, as well as the worldâs largest privately held fleet of water desalination plants. At the summit, it was involved in one of the summitâs biggest clean power announcements, a commitment by eight financial institutions to back two gigawatts of solar plants Acwa will build in TÃ¼rkiye. That plan followed Serhanâs belief that the key to global electrification, COPâs main theme this year, is to go as big as possible, so the unavoidable headaches of project development lead to a worthwhile payoff for investors and consumers.
But Serhan is clear-eyed about the challenges ahead, including investors skeptical about its extensive reliance on Chinese supply chains. There might be some little bit of a slowdown in the US, but it will really happen.

We are committing around $4 billion and we really see the value there. And weâre not just a financial investor. When we typically build an asset, we also operate it, we invest in it, and we stay in for 20, 30 years. So these ups and downs happen sometimes, but the long-term signal definitely is very strong.
Why the focus on acquisitions instead of greenfield projects?
Time, and the risks of construction, and honestly because of all of this demand for data centers means there isnât enough labor force in the [US]. EPC contractors and supply chains are a problem. Thereâs just not enough to feed the frenzy. If we buy a platform of projects, we immediately get a footprint.
And we see the energy transition is not a sprint, itâs a marathon. So some of the major oil and gas companies are going back to investing in their traditional assets. They also want renewable power, but they can hire someone like Acwa to build and operate it, and supply it to them, instead of them becoming a power company. And with the hyperscalers, they have a nice balance sheet and theyâre in a big race to lead on AI technology. So there are some dislocations in the market and weâre trying to capitalize on this.

86bc2f4feb59.text: It was random, but related, that we were hit with a tectonic election result, an epic AI-and-spy scandal , and the dramatic FAA shutdown in just over one week. This is our new reality: constant shock and awe, igniting chain reactions across politics, media, AI, business and culture. Why it matters: This month's three shocks hit separately. But their speed and spread are our new reality. Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly. We call this post-processable velocity : Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb. People's fears about AI are now mushrooming into jitteriness about civilization's connective tissue. An AP story on Sunday asked: "Could everything be broken?" Images of empty European supermarket refrigerators , cleared of spoiled food after a spate of mysterious cyberattacks, added to the sense that our connections are crumbling, with the simplest conveniences in danger. What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. The Nvidia spy scandal is a vivid example: Media, last weekend: The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang was tied to a suspected Chinese spy. Social media erupts. Business, Monday: Nvidia stock falls more than 4% at the open and keeps sliding. Fears of economy-wide AI fallout follow. Politics, all week: Trump's top team gets dragged into a "what did they know and when" frenzy. Democrats demand hearings. Policy, now: Lawmakers are scrambling to untangle the web of spies, lies and AI, and are racing to tighten China's access to Nvidia chips that gave Huang the power he's now surrendered. Tech, going forward: AI companies are rethinking their reliance on Nvidia chips and exploring financing options beyond Nvidia. ⏱️ Huang's resignation was announced just 14 days after last month's New York Times blockbuster exclusive that he was believed to be the target of a Chinese plot, and four days after he admitted an affair . One revelation, two weeks, and the most important CEO in AI is gone. Three forces make this permanent: 🔄 1. Politics swings wildly. This was the seventh straight election in which the White House, Senate or House changed hands. And this time, in truly unthinkable and historic ways. There were a number of " split districts " in 2024 that went for Kamala Harris for president and a Republican for the House. This year, every single one swung to electing a Democrat. We can't find any precedent for this. It's possible we've hit a post-ideological age where people feel very little affiliation to party tribes. How do you explain young men shifting almost 40 points from Republicans to Democrats in two years? 🤖 2. AI concentrates everything. A handful of companies are making historic bets on superhuman intelligence, and propping up the economy while they do it. That puts enormous power and risk in very few hands. One man's affair shook the whole market. Nvidia makes the vital ingredient of AI, and helps finance nearly every big player buying it. But it's not just Nvidia. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Amazon can rattle the market with one announcement too. ⛓️‍💥 3. Everything is fragile when everything is interconnected. Friday's flight shutdown had nothing to do with AI, spies or elections, but it still shook us all. It appears a contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber. Routers overloaded. Departures stopped nationwide for more than four hours. A total of 18,000+ U.S. flights were canceled over the past three days. Officials said little for hours. Rumors, speculation and gallows humor filled the void. "The aliens have landed," the novelist Stephen King tweeted . "That's the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don't want to start a worldwide panic." The bottom line: The shocks will change. The speed won't. Go deeper : New signs of rising risk.

ac5edfad2065.text: DENVER — Democrats' euphoria over their once-in-a-generation wave of midterm victories is giving way to a reality check: They were lucky to have a weakened opposition. And they might be "renting" this year's voters if they don't quickly deliver on their promises. Why it matters: If Democrats want to rack up policy wins ASAP, they'll need to work with President Trump — the guy many of them held up as what's wrong with America. That means giving him a few wins. Zoom in: Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico argued exactly that at a Democratic summit late last week in Denver — What's Next , held by the centrist group Majority Democrats . "If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history." Gina Hinojosa, who'll be Texas' first Democratic governor in more than three decades, has said she'll work with Trump on immigration . Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a frequent Trump target, is pitching the president on rebranding Medicare for All as " TrumpCare " to get it passed. And on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told Dana Bash he wants to collaborate with Trump to deliver on the president's own past promise to lower grocery prices. Zoom out: Midterm elections are usually a referendum on the sitting president, not a sign that voters are in love with the opposition party. And polls show that Democrats are still unpopular. At the Denver confab, several Democrats acknowledged that. Adam Jentleson , president of the moderate Searchlight Institute, said onstage: "The voters who decided last week's election have not yet fallen in love with us. ... They are on loan to us." Many Democratic leaders believe Congress must prioritize legislation aimed at lowering prices and ending the war in Iran, given the salience of those two issues in this year's elections. Some top Democrats are determined not to repeat the mistakes the party made after the 2022 elections, when they overperformed — and grew complacent. They lost the presidential election two years later. The other side: Merely talking about working with Trump can disillusion parts of the Democratic base. Outside the Denver event, left-wing activists protested the get-together itself. Some accused Democratic leaders of already being too conciliatory toward the Republican president. "I can't believe that Talarico said he'd work with Trump," Anna Libey, a volunteer for the progressive Sunrise Movement, told Axios. "I can't believe that he would go back on his campaign messaging immediately." (During his campaign, Talarico consistently signaled his willingness to work across party lines, while also routinely criticizing the president's agenda.) Yes, but: Many Democrats don't really believe Trump will become a serious governing partner overnight, if ever. They just think they ought to be able to say they tried to work with him. If and when Trump vetoes the priority bills of a Democratic-led Congress — as he's already threatened to do — many in the party figure it'd boost their argument that he's still to blame for high prices and his unpopular war on Iran.

2fddce45a911.text: The downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang adds an explosive new risk to an already-strained AI boom, threatening to burst a financial bubble even if the technology ultimately succeeds. Why it matters: History shows that world-changing technology and devastating financial bubbles often go hand in hand. A market reckoning won't stop the AI revolution. But as with the dot-com crash, it could vaporize trillions in investor wealth as expectations come crashing back to earth. The big picture: "No sane person questions whether AI works. And that 'working' status is precisely what makes a bubble possible," veteran technology investor Paul Kedrosky told Axios. The risks have grown as technology companies commit trillions to infrastructure, increasingly relying on debt, investments in one another and complicated financing arrangements to keep the expansion going. Driving the news: Huang's stunning resignation Thursday has shaken confidence in the company at the center of the AI boom — and raised fresh questions about the sustainability of the broader investment frenzy. Nvidia, which named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, faces a leadership vacuum at a time when the industry is already grappling with financial and political uncertainty. Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has helped finance the massive expansion of computing infrastructure by investing in its customers and providing financial backstops for major projects. A more cautious approach by Huang's successor could undermine confidence in projects that have depended on Nvidia's financial support. What they're saying: RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas told Axios that Huang's departure could trigger a "wholesale bursting" of the AI bubble. "The turmoil around Jensen Huang matters for the buildout if it makes lenders less confident that Nvidia will back the next round of projects," Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh told Axios. Zoom out: The financial and political vulnerabilities were piling up well before the Nvidia scandal. Spending is outpacing expected returns. AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over the same period, according to Axios reporting . Valuation expectations are being reset. Anthropic's newly announced IPO terms imply a valuation well below earlier hopes of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI also reportedly secured less cash and a lower valuation than it had hoped in a recent funding round. Investors are growing more cautious. Retail traders, who have routinely bought previous AI-related market dips, instead became net sellers of U.S. stocks during the sharp Nov. 5 selloff, according to Vanda Research. Financing is getting harder. The debt-fueled expansion was already showing signs of strain before the latest turmoil. Rising borrowing costs and an avalanche of new bond offerings have made lenders wary. Political opposition is growing. A wave of election victories for AI-skeptical candidates, along with widespread voter support for data center restrictions, threatens to delay construction, increase costs and undermine the assumptions behind some projects. Regulatory risks are mounting. Huang's downfall has intensified bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, which increasingly appear likely to pass. The risk: A retreat in AI investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a market correction into a much broader financial reckoning. Falling valuations and tighter credit could make it harder for startups and cloud providers to finance additional data centers, reducing demand for chips, power and other infrastructure. That could put further pressure on the investors, lenders and companies financing the expansion, spreading the consequences well beyond the companies developing AI models. Yes, but: There is considerable evidence that AI itself is a real and potentially transformative technology — and that demand is growing rapidly. Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up from $71 billion a month earlier. OpenAI grew quarterly revenue roughly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to The Wall Street Journal, even as its adjusted operating losses reached $10.9 billion. Businesses are already using AI to write software, automate tasks and perform work that previously required significant human effort. Tighter U.S. export controls could also benefit American AI developers by limiting Chinese rivals' access to advanced computing power, even as they complicate Nvidia's business prospects. The historical lesson: Some of the greatest technological transformations have been accompanied by speculative investment booms that ended painfully for investors. "I have no doubt that AI will be transformative. That does not preclude a financial bubble," MIT economics professor Ricardo Caballero told Axios. Caballero argues that excessive optimism may even be necessary to marshal the enormous investments required for a new technology to reach its potential. Such booms can leave behind valuable infrastructure and lasting economic gains, as they did in the dot-com boom-bust cycle, even if many investors suffer losses along the way. The bottom line: "AI can deliver enormous value to users while the companies building the infrastructure earn far less than their investors expected," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.
A yellow weather warning for snow comes into effect in the very early hours of Tuesday following a blast of Arctic air pushing across the UK causing temperatures to plummet.
Cold health alerts for parts of northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.
Coldest night of season so far recorded
Monday morning started on a chilly note for all parts. The coldest conditions were seen across the northern half of the UK with northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland waking up to a sharp frost with some wintry flurries over the hills.
Tulloch Bridge in Scotland recorded an overnight low of -7.7C making it the coldest night of the season so far.
Temperatures in the south generally remained a few degrees above freezing.
Cold health alerts, issued by the UKHSA, are currently in force across north-west England, north-east England, Yorkshire and the Humber until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
These alerts are only issued in England and are aimed at health and social care professionals.
A Met Office weather warning for ice from Sunday evening into Monday morning across northern and eastern Scotland as well as parts of Cumbria, Northumberland and Durham has now expired.
Though Monday will be dry and bright for many places, wintry showers will affect some eastern parts of England and Scotland, with these falling as sleet or snow over high ground.
Afternoon maximum temperatures will be a chilly 4-8C in most places - a few degrees below the seasonal average.
Later in the day, the next front will approach from the south-west bringing milder air and some heavy and persistent rain.
As this band of rain then moves northwards overnight into Tuesday, a further spell of hill snow may develop.
Met Office warnings for snow on Tuesday
A yellow weather warning for snow is set to come into effect on Tuesday from midnight until 11:00 GMT, covering parts of the Midlands, north-east and north-west England, North Yorkshire and south-west Scotland.
Where snow does accumulate, depths of 1-5cm are likely, although some locations above 300-400m could see 5-15cm.
Some roads and railways are likely to be affected, resulting in longer travel times by road, bus and train services. Power cuts are also possible.
Further south, Tuesday will be a very different day with blustery conditions and some heavy showers.
This battleground of colder, drier conditions in the north and milder, wetter weather in the south will continue into the middle of the week.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

a726d6370471.text: Prominent conservative thinkers and MAGA figures are seizing on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy to pull President Trump away from his alliance with the tech right. Why it matters: The Nvidia scandal highlights some of the political weaknesses for Trump in allowing himself to be defined by his connections to an increasingly unpopular group of companies. Right-wing players are hoping the bombshell revelations about Huang's affairs will chip away at the president's embrace of the tech industry and offer an opening for anti-tech voices in his administration. What they're saying : They view the midterm elections as proof that people across the political spectrum hate AI, data centers and view Silicon Valley as too powerful. President Trump's perception of China "has always been entirely commercial and transactional. His view was, 'we're getting screwed. I'm going to get a better deal,'" Oren Cass, founder of conservative think tank American Compass, said. Cass, who has warned about Nvidia risks for more than a year, said the allegations of espionage are the strongest evidence yet that China is not a commercial partner but an adversary that is going to "subvert the American political process in ways that end up humiliating the President." MAGA figure Steve Bannon, meanwhile, said in a text he has called Jensen Huang "a CCP 'Agent of Influence' a thousand times." and that it's an OPEN SECRET." "We need to actually cut OFF ALL THE CHIPS NOW," Bannon added as Congress warms up to legislation aimed at that. Reality check: Amid daily revelations about Huang's affairs and the negative consequences for the AI boom and U.S. economy, Trump has created some distance. He backtracked on a suggestion that Jensen could go on a trip to China later this month. Other than that, he has kept it friendly. The president earlier this week called him "honorable" and on Thursday, following Jensen's resignation, the president said he "has done a fantastic job" and called him a "Legend." On Thursday, he said in an interview with Stephen Smith that Jensen is "a tremendous talent" who's done "incredible" and "brilliant" work at Nvidia. What we're watching: Supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying the White House to support his reinstatement as CEO, according to the Financial Times. What's next: Conservatives are hoping the scandal changes who gets a seat at the table for the remainder of Trump's presidency as 2028 and mounting AI unpopularity approaches.

These Governors-Elect Campaigned on Expanding Medicaid. It Won’t Be Easy.
Early in her election-night victory speech, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, Georgia’s next governor, alluded to one of her main campaign promises: granting more low-income adults access to government health insurance.
“This win is for the caregiver who can’t afford healthcare and needs Georgia to finally expand Medicaid,” she told a crowd of cheering supporters.
The national Democratic landslide that will give the party control of Congress will also sweep Bottoms and other Democratic gubernatorial candidates into office in a handful of states that have for years resisted fully expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
Like Bottoms, governors-elect Cindy Holscher in Kansas, Gina Hinojosa in Texas, and David Crowley in Wisconsin campaigned on finally broadening access to the joint federal-state insurance program for those with low incomes or disabilities. More than a million people collectively in Georgia, Kansas, Texas, and Wisconsin could be covered by full Medicaid expansion, according to 2024 data from KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
But expanding their Medicaid programs is no small task.
These Democrats would have to surmount political and legislative hurdles at a time when the realities of Medicaid expansion have changed. Last year’s GOP budget law eliminated a financial bonus for states to expand, imposed a work mandate, and implemented funding restrictions that are tougher on full expansion states.
“It’s so messy,” said Caylee Noggle, a former Georgia Medicaid director who is now president of the Georgia Hospital Association. “We’re in this real moment where there are benefits and trade-offs to traditional expansion.”
Federal Changes
The Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, required states to expand Medicaid to millions more low-income adults. But a 2012 Supreme Court decision made that choice optional.
Forty states plus Washington, D.C., have expanded Medicaid, most recently North Carolina in 2023. Ten states, including Georgia and Wisconsin, have declined to fully expand eligibility for the program. But those two states have offered coverage to some who would be covered under full expansion.
The calculus for expanding changed last year. Along with eliminating the expansion bonus, President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act imposed restrictions on how much federal money states can draw down to help prop up doctors and hospitals that treat large numbers of Medicaid patients. And the limits are lower for expansion states than non-expansion states.
Those funding restrictions will likely be a focal point for lawmakers in Wisconsin. Fully expanding Medicaid could threaten hundreds of millions of federal dollars flowing into the state, according to estimates from the Wisconsin Hospital Association.
Bobby Peterson, a Madison-based attorney who helps clients navigate benefit programs, said any plan to cover more people with full Medicaid expansion in Wisconsin would likely hit headwinds, even with Democrats controlling the governor’s office and both branches of the state legislature starting in January.
“These are going to be hard conversations,” he said.
Crowley, the state’s incoming Democratic governor, embraced full Medicaid expansion early in his campaign. Later, he called for opening the state’s partial Medicaid expansion to anyone who wants to buy a plan. Since his win, he’s moved further away from full expansion.
The Crowley campaign did not answer specific questions from KFF Health News about which policy he would pursue, and spokesperson Jonathan Fera said the governor-elect would share more about his agenda after his inauguration.
When states expand eligibility, they get a larger federal funding match per enrollee in the expansion pool than for other people in their Medicaid programs. And having fewer uninsured patients can reduce the financial strain on hospitals and other players in the health system, which can win support for expansion from the hospital industry and rural politicians worried about facility closures in their communities.
Still, states must find the money to pay their share for this bigger group of enrollees while wrestling with the new funding restrictions.
“It’s a lot of complicated math,” said Lawson Mansell, senior health policy analyst at the Niskanen Center, a think tank focused on free-market policies.
Expansion also comes with new rules from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act requiring enrollees to prove they’re working or completing at least 80 hours of other qualifying activities a month. Democrats would need to grapple with the politics of rolling out rules pushed by Republicans — and the potential of their congressional counterparts to change course again.
The political landscape in Washington, D.C., has shifted with the blue wave entering Congress. Democrats have already pledged to roll back the Medicaid cuts in the GOP budget law but haven’t said how. And it’s unclear whether Trump would be on board.
“When states operate in an environment where they’re uncertain about federal policy, that makes it harder for states to legislate,” said Brian Blase, president of the right-leaning Paragon Health Institute.
States would also need to figure out how to enact those work requirements if they hold. In Georgia, administrative hurdles for similar work rules made it difficult for people to enroll in the state’s limited expansion program, which is set to expire at the end of the year. And many states that have already expanded Medicaid are struggling to implement the rules.
On Nov. 13, the White House allowed states to delay the new work rules, originally set to take effect Jan. 1, by six months after pushback.
“Even if a state adopts the expansion, unfortunately, this could result in people still remaining uninsured just because of all these changes that essentially add more red tape,” said Edwin Park, a research professor

LĪHUʻE, Hawaiʻi — Dylan Lawton realized something was wrong when he struggled to use his right leg to hit the brakes while driving.
Within a matter of hours, scans showed the third-year medical student had a brain tumor. But the island of Kauaʻi, where he was completing his clinical rotation, has no neurosurgeons. So Lawton was medically evacuated on a plane to Straub Benioff Medical Center on O‘ahu, Hawaiʻi’s most populous island. There, the then-27-year-old was diagnosed with a type of lung cancer commonly found in nonsmokers, which was stage 4 and had spread to his brain.
Lawton said he wasn’t surprised by the extent of the healthcare shortages on Kauaʻi. Although he’s from Oʻahu, he grew up aware that his uncle on Kauaʻi needed to travel off-island to receive cancer treatment. It was one reason Lawton chose to participate in the University of Hawaiʻi medical school program that trains students on rural Kauaʻi, his grandparents’ home island. The cost of medical school is covered if the students practice medicine for four years on Kauaʻi after completing their residency. But now he needs ongoing, specialized treatment in a place with limited resources and only one full-time oncologist, who practices outside the hospital system where Lawton receives his treatment.
“I am experiencing the very thing that I was brought to fix,” Lawton said. “It crosses my mind all the time.”
Similar recruitment and retention programs to attract healthcare professionals to work in rural areas received a significant boost from the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, created by President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. At least 38 states, including Hawaiʻi, plan to use some of those dollars to incentivize more healthcare providers to practice in their rural areas.
Under the law, providers who get such incentives must practice in rural spots for at least five years, longer than in Lawton’s program. States hope the effort will address rural healthcare workforce shortages.
But juggling partners’ jobs, family obligations, and even medical issues — as Lawton’s extreme case shows — can shift medical providers’ willingness or ability to stay. And critics are calling the five-year federal requirement unrealistic, adding to the question of whether such incentives can even solve the problem.
Some students may not fully grasp the implications of the commitment. If they don’t complete the five years, they may have to pay back the funds, which states can prorate to reflect any years of service completed. States must provide “documentation substantiating a provider’s death or disability” to request permission from federal officials to forgive the debt, according to the federal rules.
A Five-Year Commitment
The Bipartisan Policy Center released a report that questioned the likely effectiveness of the rural fund’s five-year service requirement. Maya Sandalow, who worked on the report as director of the organization’s health program, said she heard from many healthcare providers that the five-year service requirement was too rigid, especially for lower-paid medical professionals, such as behavioral health support specialists or community health workers.
“The requirement might be a pretty big one compared to the level of award that that individual is receiving, no matter what the degree is,” she said.
For example, Michigan is offering scholarships to students training to be emergency medical service professionals. But even though less training is required to become an EMT, those students will be held to the same five-year service commitment as physicians.
Few programs have required such a long commitment. One of the longest is for the National Health Service Corps, which requires a service commitment of two to four years.
Although about 80% of Health Service Corps participants continue to work in a health professional shortage area one year after completing their service obligation, according to a federal report, fewer than half stay in the same county. The retention rate of clinicians who continue to work in health professional shortage areas continues to drop in years two and three after they complete service obligations.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which oversees the Rural Health Transformation Program, declined to comment on the record about the five-year service requirement.
Donald Pathman, a professor at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine who studies workforce incentive programs for physicians, pointed to two provisions in the Rural Health Transformation Program service requirements that allow for flexibility. One allows participants to move around the state throughout their service as long as they continue to practice in rural areas. The other largely leaves it to states to create the incentive programs in whatever way suits their needs, outside of the five-year service commitment.
“There’s not any heavy hand in federal requirements with this,” Pathman said, adding that the flexibility may come with some risk. “We’re hoping 50 states get this right.”
Retention Efforts
Federal officials list workforce development as a main goal of the Rural Health Transformation Program. Over 100 million people nationwide live in areas with a health professional shortage, according to the federal Health Resources and Services Administration. And rural areas represent 62% of the places with a shortage of primary care professionals.
States are trying various tactics beyond direct incentives to fill those gaps with money from the program. For example, Wisconsin, Idaho, and Kansas are developing programs that target children as young as middle school to create clearer pathways into health-related careers. And Rhode Island is using some of its funding to renovate housing for healthcare workers.

Trial by Fire: Second in a series about the impacts of wildfire litigation.
A week before Christmas 2025, 100-mile-per-hour wind gusts punished the foothills of Boulder, Colorado. An unusually dry summer and fall had parched trees and tall grasses. Snowfall across the county was roughly half the long-term average, and record-warm temperatures left none on the ground in the city below the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains. When the National Weather Service warned of exceptionally high wildfire danger, Xcel Energy cut power to more than 50,000 customers.
The utility’s caution came from experience. Under similar conditions almost exactly four years earlier, the Marshall Fire had burned more than 1,000 homes to the ground within hours, totaling over $2 billion in property losses. Investigators with the Boulder County Sheriff’s Office later concluded that an unmoored Xcel Energy power line was partially to blame for the blaze. Homeowners, businesses and insurers sued Xcel, which denied any fault, wrongdoing or negligence, but nevertheless settled for $640 million one day before a major civil trial was set to begin in September 2025.
In the aftermath of the fire, Xcel Energy implemented “Public Safety Power Shutoffs” on days when weather conditions are especially conducive to wildfires. Utilities in California have been doing the same since 2019, after their power lines ignited a series of catastrophic wildfires that brought billions of dollars in legal claims against the companies.
Xcel calls such proactive shutoffs a risk reduction measure. But the strategy—which has been used in Boulder County four times since 2024—left some residents furious. Many business owners lost revenue as the shutoff fell during the busiest shopping season of the year. City council members voted to send a letter to Xcel noting that “many residents feel the increasing instances of power outages when we have high winds … as being a consequence of prioritizing litigation avoidance ahead of protecting our community.”
“We understand that losing power for any amount of time is impactful and frustrating, but the safety of our customers, crews and the communities we serve remains a top priority,” an Xcel Energy spokesperson said.
Such criticism highlights the difficult situation utilities now find themselves in. Either cut power and enrage customers, or keep electricity flowing and risk igniting a devastating wildfire that could leave them exposed to multibillion-dollar lawsuits.
U.S. utility companies have faced more than $18 billion in wildfire liabilities over the past decade. As governments and communities struggle to respond to the staggering losses caused by the wildfire crisis burning the West, lawsuits against the utilities that ignite the blazes have emerged as the de facto recovery strategy. But the steep increase in wildfires’ destructiveness is the result of a combination of factors: a climate warmed by the burning of fossil fuels; decades of fire suppression and forestry policies that have increased the amount of flammable fuel in forests; and rapid development into fire-prone landscapes.
With another historic fire season gripping the West, and lawsuits already filed against electricity providers, states—from Oregon to Montana—are facing a reckoning over how much utilities can be expected to bear the costs of ever-worsening wildfires. Even California, the ground zero of sky-high wildfire litigation against utilities, appears to be coming to terms with the idea of offering some protections to utilities. Such reforms have become a key aspect of Governor Gavin Newsom’s political mission as he nears the end of his term in office, working to get a deal with legislators.
Attorneys behind cases against utilities argue high-dollar lawsuits force companies to operate more safely and deliver much-needed payouts to victims. But with those costs often passed onto customers through higher electricity rates, state governments are now considering how best to intervene. Policy experts observe that placing full blame on the entity responsible for sparking a wildfire may create a disincentive for homeowners and communities to carry out wildfire mitigation measures that could reduce destruction. And the approach raises questions of fairness in the judicial system—even for multibillion-dollar corporations.
Fanning the Flames
Relying on lawsuits to cope with worsening wildfires has worked, in part, because ignition is everything in the U.S. legal context.
But the spark that ignites a wildfire has little to do with how much damage it ultimately does.
The actual number of U.S. wildfire ignitions has not dramatically increased over the past half-century. Around 50,000 to 70,000 wildfires burn across the country every year. The difference is that many more of these fires are growing into huge conflagrations—U.S. annual burned area is up roughly 60 percent since 1990.
Many of today’s catastrophic fires have been made more intense and more likely by climate change. Warmer temperatures, reduced humidity and greater aridity have bred increasingly favorable conditions for wildfires across the American West. In California alone, the average summer burned area is now five times larger than it was in the latter half of the 20th century. And nine of the largest wildfires in state history occurred in the last 10 years.
“We’ve been burning fossil fuels as a global society, and that’s really what’s driving it,” said Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “Greenhouse gas molecules are not zapping the ground, starting fires on their own. But what they are doing is loading the dice for a fire to grow large quickly.”

More Americans now say Washington, DC, is safe than have said so in 36 years, a statistic that the White House will likely view as a testament to President Donald Trumpâs federal crime crackdown in the nationâs capital.
Sixty-four percent of US adults currently view DC as a safe place, according to Gallup, a 12-point increase since 2023. Thatâs been driven by Republicans: In 2023, 77% of Democrats and only 29% of Republicans said DC was safe; today 70% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans say so.
The poll was taken before a recent shooting in DCâs Logan Circle made national headlines.
Crime has generally been on the decline in DC, though at least one study found that Trumpâs National Guard deployment had minimal effect on violent crime. Another city seeing its highest perceived safety rating since 1990: New York City.

The tech association Chamber of Progress is expanding an initiative launched last year to improve the relationship between the tech industry and Democrats, adding a former adviser to former President Joe Biden and former aide to Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., as senior advisers.
Steve Benjamin, Bidenâs former director of the White House Office of Public Engagement, is joining the Blue Horizon Project, along with former Fetterman chief of staff Krysta Juris, according to an announcement shared first with Semafor.
The group is trying to steer the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress away from heavily regulating and investigating the tech industry; a poll it commissioned from Morning Consult found 84% of voters want Democrats to focus on fighting inflation rather than regulating AI and technology.
âTech and Democrats had a long honeymoon in the Obama era. There was a divorce in the Biden era, and now Democrats have to craft a relationship thatâs somewhere in between,â Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, told Semafor.
The group is among a handful trying to influence Democrats as they take power and weigh policy positions ahead of 2028. Who Decides, an outfit founded by unsuccessful New York congressional candidate Alex Bores that is calling for more stringent AI regulation, is already organizing across battleground states.

Democrats are debating who will have a piece of investigating and overseeing AI and chip export controls next Congress in the wake of the controversy enveloping Nvidia.
Incoming House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., is floating creating a subpanel on chips and AI, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said Meeks and incoming Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., are taking the lead on the Nvidia fallout.
But other committees have jurisdiction and also want to lead on AI â including the House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, or Science, Space and Technology Committees.
âIt seems like every chairman â¦ or chairwoman is wanting a piece of the pie with AI now,â grumbled one congressional aide, who questioned how that would work logistically, âconsidering itâs going to be spread out over â how many different committees?â
One solution to settle the jurisdictional issues would be to set up a select panel overseeing AI, though a key committee chair has already registered his opposition to that idea. Itâs also possible that multiple committees will pursue their own investigative efforts within their jurisdictions anyway, regardless of the turf wars that creates.

Senate Democratsâ leadership fight between Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is taking place against the backdrop of a major policy decision: how hard to push to include a spending prohibition on the Iran war in a broader funding bill.
Schumer lists the âpower of the purseâ as an option for curbing the conflict, while Van Hollen is a leading proponent of a funding restriction. This could all lead to a shutdown on Dec. 11, the current funding deadline.
Itâs important to remember that the anti-Schumer sentiment among progressive activists increased when he supported advancing a spending bill early on in Donald Trumpâs second term, after House Democrats came out in blanket opposition.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said that he wants to figure out what the âstrategy is to get us out of the war, and it is understanding the differences between what takes place now and what takes place when we are back in charge.â

The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy have issued a joint statement urging Israel to "allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza", where they say the situation on the ground is "dire".
The foreign ministers warn recent floods have brought "further suffering" to the war-torn territory, which recently had its first winter storm.
The statement says 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border.
The Israeli military authority which controls the Gaza crossings has said it is co-ordinating with the US-led Board of Peace and the UN on a winter plan, and that 93,000 tents and 8,600 aid trucks with winter supplies had entered the territory.
It added that reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".
The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the widespread flooding and a landslide led to a number of deaths, thousands of damaged shelters and the suspension of critical services.
The statement from the British, Australian, Canadian and Italian foreign ministers says, external: "This situation is entirely reversible - and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in."
"The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late."
The European Union issued a similar statement on Saturday, external, reiterating its "grave concern" over what it called the "persistent and devastating humanitarian crisis".
The EU also urged Israel to comply with international law.
The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 74,690 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israeli air strikes and other attacks have continued to take place almost every day despite the ceasefire agreed in October last year.

A basketball player from the US has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".
In statement on Sunday, the agency said he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.
The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.
A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.
The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.
Greene played with the Reinhardt University's basketball team in the US in the 2017-2018 season, before he went to play at the South Georgia Technical College.
He was the leading scorer with Georgia Bombers semi-professional basketball team during the 2023-24 season before he moved to Thailand.
Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.
Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.
In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.
In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (Â£21m), which was destined for the UK.

A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.
The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.
The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.
Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.
Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.
Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.
But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.
Beavers have been reintroduced already in Norfolk at enclosures at Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve near Fakenham, Wild Ken Hill near King's Lynn and on the River Glaven near Holt.
A pair of beavers have also been spotted in the wild at Pensthorpe Natural Park, which is a short distance downstream from Sculthorpe Moor.
In Suffolk, a colony was introduced at Little Haugh Hall at Norton, near Bury St Edmunds.
River Waveney Trust is holding a series of events to discuss the proposals and it hopes to engage with local landowners in Bungay, Palgrave and Eye.
Lamb added: "Our aim is to ensure that local communities, landowners, anglers and conservation groups have the opportunity to be part of the discussion from the beginning."
While talks are beginning, Lamb said it would be years before any decision would be made, which would require a licence from Natural England.
More information about the events can be found on its website., external
