Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.
Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.
It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.
The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.
"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.
"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."
Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".
She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.
"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."
Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".
She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".
Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing â known as a tie-back in industry terms â before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add Â£2.9bn to the economy.
The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank
The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.
Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.
This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.
He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".
A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.
The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.
The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.

Indians see AI as less of a threat than people in the US because fewer workers hold the âcognitive and office-oriented jobsâ that the technology could replace, one of the countryâs top tech officials said.
Young Indians are drawn to technology and see AI as a way to raise productivity, reduce poverty, and help India become a developed country within two decades, S Krishnan, secretary of Indiaâs Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
The gains, he predicts, could touch sectors such as agriculture, education, healthcare, and government. Krishnan told Semafor Deputy Editor-in-Chief Shelly Banjo that AI tools could help advise farmers with the expertise thatâs only available to the largest companies, or screen chest X-rays for tuberculosis to enhance the productivity of the stressed healthcare sector.
With around 6 million people in IT and related services, Krishnan said India has the workforce that can diffuse the technology throughout the economy. But the constraint, shared in many countries, is that âAI compute is still in short supply and expensive.â
Krishnan said India and the US were âpretty closeâ to a trade deal, with one or two issues left to resolve. âWeâd prefer to have it by yesterday, but, yes, as quickly as we can,â he said.
Asked about a potential bilateral visit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump, which hasnât happened in Trumpâs second term, he said: âWell, I think they still share a very good relationship.â

Jersey primary school children have enjoyed learning about space in a lesson delivered by an astronomer.
Dr Robin Catchpole of the Cambridge Institute of Astronomy was invited to the island by the Jersey Astronomy Club and shared his extensive knowledge with pupils aged 10 and 11 at First Tower School.
Year 6 pupil Lola, 11, said her favourite part was learning about how the planets were created while Vihaan, 10, said he was fascinated by black holes and how they were formed.
Catchpole, who has written and co-written more than 100 research papers and articles on astronomy, said his trick for making space accessible to children was to show them planets they would be familiar with.
Catchpole said he first became interested in astronomy when his grandfather gave him a book about the subject and his mother showed him the Moon through a telescope on the beachfront in Torquay, Devon.
"I saw craters and shadows of mountains and I thought that was very exciting," he said.
Year 6 teacher Lee Bradshaw said it was a great opportunity to have an expert like Catchpole answering questions and children proved inquisitive about the subject.

The scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sparked a wave of sadness in his native Taiwan, the islandâs deputy digital minister said Sunday.
Huang had a close relationship with Taiwanese tech companies, meeting with them every year, Isabel Hou said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & the World.
âThe relationship is very personal,â she told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. âThe supply chain leaders, I think, were concerned about how this kind of trust can be replaced. It will be tough.â
Those ties went beyond business: Hou referenced a New York Times article in which Huangâs longtime hairstylist admitted he was too upset to sleep, drank a bottle of red wine, and prayed for the former chip CEO after his resignation.
âWe feel sad,â she added.
The Nvidia ordeal has fueled calls in Washington for tighter chip export controls, given Huangâs years of lobbying to sell chips to China, and the revelation that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect spying for Beijing. US authorities are probing whether Megaspeed, the company the woman formerly led, smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Singapore-based Megaspeed has denied the allegations.
US lawmakers from both parties have pushed for tougher export restrictions, and Democrats have opened an inquiry into the Trump administrationâs approval of Nvidiaâs H200 chip sales to China.
Taipei has been aligning its export control policy with the US. Hou said Taiwanese donât want frontier chips going to China, where they could end up in military equipment aimed at the island. Reading a line prepared by her staff, she called for a policy thatâs âprecise, predictable, and coordinated with partners.â
China, once the destination for the vast majority of Taiwanâs outbound investment, now draws less than 1%, Hou said, as companies expand elsewhere, many in the US. In AI especially, Taiwan needs âtrusted partners.â

The US government has a responsibility to explain AIâs benefits to the public after the midterm elections showed widespread antagonism to the technology, a top State Department official said Sunday.
Jacob Helberg, the undersecretary for economic affairs, said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & the World that the election, in which many voters were opposed to AI and data centers, should be seen as an âopportunity.â
âThe onus really is on everyone serving in government at all levels, local, state, and federal, to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology,â Helberg told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith.
Helberg pointed to data showing that AI has helped prop up the US economy through investment and productivity gains. He said AI hasnât caused mass job losses, and âwe havenât seen any evidence at all that super intelligence has had an inflationary effect,â using the Trump administrationâs preferred alternative term for AI.
Competitor obsession
Helberg, who has spearheaded the Pax Silica effort with US allies to secure global supply chains for critical industries, also said US global tech policy shouldnât âobsessâ over China.
âGreat companies donât try to succeed by obsessing over their competitors,â he said. âOne of the temptations in policy roles is you spend so much time studying what competitors do that it almost becomes easy to over-obsess on them.â
While Pax Silica is building a bloc of US-allied nations to reduce their dependence on China, Helberg said the effort is intended to be âan America-centric initiative, not a China-centric initiative.â

The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.
Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.
Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.
Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.
Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.
Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."
A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.
Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021, allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.
Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.
The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.
Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.
Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.
At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.
Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.

The Scoop
Last week, while shouting out supporters at the Muslim Public Affairs Council gala in Washington, DC, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed singled out a figure in the crowd for special thanks: the founder of Zeteo, Mehdi Hasan, whose posts and videos pushed back against claims that progressives had underperformed more moderate candidates.
Three days later, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told the anti-Trump digital outlet MeidasTouch that the network had given him a key boost at a moment when few people believed Mississippi would be in play for a Democratic candidate.
âThank you for giving me the opportunity very early on, when nobody thought Mississippi would be on the radar, to tell my story, tell my message,â Colom said.
The first two years of President Donald Trumpâs return to power were a waking nightmare for the Democratic Party. But in Trumpâs shadow, oppositional media on the left has seen a period of extraordinary growth. Creators like Aaron Parnas, Keith Edwards, and Jack Cocchiarella gained millions of followers railing against Trump on YouTube. Independent media companies like The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and Zeteo gained millions of combined subscriptions on Substack, which grew from a platform largely favored by right-leaning or âheterodoxâ publishers to one dominated by left-leaning new media outlets and voices.
Scarred by Trumpâs 2024 podcast tours, Democratic donors are pouring money into the independent media space, and Democratic candidates have new media figures on speed dial. And now this ascendant new media ecosystem is positioning itself to help pick the next Democratic presidential nominee â or at least weed out a few of the duds. Progressive outlets are aiming to serve as a check on traditional media that they feel wants to knock out left-wing candidates, while moderate forces are starting up their own media to try and counter a zealous left flank that has shouted down moderates online.
âThatâs going to be the war more than anything: the attention fightâ¦ How can I, with the least amount of friction, get these people to start sharing clips?â Cocchiarella told Semafor.
The Left
While many legacy outlets that had experienced ratings and subscriptions growth during Trumpâs first term have seen little to no meaningful gains in his second go-around, independent media outlets critical of Trump, the mainstream media, and Democratic Party leadership saw huge gains.
Since the beginning of Trumpâs presidency, Zeteo has added almost 2 million YouTube subscribers. The Bernie Sanders-ite outlet More Perfect Union has added 3 million. Hasan Piker, the leftist Twitch streamer who became a midterm campaign fixation, has gained millions of followers on YouTube and increased viewership of his stream.
Now, both MPU and Zeteo are hoping to bring different issues â or candidates â to the front of the Democratic presidential primary debate.
Over the last two years, Zeteo has provided early coverage and political air cover for left-wing and socialist candidates, particularly those that have expressed aggressive criticism of Israel. In an interview on Thursday, Hasan pointed to the companyâs early interviews with then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and El-Sayed as examples; both were able to gain exposure to like-minded voters while other outlets were skeptical of their candidacies.
âFrom Zohran Mamdaniâs race, to AOCâs rise, to Abdul El-Sayedâs victory, I think itâs been very clear â Iâm not saying they wouldnât have happened without us; thatâs a little bit too arrogant and not accurate â but certainly they were aided and abetted and strengthened and bolstered by the fact that we exist,â he said.
Hasan said potential 2028 candidates clearly have taken notice.
Before the midterm elections, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a candid rare interview on Zeteo that he was considering running in 2028, an admission he hadnât made on-camera anywhere else. Hasan said although his political views are clear, multiple likely candidates who do not necessarily share Zeteoâs progressive, Israel-critical stance had nonetheless been in touch in recent days about appearing on the outletâs show.
âDemocratic presidential [hopefuls] and their teams have reached out to us, not the other way around, even people weâve criticized,â Hasan said, noting that heâs angling for an interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a pro-Israel Democrat.
Other outlets are more interested in highlighting specific issues, but could end up tipping the conversation in favor of certain candidates that they choose to spotlight.
More Perfect Union, the viral video channel founded by Sanders advisor Faiz Shakir, has not outright endorsed candidates in races, but its story selection and tone have bolstered candidates on the left. During the midterms, the organization published a video on then-Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner titled We Investigated The Most Controversial Candidate In America. It was less investigatory (the piece did not uncover the various scandals that later led to Platnerâs decision to drop out), and more complimentary; it gave space for Platner to explain his view on various media controversies, and showed working class Platner supporters who were unbothered by the unfolding scandals.
Over the last few months, More Perfect Union has interviewed Sanders and Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. In an email, More Perfect Union Editor-in-Chief Josh Miller-Lewis told Semafor that although the organization had not finalized its 2028 plans yet, it was hoping to host multiple events with candidates. The organization also hopes to grow its More Perfect University program, which hosted town halls where candidates faced college student questioners. But primarily, Miller-Lewis said, it plans to create content that would âput candidates in conversation with working class audiences and force substantive policy discussions that are often lacking in election coverage

"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.
Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.
Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.
It is part of a rapid $2bn (Â£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.
The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.
Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.
The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.
In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum â including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.
He survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [new flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster."
Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region.
"Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," says Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'"
The complex includes a new mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.
Among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.
His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.
He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles.
"This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord."
To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast new flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed.
"I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he says. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them."
Belkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.
Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.
Building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and AtlÃ©tico Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean."
Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration.
"Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he said. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need."
International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances.
The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.
Critics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency.
"There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.
Belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground."
He agreed to show the BBC the audits. But he has not provided them, despite repeated requests.

For Mirra Andreeva, the thought of her first WTA Finals singles campaign was so stressful that it gave her "a little breakdown" in a practice session before the tournament.
The 19-year-old may have been nervous on arrival at Indian Wells, but she leaves California as the champion, having been the standout player of the week.
The French Open winner produced a hard-fought 7-5 6-3 victory over Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final to become the youngest champion of the event in 22 years.
The Russian has now risen to second in the world rankings - and she will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina.
Andreeva did not drop a set on her way to the title and lost only 26 games across her five matches.
She raised her arms in celebration after beating Svitolina before racing to celebrate with her team, which includes 1994 Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez.
"I am super thankful to my team for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don't want to do anything," Andreeva said.
"Thanks for fighting with me, thanks for forcing me to do everything that I have to do and not asking any questions!"
As well as Â£2.55m in prize money, Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes - and joked she was happy to remain a "passenger princess" until she passed her test.
Andreeva thanks herself again after stellar season
One of the most notable parts of Andreeva's performance has been her increased maturity.
In March, she swore at the Indian Wells crowd after suffering an early defeat in the venue's WTA Tour tournament, and she has struggled to control her emotions, external on court in the past.
However, she showed little sign of that during this tournament.
Against Svitolina, one of the grittiest players on the women's tour, she lost a break lead three times across the two sets. Each time, she reset admirably, upping her aggression on her backhand in particular to put pressure back on her opponent.
After losing serve in a mammoth nine-minute game in the second set, Andreeva marched back to her chair and then broke Svitolina from 40-0 down in the next game to stay in front.
While her serve was not at its best, Andreeva still saved nine of the 12 break points she faced and hit 19 winners to Svitolina's 10.
"This fighting mindset helped me to get more brave and aggressive in the important moments," Andreeva told Sky Sports.
"This is just a dream. I had a little breakdown in my practice just before Indian Wells because I was so stressed.
"I didn't want to lose a match in the group. It's amazing."
Andreeva had only won one of her six matches against top-10 players in 2026 coming into the tournament.
She has beaten three top-10 players en route to the title, including a demolition of four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday.
She also laughed off an incident before the tournament where private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about Andreeva - including calling her a "diva" - were live-streamed.
Just as she did when she won the French Open, Andreeva ended her speech by thanking herself - a twist on a quote she "stole" from rapper Snoop Dogg.
"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work and for never quitting," she said.
"For not taking the days off, for working every day and committing to what I have to do - just thanks to myself."
Ukraine's Svitolina was tearful after the defeat, but reaching this stage capped a fine turnaround after she lost 6-4 6-0 to Andreeva on the first day of the tournament.
She pushed Andreeva throughout, drawing her into lengthy baseline rallies before fatigue set in.
She will finish the year at six in the world rankings, having made it back into the top 10 for the first time since 2021.
Svitolina returned from maternity leave in 2022, and joked that daughter Skai would have some questions for her after the match.
"She's probably still awake and is going to ask me why I didn't win today," the 32-year-old said.
"I'm really happy to be in great form and coming back after pregnancy. Hopefully it inspires some ladies and athletes around the world to believe that it's possible.
"I also want to say thank you to people in Ukraine for supporting me and being on this journey with me."

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.
Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.
Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.
The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.
Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.
But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.
When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.
The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.
But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.
On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.
Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."
He warns that if the port of Aden â a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants â was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".
But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.
"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."
"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."
It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.
The former British defence attachÃ© to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.
He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.
"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.
"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

12fb50528067.text: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing. Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies. International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk. Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report . Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition. Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students. A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices. Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit. The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue. The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent. "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect." Go deeper: What to know about the wave of student visa cancellations

Elon Muskâs âdifficulty in understandingâ a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africaâs biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday.
Under the countryâs Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy âopenly racistâ and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country.
âAll countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,â Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. âYouâve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.â
Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss âdoesnât fully understand the extentâ of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans.
Ramaphosa also said Musk should be âloyalâ to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years.
An âambushâ
Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trumpâs second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Muskâs guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washingtonâs increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria.
South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administrationâs ire over Pretoriaâs criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office â an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide â was an âambush.â He said Trump was âseriously misinformed.â
Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US presidentâs belief in a white genocide â a widely discredited allegation â underpinned Washingtonâs approach to South Africa.
The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google.
Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has âpersonal strong empathyâ for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant.
Altman â who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter â said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has âlong been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.â
Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semaforâs Reed Albergotti: âI donât think I know enough to answer that question.â
Altman said itâs hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is âa behemoth of a company,â and people still trust its guarantees as an investor.
In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout.
On public sentiment toward AI
Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a âstrong stanceâ on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI.
He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay âin control of the future.â
âWe should not want to have a âhandoverâ â¦ either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,â he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are âteam human.â
He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that âthe engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.â
Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. âWe have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.â
On going public
Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasnât concerned.
OpenAI âwill go public at some point,â even if there are âreal downsides to being public,â including intense volatility.
Altman said he isnât concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week.
âThat is not a worry,â he said. âThereâs been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.â
On espionage
OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. Itâs clear that âpeople are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,â Altman said, adding that the companyâs operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. âWe have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.â
On memory and RAM
Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that itâs a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage.
His comment, he said, got âmisinterpreted,â and that he wants people to have RAM at home: âI think the home tinkering is great.â
Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to âshare this memoryâ with people who need it.
On the next generation of tech
Altman said the world is âunderpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.â
âWe had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,â he said. âI think weâre going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.â
OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientistsâ access to frontier AI.
âThe world can get so much better,â Altman said.
On AI safety
Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement â the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve â but added, âI donât think we could safely do that right now.â Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI.
OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labsâ safety work âis going to be increasingly important and valuable,â he said.

Pope Leo hit by flying rosary while waving to crowds in Peru
Pope Leo XIV was struck in the face by what is thought to be rosary prayer beads while travelling in the popemobile to deliver a farewell Mass in Peru.
Photos and video show the pope rubbing his eye shortly after the object was tossed toward him. He sustained no injuries and the Mass went ahead.

President Donald Trumpâs trip to Asia may include a sitdown with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Though Trump floated that possibility today, telling reporters that Kim âmight come,â one senior US official said days ago that there are âno plans at all for engagement with North Korea.â
The White House declined to comment further on the prospect, pointing to Trumpâs earlier comments.
While the president met with Kim during his first term, he has yet to organize a second-term meeting. Trumpâs trip will culminate with an unprecedented trilateral meeting between the US, China, and Russia.
Trump is not expected to discuss Ukraine at that sitdown, the senior US official said. Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin are instead expected to discuss âthe reduction of nuclear weapons in the world,â White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said.

9a1718d17ac2.text:
This monthâs midterms were the âcare election,â according to a sweeping new report by Care Canât Wait Action that was shared first with Semafor.
The coalition points to its role in boosting turnout â citing nearly 24 million impressions via events, media and other outreach â as well as exit polling that found voters want the next Congress to focus on issues like paid leave and child care.
âThereâs this undeniable sense of momentum,â leader Ai-jen Poo told Semafor, adding that she is âlooking to Congress to pass a whole set of bills that will address the entire care agenda, because I think voters are ready.â
Seven in 10 voters said itâs important for Congress to pass a paid family and medical leave bill in the next six months, according to included polling by Lake Research for MomsRising Together and Paid Leave for All Action.
Eight in 10 voters who are mothers said it was important to their vote that the federal government âimmediately works to lower the cost of raising a family,â including by tackling child care.
Nearly 8 in 10 voters said presidential candidates should make paid leave a top priority, according to separate post-election polling by Change Research. That includes 95% of Democrats and 69% of men.
âDemocrats won on these issues, and now they need to take action within the first 100 days of this new Congress,â Sondra Goldschein, executive director of the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, told Semafor. She called for lawmakers to âput them on the presidentâs desk, and then force him to decide whether he wants to veto.â
GOP cuts to Medicaid funding helped mobilize âmany first-time care-worker activists,â SEIU Executive Vice President Leslie Frane said. Advocates are hopeful the Trump administration agrees to repeal some of those cuts â but theyâre not holding their breath on other issues.
âWhen the time comes to be smart about making choices and tradeoffs, we will. But I think weâre really far from that time,â Poo said. âSo this is a moment where we have the momentum to do big things, and thereâs no reason why we should not.â
Democrats had tried to enact paid leave and universal pre-K amid the pandemic, but fell short given their narrow Senate majority. Advocates are now optimistic that the latest wave of policymakers will see more success.
âWe have a whole crop of new leaders coming in with a clear mandate on these policies â and that was intentional,â Poo said. âThat was a big lesson from Build Back Better, is that we need a whole different level of consensus.â

ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic U.S. House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.
Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for U.S. climate and energy policy.
“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.
President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the U.N. talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes and universities.
Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.
Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the U.S. from the U.N.’s climate framework, the extent of U.S. participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, U.S. congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.
“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.
The U.S. would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman said.
“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners … and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).
The new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the U.S. has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).
Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.
“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).
“I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the U.S. can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said.
“But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are … supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”
Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.
“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”
Singh said the U.S. has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.
“As the world’s largest historical emitter, the U.S. carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”
Singh said until the U.S. pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”
Brandon Wu, with ActionAid USA, said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.
“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.
While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible U.S. return to the climate talks.

e135f3f56587.text: By — Liz Landers Liz Landers Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/read-the-full-white-house-memo-requiring-agencies-to-get-approval-before-testifying-in-front-of-congress Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Read the full White House memo requiring agencies to get approval before testifying in front of Congress Politics Nov 16, 2026 4:00 PM EST In a new memorandum obtained by PBS News on Monday, White House counsel Will Scharf is directing all federal agencies and executive departments to get approval from White House legal and legislative affairs offices before agreeing to testify before congressional committees. Read the full memo by clicking the image below. The directive comes as both chambers of Congress prepare for incoming Democratic leadership, which has promised robust oversight of the Trump administration after sweeping victories in the midterms. A White House official told PBS News in an emailed statement: "The Trump Administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations. We are ready to engage with Congress, this process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats' who want to slow the administration down from its historic work." Stand with free and independent journalism. The latest directive from Scharf follows a separate letter he sent last week to Rep. Garcia says voters gave Democrats a mandate to pursue accountability The White House official pointed to four letters that House Democrats have sent to federal agencies like the Department of Homeland Security asking for documents to be preserved, referring to them as "exorbitant demands Democrats have sent the agencies." This article contains distressing details and references to suicide
A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.
The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.
Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.
Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.
Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.
He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.
Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.
Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.
He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.
Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.
He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".
He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."
The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General , externalthat Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.
Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.
According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.
Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.
When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".
"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.
Challenged on whether his views veered into conspiracy theory, Freeman said: "I have the luxury of being able to say, don't take my word for it, let everybody look at it."
"If you think I'm still a conspiracy theorist because I'm looking at something that looks like a strangulation and say, I think it is a strangulation and I don't think it could be a hanging, show me where I got it wrong."
"I'm wide open to that. I'm an academic. I'm quite happy to hear people's theories on things that are informed," he said.
Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.
Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

President Donald Trumpâs former AI and crypto czar, David Sacks, argued on Monday the public was too quick to judge former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, though he stopped short of saying whether the board should reinstate Huang as CEO.
âYou have the right to have allegations against you adjudicated in a proper court of law,â Sacks, a longtime venture capitalist and co-founder of Craft Ventures, said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World on Monday.
Sacks went on to say that the public âshould wait until thereâs a proper determination by a legal authorityâ on the allegations against Huang. The Trump administration and Congress have launched investigations related to the controversy.
Huang resigned as Nvidiaâs CEO last week following revelations that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset as well as a Nvidia employee who had reported directly to him, sending shockwaves throughout Silicon Valley. Huang acted as a linchpin of the AI trade, deploying nearly $99 billion across the tech ecosystem to fuel the AI infrastructure buildout.
Sacks cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Huang admitted to having an affair, was spying on Nvidia, citing reports that US intelligence hasnât arrived at a definitive conclusion. âThis narrative of the Chinese spy is falling apart,â he claimed.
Sacks is a staunch proponent of the AI buildout, and has argued that any guardrails on the technologyâs development would hamstring the US in its competition with China. The venture capitalist played a decisive role on US policy while in the White House, pushing for softer AI regulation.
Sacks drafted parts of Trumpâs âAI Action Plan,â a comprehensive blueprint that involves cutting red tape and prioritizing private-sector growth over federal oversight.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng acknowledged Monday that the $6.3 billion hack his firm suffered â one which roiled cryptocurrency markets and raised existential questions about industry security â resulted from the companyâs own failings.
âIt shouldnât have happened,â Teng said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. âThis was a multi-month, sophisticated campaign,â he continued, referring to the attack, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea. (Pyongyang has denied involvement in the hack.)
The hack raised questions about what is fundamentally the weakest link in most cybersecurity and business operations: humans themselves. Binance said that it was compromised in part because of a sophisticated phishing attempt that involved a Binance employee undergoing a fictitious interview process that resulted in âmalicious softwareâ being loaded onto a corporate machine, Teng noted.
Teng also acknowledged Binanceâs checkered reputation, involving billions in fines for anti-money laundering violations and the imprisonment of its primary shareholder and founder Changpeng Zhao. âWe had really underinvested into the area of compliance,â Teng said. âSince the record fine and settlement, we have really invested a great deal.â
Whether that investment is enough is an open question: The New York Times reported in September that Chinese firms continue to use Binance to launder illicit proceeds for the Iranian government.
Binance, like most cryptocurrency firms, has also benefitted from a laissez-faire environment in Washington. A pro-crypto mentality adopted by the Trump administration has come up short of what many crypto executives had hoped for, but has still allowed for major regulatory wins for the industry.
âWe would have hoped that the Clarity [Act] would have passed,â Teng said. âWe do hope there will be more transparency and visibility on that front moving forward.â
Binance is a sponsor of Silicon Valley & The World. Richard Teng made his comments during Silicon Valley & The Worldâs partner session.

Recent jitters in the markets about AI represents a shift among investors to becoming more selective about where they allocate their money, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup said Monday, and sheâs not worried about it.
âIn a market priced to perfection, getting the air out of tires is not a bad thing,â Fraser said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World, adding that investors are absorbing huge amounts of change even over the past two weeks â the FAA shutdown, a high inflation reading and the midterm US election. âIâm hoping for a boring week,â she said.
On the fallout of Jensen Huangâs departure from Nvidia, Fraser said sheâs ânot going to pile onâ to the commentary, but that the company is in âvery capable handsâ with his successor, Colette Kress, which was met with applause in the room.
Fraser told Semaforâs Liz Hoffman that she sees AI companies being âthoughtful about their capital stack,â and that itâs not terrible that any pullback is âa demand side rather than a supply side problem.â
Partner with China
Citi just recently got its China securities license and told rivals to âwatch out.â The bank is prioritizing relationships in the country, Fraser said, while emphasizing the importance of a stable relationship as well.
Citi has been in China for 124 years, and Fraser said sheâd work with Chinese companies if they are complimentary to the bankâs client base. As for AI and China, she noted that the tech supports a more service-driven economy in the US, whereas in China, the focus is more about physical AI and robotics. âThe two are very complimentary,â she said.
âThereâs far too much for both sides to lose,â Fraser said. Noting that the sheer number of meetings between the countriesâ presidents is unprecedented and can only mean âgood things.â US President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China this week.
Fraser feels the bank is prepared for a Democratic-controlled Congress, as the bank has taken pains to de-risk and modernize.
âWeâve put ourselves in a position for a global bank to operate and be a source of strength in choppy times rather than a source of problems.â
The same goes for cybersecurity risk, said Fraser, adding that banks donât compete on protecting against hacks and cyber attacks so they have collaborated to make sure the financial system is safe. âWeâve been in a window where we can do a lot of hardening,â she said.

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidiaâs board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huangâs ouster, saying the board needs âto get this right.â
Gerstner said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World that he wasnât calling for Huangâs immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that âeveryone is rushing to judgmentâ¦and I simply donât know the facts.â
Gerstner acknowledged that Huang âengaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,â but that heâs messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidiaâs success is âtoo critical to the future security of our countryâ for the board to make a wrong decision.
People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isnât considering a return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for âa slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.â
Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huangâs immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. âWe donât want to take shortcuts,â Gerstner said.
An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capitalâs largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC.
On âTrump accountsâ
Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. âElonâs always told me he wants to do something big here,â Gerstner said.
