Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.
The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.
Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.
Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.
"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.
Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.
Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.
The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.
A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.
Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.
The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.
Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.
It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.
She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.
The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.
Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

a2e513e28efa.text: A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide. Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel. Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said , with thousands more delayed. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday. Read more below. What caused the nationwide groundstop? What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds." Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal . The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris , has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide. After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement. How did a router disrupt flights nationwide? How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft. The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft. A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications. The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds. The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights. What to know about radio frequency outages One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions. Some reports described this as a " rolling frequency outage ," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time. This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers. Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy. What happens to pilots during the outages? Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail. These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual . The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage. Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities. Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected. What does this mean for flights? Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions. Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports. Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft. What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris. The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

48b8ccc2d0a0.text: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear three conservative appeals tied to battles over diversity, equity and inclusion , leaving lower-court rulings intact in disputes over federal research grants, medical training and transgender-related speech. The big picture: The denials mark a reprieve after years of backlash against DEI, though the justices stopped short of settling the underlying constitutional debates. One of those Monday decisions set back President Trump's administration push to cancel swaths of DEI-related research grants. Driving the news: The justices rejected President Trump's bid to revive cuts to federal research grants awarded to University of California researchers over their perceived DEI-related viewpoints. A U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled in May that challengers were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim that their grants were terminated because of the "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints." That decision partly upheld a preliminary injunction from U.S. District Judge Rita Lin reinstating grants terminated over perceived DEI-related viewpoint, while reversing relief for a separate group. What they're saying: Trump's DOJ argued to the high court that allowing the grants to continue would force taxpayers to fund ideologies "their public stewards reject." A DOJ spokesperson told Axios the department will continue fighting the preliminary injunction and "will continue to advocate for the Executive Branch's lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives." Catch up quick: The challenged funding represents just a slice of the DEI-related grants ensnared in the administration's terminations and ensuing litigation. Trump has led a top-down campaign to undermine federal and corporate DEI efforts, disputes over state policies have also crept onto the national stage. Case in point: The Supreme Court also declined to hear a challenge from the anti-trans Gays Against Groomers against Colorado lawmakers' restrictions on misgendering and deadnaming during legislative hearings. The Tenth Circuit had found lawmakers were shielded by legislative immunity. Meanwhile: The justices also declined to hear a challenge to required implicit bias training for California continuing medical education courses. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated he would've heard the appeal brought by an ophthalmologist and a conservative medical advocacy group. Justice Clarence Thomas penned a dissent, joined by Justice Samuel Alito. Thomas' argument indicates there may be an appetite for a similar question about government speech in the future: "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote. What we're watching: Both in the courts and in the public arena , disputes over the federal administration and state leaders' handling of DEI initiatives are still playing out with many more sure to come. But on Monday, a high court that hasn't always sided with DEI initiatives declined to further some key debates — for now. Go deeper: Trump says he "ended DEI." Courts disagree

US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.
Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's âaccess to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
'China plays games with us, so we play games with China'
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
'A handshake with Jensen'
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

ae0ba84a5212.text: By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/freeman-johnson-the-oldest-of-the-dwindling-number-of-pearl-harbor-survivors-dies-at-106 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106 Nation Nov 16, 2026 2:12 PM EST BOSTON (AP) — Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died. Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson. "It's going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving," said Diane Johnson, 72. "He's going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom." Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn't hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane. "While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn't see anything, absolutely nothing," said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship. Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. By the time he was topside, the St. Louis, a light cruiser, had evaded midget submarines and safely set out to sea. "We were way out to sea, way out. You couldn't see any land at all. All you saw was ocean," he said. "I was just a sailor, just a swabbie, I was not an officer. They don't tell you anything if you don't need to know. And I didn't need to know it. So they tell you nothing." The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira "Ike" Schab, who was 105. While Johnson didn't see the Pearl Harbor attack, which killed just over 2,400 Americans and propelled the United States into the war, he was witness to other historic moments during World War II. He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship's preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin. The ship was equipped with two elevators and a bathtub. All the ammunition and much of the oil was removed to lighten the ship as it made its way down the Potomac River to pick up Roosevelt. It was reloaded before the ship headed out to sea. READ MORE: Lou Conter, last living survivor of the USS Arizona during the Pearl Harbor attack, dies at 102 Johnson also witnessed the war's end while aboard the Iowa. He was on the Iowa's mast watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away in Tokyo Bay aboard the USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945. "I could see the boats coming up with the Marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table," he said. "It was all over. That was the end of the war. A bunch of us got together — the war is over. Let's go home." For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn't see it as one of the defining moments in his life. Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors — all jobs he retired from, the last one at the age of 90. "Pearl Harbor just happened. I can't put it any other way," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The US government has âno plansâ to target or âorchestrate the deep pruningâ of technology companies headquartered in allied countries from American supply chains, Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said Monday.
Speaking alongside ASMLâs President and CEO Christophe Fouquet at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World, Helberg rejected âtop-down government-mandated plans that intentionally discriminateâ against companies based on their country of origin in comments to Semaforâs Ashley Gold. He named ASML, Samsung, and SK Hynix as key partners to US firms in the technology supply chain.
Discussing Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains, Helberg said that the Trump administration wants to ensure companies across allied economies benefit from a âlevel playing field.â He described the initiative as a âcapability-centric coalitionâ that draws on the comparative strength of participating countries.
Helberg also argued that Washington must balance technological leadership with global market share of AI-focused companies, warning that innovation alone will not secure Americaâs dominance in the fast-growing technology field.
âWe need both in order to win the AI race,â Helberg said. âWe need to lead the world qualitatively and have the best innovation out there. But we also need market share, and those two things need to happen in conjunction.â
Helberg also stopped short of endorsing three bipartisan bills that lawmakers are considering including in the year-end defense bill that would tighten AI chip export controls following the Nvidia controversy.
Asked about the investigation involving Nvidia, Helberg described the company as critical to US technological leadership, saying âthere is a really compelling argument for national security to have Nvidia continue to be a leading beacon of innovation.â
He called for investigations to establish the facts quickly, adding, âOur hope is obviously to see serious work being done through the investigations to uncover the facts and get to the truth quickly in order to get to the right outcome.â Nvidia has attracted scrutiny from Congress as well as the administration amid revelations that now-former CEO Jensen Huang had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

e0b0bce43c5d.text: Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/third-u-s-aircraft-carrier-in-middle-east-as-trump-keeps-options-open-in-iran-war Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Third U.S. aircraft carrier in Middle East as Trump keeps options open in Iran war World Nov 16, 2026 2:02 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — A third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, a U.S. official said Monday, in a dramatic show of military might as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war. The U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations, confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt's arrival in the region. It brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than 8-month-old war "militarily is effectively over." The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping. Three aircraft carriers deployed in the Middle East is rare The H.W. Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003. In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the Navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea. The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 Marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region. The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump's Republican Party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led Vice President JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that "the reason we lost is the war." Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months. Trump says the US is prepared to strike but might not need to Last week, Trump warned Iran that the U.S. military is "locked and loaded" and that the U.S. was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran's nuclear program, for signs of activity. "If something does not work out, I would not hesitate" to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday. Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war "militarily is effectively over" after meeting with Qatar's prime minister. WATCH: After midterms, world leaders await Trump's next move in Iran Trump also declared that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance — who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks — instead to focus on the administration's domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states. Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran's nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the U.S. first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets. The conflict simmers in the Strait of Hormuz In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world's oil passed before the war. Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the U.S. has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters. Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a U.S.-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines. Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait's coastlines, according to the Revolutionary Guard's navy. Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said. U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade. Independent assessments from Lloyd's List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels. 0f7e9c617eb5.text: By — Didi Tang, Associated Press Didi Tang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/trump-administration-moves-to-block-china-from-indirect-access-to-american-ai-tech Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI tech Science Nov 16, 2026 1:51 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China's abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. The rule also was issued days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. "The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. READ MORE: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be an additional, case-by-case licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allow China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress "physical export controls" under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to "access our tech through the cloud" and giving it "a real tool to sidestep" U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. d393c1eea8a4.text: By — Maria Sherman, Associated Press Maria Sherman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/raye-leads-2027-grammy-nominations-as-women-dominate-top-categories Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Raye leads 2027 Grammy nominations as women dominate top categories Arts Nov 16, 2026 1:32 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Call her a Raye of sunshine. The English singer-songwriter leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday. Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video. Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist. Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category. Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award. Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video. Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each. Women dominate the top categories In addition to Raye's "This Music May Contain Hope" and Rosalía's "Lux," the album of the year category is rounded out by Bridgers' "Lost Weekend," Dean's "The Art of Loving," Langley's "Dandelion," Mars' "The Romantic," Rodrigo's "You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love" and Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl." Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar. Only recordings commercially released in the U.S. between Aug. 31, 2025, and Aug. 28, 2026, were eligible for nominations. The final round of Grammy voting, which determines the winners, will take place between Dec. 10 and Jan. 7. The record of the year category is made up of Dean's "Man I Need," Langley's "Choosin' Texas," Mars' "I Just Might," Raye's "Where Is My Husband!", Rodrigo's "The Cure," Rosalía's "Berghain" featuring Björk and Yves Tumor, Swift's "The Fate of Ophelia" and Tame Impala and Jennie's "Dracula." WATCH: Sasha Alex Sloan performs 'Empty' and discusses the craft of songwriting Jennie, perhaps best known as one-fourth of the juggernaut girl group Blackpink, is also a first-time nominee at the 2027 Grammys. Last year her bandmate Rosé became the first K-pop artist to ever receive a nomination in the record of the year field for "APT.," her megahit with Mars. Jennie's "Dracula" nomination makes her the second. Song of the year — an award for a track's songwriters, which sometimes includes the performer but not always — is made up of an almost identical list to record of the year, featuring the same song selections from Dean, Langley, Raye, Rodrigo and Rosalía. But it also includes Ariana Grande's "Hate That I Made You Love Me," Swift's "Toy Story 5" song "I Knew It, I Knew You" and Mars' "Risk It All." In the best new artist category, Langley, Angine de Poitrine, Geese, Slayyyter, Sienna Spiro, Don Toliver, Remi Wolf and The Womack Sisters will go head-to-head. "It's a privilege to congratulate all the incredible music creators recognized in this year's Grammy nominations," said Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason jr. in a statement. "From first-time nominees to artists reaching career milestones, it's inspiring to see musicians at every stage of their careers represented. Together, they reflect the extraordinary diversity of genres, crafts and backgrounds that make up our community. We look forward to a remarkable season of celebration, and I'm grateful to our Voting Members for their continued commitment to honoring the music that moves us year after year." There are a number of other first-time nominees this year, including Geese, Tinashe, Slayyyter, Angine de Poitrine, Ryan Castro, Milo J, Megan Moroney, John Cale — who accepted the Recording Academy's Lifetime Achievement Award on behalf of his band The Velvet Underground in 2017 but has never been nominated before — and many more. The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 at 7 p.m. Eastern, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu. Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.
These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” says Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.
In November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.
In June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.
Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.
Many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” says Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is important, because you never know where some advance will come from.”
Through Genesis, the DOE plans to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” says astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”
This year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.
Other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have launched their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.
Many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” says John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.
Compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” says Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing shows promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.
Accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.
AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston says. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.
In the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.
As excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she says. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.
In response to these concerns, Gil says that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.
Sarrao says that it’s important to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”

55a493454221.text: By — Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/the-nvidia-scandal-is-heightening-americas-ai-rivalry-with-china-ahead-of-trumps-visit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit World Nov 16, 2026 12:50 PM EST HONG KONG (AP) — Well before reports emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the advanced chips made by his company were at the center of the race between the U.S. and China to dominate artificial intelligence. The scandal now threatens to intensify that rivalry. As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in China, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Congress are seizing on the affair to press for tighter restrictions on technology exports to protect America's edge. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The scandal, in many ways, encapsulates the rivalry, where concerns around national security, export control, and foreign policy get intertwined," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at London-based technology research and advisory group Omdia. At the heart of the competition to build the most advanced artificial intelligence is the race to access the most powerful AI chips. U.S.-led restrictions have barred China from getting the world's most advanced AI chips, a strategy that has led Beijing to accuse the U.S. of pursuing an AI monopoly. READ MORE: Trump's Asia reset: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, then a rare nuclear summit with Xi and Putin Once commanding some 95% of market share in China, Nvidia's sales to China have plummeted due to the export restrictions, first applied during the Biden administration. After Huang lobbied Washington to loosen the limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Trump earlier this year greenlighted the export of its highly-advanced, though not the most powerful, H200 chips. Trump has spoken admiringly of Huang — a man at the center of the AI boom Trump has been keen to promote — and the two have talked regularly during his second term, including at least twice this week as the scandal grew around the tech executive. Supporters of stronger export controls have a new rallying cry The strategy in Washington has been largely focused on hardware, with officials believing if they controlled where California-based Nvidia's best chips go, they'd be in control of the race for the most capable AI, said Shaoyu Yuan, an assistant professor at New York University's Center for Global Affairs. That strategy was effective in slowing down Chinese companies, Yuan said, but it assumed the primary threat was the physical hardware, not access to leaders like Huang. Yuan said what he called "China hawks" in Congress — who have been bullish on oversight and stronger export controls long before this incident — will now have "a story with a name and a face" to support their argument. "I don't think anybody in Washington wants to be seen as loosening the controls on chip exports to China right now," he added. This week several congressional Democrats wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to ask what officials knew of Huang's affair with a reported Chinese spy — and to demand an immediate halt to exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips Lawmakers from both parties have become more outspoken in their calls for tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. The Senate version of a defense policy bill includes authorizing Congress to review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, authorizing the Commerce Department to track AI chips to ensure they aren't diverted to unauthorized regions, and compelling U.S. allies to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers. Beijing has warned the U.S. against using the episode as a reason to impose new restrictions, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning telling reporters on Thursday: "The U.S. should stop fabricating the 'Chinese spy' narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions." China and the US have been pursuing common ground on AI safety The woman in the relationship with the Nvidia chief is reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to reporting by The New York Times, U.S. officials suspect she was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its cutting-edge chips more available to China. Beijing has refuted claims she was a Chinese spy and called the allegation "unsubstantiated." Trump doe s not plan to confront Xi on the Nvidia issue, according to senior U.S. officials who briefed reporters Friday on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House. The officials also said they do not expect Chinese retaliation if they close loopholes to existing measures that prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips. WATCH: Trump pushes back as AI leaders fuel calls to rein in rapidly advancing technology Huang has been a frequent visitor to the White House, and in May, he jumped onto Air Force One in Alaska, joining Trump at the last minute for a state visit to Beijing, where he captivated locals by sampling street food. He and his wife, Lori, were seated at the head table with the two leaders when Trump hosted Xi in September in Washington. At a tech summit that month, Huang took a phone call from the president while he was in a live appearance. 36dcd8e621fd.text: By — Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/preliminary-study-finds-a-clue-in-the-quest-to-help-diagnose-cte-in-the-living Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living Science Nov 16, 2026 12:14 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer's disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head. Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer's, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn't have Alzheimer's but advanced CTE instead. The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE. WATCH: New study reveals widespread signs of brain trauma among former NFL players Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn't reliably identify early-stage CTE. It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn't involved with the research. Abnormal tau is found in several brain diseases, many of which can overlap in older adults, adding to the difficulty in teasing apart its role in any one disease, including CTE. Sato, who studies such tauopathies, also stressed much more research is needed. The findings were published late Friday by the medical journal JAMA and presented at a scientific meeting in Japan. d34477c2e823.text: The White House counsel has instructed all executive branch agencies to get permission from their chief legal counsel and legislative affairs offices before allowing any employee to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Monday's memo from White House Counsel Will Scharf is the latest sign President Trump is ready to fight the many investigations being promised by Democrats, who will have significant majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. "The Trump administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations," a White House official said. Zoom in: Scharf's memo to staffers follows a letter he sent last week to the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif). In that letter, Scharf warned Democrats to limit their investigations to "legitimate" inquiries. "The Supreme Court has held that '[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to 'punish ' those investigated are indefensible," Scharf warned. "Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary," the letter said. Between the lines: Partisans will likely differ on what's "legitimate," but it's clear that Scharf's office will use its interpretation in deciding whether to allow executive branch employees to testify. "We are ready to engage with Congress," the White House official said, "This process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats' who want to slow the administration down from its historic work." In his Monday memo, Scharf said the administration "will remain disciplined in pursuing the work and service the American people deserve by ensuring that all Executive Departments and Agencies follow the established White House consultation process ... before any agency personnel may agree to appear before any congressional committee." Zoom out: For more than a year, Trump's administration has planned for the day congressional investigations ramp up. Trump knows he also faces the prospect of impeachment. But advisers say that's no longer threatening to Trump, and he doesn't believe there would be the 67 votes needed in the Senate to remove him. "The president can count, and he won't be cowed," a Trump adviser said. Trump also has promised to pre-emptively pardon staffers and allies he believes will be unfairly targeted by Congress or prosecutors in future Democratic administrations.

The coalition, launched in the Colombian coastal city of Santa Marta in April, is expected to release a progress report this week outlining steps taken by participating countries, including additional national plans to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas. The announcement comes as Ireland and the Pacific island nation of Tuvalu prepare to take over leadership of the initiative from Colombia and the Netherlands, with a second international conference planned for July 2027. A statement from Ireland's Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment confirmed Colombia's withdrawal and said preparations were well advanced for a program of events in both countries next year. Neither the Environment Ministry nor the presidential office responded to questions about Colombia's withdrawal or its plans to attend the next conference. "This process is bigger than any one country," the department said, adding that further details would be announced at a formal handover during COP31. A coalition seeking to turn promises into action The Santa Marta conference emerged from frustration over the slow pace of international efforts to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas, the fossil fuels that are the main drivers of global warming. The initiative brought representatives from 57 countries together to explore ways of turning international commitments to move away from fossil fuels, the main drivers of global warming, into concrete national policies. Unlike formal U.N. climate negotiations, the gathering was designed to encourage open discussions without pressure to reach binding agreements or commit to specific deadlines. Colombia's withdrawal follows the election of President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August promising to strengthen the country's oil and gas industry and revive exploration. He succeeded leftist President Gustavo Petro, who had made moving away from fossil fuels a central pillar of his environmental agenda and stopped awarding new oil and gas exploration contracts. WATCH: Colombia's new president reflects Latin America's right-wing shift Colombia's Environment Minister Fabio Arjona said in the past week that the previous administration's restrictions on gas development had contributed to domestic shortages, forcing some industries to rely on more polluting fuels. He argued that expanding supplies of natural gas, itself a fossil fuel, would help reduce emissions by replacing dirtier alternatives while ensuring the country's energy security. Irene Velez, Colombia's former environment minister and one of the initiative's leading advocates, said the coalition had developed momentum beyond the government that helped establish it. "Santa Marta has a life of its own, beyond the change of government in Colombia," Velez said. From international pledges to national road maps The coalition's future is being discussed as governments at COP31 confront renewed disagreements over how to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels. At the 2023 U.N. climate summit in Dubai, known as COP28, nearly 200 countries agreed for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. But the agreement established no binding timetable, leaving governments to determine how to fulfill the commitment. Since then, little has happened on the international level toward reducing greenhouse gases. This year at COP31, an initial outline of a possible agreement includes proposals to recognize a global fossil fuel transition road map developed by Brazil's COP30 presidency in 2025 and establish a process for advancing its recommendations. Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said 23 countries had announced national or regional road maps or plans to develop them and the Santa Marta coalition was advancing work on national road maps, trade, economic policies and financial incentives. "Planning is the first step towards delivering the transition," Jones said. Velez pointed to initiatives in Finland, Germany, Ireland and the Netherlands, alongside efforts by the United Kingdom and Brazil to develop their own road maps, as evidence of growing momentum. Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said progress since Santa Marta had been limited, with only a handful of countries publishing national transition road maps. The secret terms of Trump’s Venezuelan oil deal
Signed in August by Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth, the agreement sets up a small group of people to govern and profit from it.
This story was originally published by ProPublica.
In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.
ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text.
One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.
The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.
The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial 15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.
Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to the Miami Herald, federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company.
NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr. Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims against them are baseless.”
Key aspects of the plan differ from the Trump administration’s public pronouncements. Trump has said the deal will secure America’s energy dominance for the next century. But the text indicates that U.S. purchasing rights expire in half that time and that the underlying operating rights appear to run afoulof Venezuelan laws limiting oil concessions to 25 years.
The agreement does ensure the United States a deep discount from fair-market value on 20% of NABEP’s oil, as Trump has said. It does not, however, explicitly guarantee that Betancourt’s company is obligated to pay the estimated $200 billion in royalties and tax payments to Venezuela that the White House has said would benefit the country.
There are also significant caveats related to Trump’s central selling point to Americans — that the deal will bring a gusher of low-cost oil imports.
The agreement gives the U.S. the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s oil at a discounted rate of $30 a barrel, or less than a third of what oil has sold for in recent months, according to one of three supporting documents reviewed by ProPublica.
But this fee does not account for the cost of getting Venezuela’s oil out of the country. Much of Venezuela’s raw crude is so thick that it won’t flow through pipelines unless it is first blended with 20% or more of oil thinner products. Under the deal, the potentially significant cost of importing millions of barrels of those blending materials is not included in the price.
The White House, the State Department, the Pentagon and the energy company NABEP all defended the agreement, saying in statements that their new public-private venture will provide meaningful and lasting economic benefits to both countries that cannot be captured in a legal document.
“This historic deal marks a major step toward stabilizing Venezuela’s economy after years of hyperinflation and almost no new investment, while more than doubling the United States’ oil reserves,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers.
Wade emphasized that NABEP was chosen because of its track record of expanding oil production in Venezuela in recent years and that the agreement was between the company and the U.S. government, not Venezuela.
“Thanks in large part to the agreement,” Wade said, “there is a surge in confidence about the future of Venezuela’s oil industry and, as a direct result, substantial new investments are flowing into the country.”
He added that much of NABEP’s oil comes from fields that require little or no blending materials and that blending costs would not meaningfully impact the price of production. “Our barrel economics are strong.”
The newly revealed details of the agreement are nonetheless likely to raise more questions about whether the unorthodox marriage of the United States and a foreign energy baron can bring lasting benefits to either country — and which private parties might benefit along the way. Trump’s oil deal is likely to face scrutiny in both the United States and Venezuela, especially if Democrats win one or both chambers in the midterm elections, according to former U.S. diplomats and congressional staff.
“Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?” said former Ambassador James Story, who served as the top U.S. diplomat in Caracas from 2018 to 2023, in an interview.

The bloc also imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, and targeted several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil and petroleum products. Please check your inbox to confirm. At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority in Ukraine should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must back down rather than make fresh demands of Ukraine and its Western supporters. READ MORE: Europe to send a diplomat team to Ukraine talks as leaders push for a voice "Let's not blur the picture right now. What we need to see is a ceasefire," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said before chairing the meeting. "We don't see it at the moment. We see that Russia is really escalating." After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace. READ MORE: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large prisoner exchange as talks end with no major breakthrough But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999. Russia again accused of delaying tactics That demand is "really absurd," Kallas said. "If we look at the history, none of these countries has ever attacked Russia." She said Russia's tactic is always to demand more even though "they started the war. They are the aggressor. And there's one victim." German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: "Europe has a security architecture – we don't need a new one, we just need respect from everyone for the existing security architecture." He said that is "the foundation for any conceivable agreement, from the European point of view." Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys also insisted that Europe does not need another security framework, saying that Russia cannot be trusted and has already broken past agreements anyway. "It's very clear that we don't need another one. We already have one. Secure Ukraine, strong Europe, strong trans-Atlantic bond," he told reporters. "It's not about the rules. Rules are working. The problem is that Russia is breaking them." Little progress in US-led talks U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have positioned themselves as mediators and have been talking to Russia and Ukraine for just over a year. In that time, no lasting ceasefire has been agreed, and little obvious progress has been made toward peace. Major differences remain over the control of territory and future security arrangements. European leaders and officials, including Kallas, have expressed skepticism about the talks. The only tangible progress has been exchanges of prisoners, which are often used by warring parties as a trust-building measure during peace talks. READ MORE: Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by U.S. could benefit Putin At a summit in Dublin last week, EU leaders agreed that Europe should be represented in future talks by a team of security advisers from France, Germany, the U.K., Italy and Poland as well as senior officials from the EU's main institutions. The Europeans concede that as Ukraine's biggest backers they cannot also act as mediators. Their role will focus on security arrangements, reconstruction and Ukraine's future. Only Ukraine itself can decide on matters involving its sovereignty, they said. Associated Press writer Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report. AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?
Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.
The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.
AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”
Morphing simple worms into shrewd attackers
Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.
Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.
That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.
Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.
And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)
Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.
“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.
Spreading like octopuses or slime molds
The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.
Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.
Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.
The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.
How an octopus-worm spreads
An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image).
