In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.
Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label âEireâ.
It has been this way since Brexit.
Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.
It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.
Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.
All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnsonâs 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.
That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.
The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of Â£5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.
But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?
EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a âchoiceâ is being made.
In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.
The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.
But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.
Exit clause
A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.
He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.
"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.
The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.
The reset means they will be dismantled.
The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.
Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".
He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.
Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.
The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.
The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.
Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.
Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.
But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.
He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.
UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.
Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.
Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.
Contentious crisp flavourings
Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.
"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.
Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.
Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.
"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.
"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

b1ba0716124b.text: A U.S. attorney put likely incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on notice about her intent to investigate corporations and expected probes into the president's inner circle. Why it matters: The letter demanding Warren preserve documents related to her congressional oversight is the latest in a string of threats levied against congressional Democrats ahead of the party assuming the congressional majority — and gavels — next year. Congress' authority to investigate, hold hearings and gather testimony is a core legislative power. Analysts have long forecasted a Democratic subpoena storm into President Trump's lucrative presidency. But Democrats' plan to exercise that power and hone their focus on the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption," as reported by Axios' Hans Nichols, is already facing Justice Department pushback. Driving the news: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas contended in his Sunday letter that Warren appeared "eager to wield" her "gavel like a tomahawk," instructing her to preserve oversight records. In the strongly worded letter, he warned Warren about targeting private citizens close to the president and reiterated that any probes must serve a legislative purpose or risk violating those individuals' First Amendment rights. Those arguments echo his prior letters to Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller , shared Reitz's letter and referenced two civil rights statutes. Warren's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: Reitz's letter referenced Warren, Blumenthal and incoming Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia's (D-Calif.) recent inquiry into Trump fundraiser Meredith O'Rourke's role in coordinating contributions for the president's ballroom and other projects. It also referenced letters Warren, with Slotkin and other lawmakers, sent to tech CEOs probing the extent to which their AI investments were subsidized by GOP-led tax breaks. What they're saying: The White House did not respond to detailed questions but referred Axios to White House counsel Will Scharf's letter to Garcia that argued Democratic threats of investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality." Asked if Warren was the subject of a criminal probe or other proceedings, a Justice Department spokesperson told Axios that "the Department does not confirm or deny the existence of ongoing investigations." "The Department has both the statutory authority and the responsibility to examine potential violations of the law," the spokesperson added. Asked if DOJ leadership authorized or reviewed the letter, the DOJ referred Axios to Attorney General Todd Blanche's prior statement that "DOJ leadership is working with every U.S. attorney, including U.S. Attorney Reitz, on ongoing investigations." Friction point: Blanche refused to rule out prosecuting Democrats set on investigating administration officials in an interview earlier this month, claiming lawmakers' rhetoric had overstepped their authority. That came after Trump demanded the DOJ look into what he labeled as "Weaponization and Lawfare" from his political opponents. What we're watching: Reitz asked Warren to respond to his letter by next Monday. He described the letter as his "first arrow shot." Go deeper: Corporate America's Trump trap

Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit
The Prince and Princess of Wales have played street cricket and taken a trip on the metro during the first day of their three-day visit to India.
In the coming days, the royal couple will be attending events for the Earthshot Prize, which William founded, as well as meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
It marks the first time in four years that William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together - following Catherine's treatment for cancer.
The BBC's senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph explains more.

09d3cc1a432a.text: By — Mogomotsi Magome, Associated Press Mogomotsi Magome, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/at-least-17-people-killed-in-2-mass-shootings-on-the-same-day-in-south-africa Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter At least 17 people killed in 2 mass shootings on the same day in South Africa World Nov 16, 2026 10:04 AM EST JOHANNESBURG (AP) — At least 17 people were killed in two mass shootings on the same day in South Africa. Motives have not been immediately established for the crimes some 530 kilometers (330 miles) apart, police said Monday. Eight people were found dead inside a bullet-riddled vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, according to police, who said they had not immediately identified the victims or any suspects in the shooting Sunday. Nine people were found dead with gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville near South Africa's capital, Pretoria. The shooting reportedly took place Sunday night and no arrests have been made. The Jeffsville case is being investigated by the serious and violent crimes, murder and robbery unit in Gauteng province. The incident is reported to have occurred between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m., police said. "Police were alerted at approximately 07:30 this morning, 16 November 2026. On arrival, members found the bodies of nine people, six males and three females, inside the four-roomed shack with gunshot wounds," said police spokesperson Brenda Muridili. Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said the killings could be related to a previous shooting at a nearby informal settlement in Saulsville last year where 12 people were killed and 13 injured. He said one of the people who was killed during the shooting was a "person of interest" in the shooting that happened in Saulsville last year. READ MORE: Mass shooting at South African hostel bar leaves 11 dead, including 3 children "We cannot rule out that they may be linked, and may possibly have been a retaliation attack," Mthombeni said. In the Saulsville case from last year, Mthombeni said police had made a breakthrough and arrested one suspect who is believed to be one of the mass shooters. Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi, who visited the crime scene with the police on Monday, said the provincial government was coordinating with other provincial departments to support the police in their investigations of similar crimes happening in the province, which includes the city of Johannesburg. In the Pietermaritzburg shooting, police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said some families had come forward to help with identifying the victims but it was yet to be confirmed. "It's still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims," said Netshiunda. Several mass shootings linked to criminal gangs have occurred in the past year. READ MORE: South African police make multiple arrests after deadly mass shooting at a pub In September, three gunmen barged into a small house in an impoverished neighborhood near the coastal city of Durban and opened fire on people attending a party, killing at least 11, including a pregnant woman. In the same month, 17 people were killed and several others wounded when gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles stormed a tavern and opened fire at patrons outside the bar before moving inside and continuing to shoot. In June, multiple shooters killed 12 people in a poor neighborhood in Johannesburg in an attack that police linked to criminal gangs. Also in June this year, an armed gang opened fire in a poor neighborhood in Johannesburg, killing 12 people and wounding at least nine, before fleeing in a minibus. Mthombeni said police had arrested three people in that shooting. They believe that it was linked to territorial battles between rival illegal mining gangs. Two mass shootings two weeks apart in December last year killed 21 people. They also were carried out by multiple gunmen. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.
He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.
At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.
His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.
Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.
He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability, external".
Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance", external. It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.
Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.
His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.
"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external.
"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.
"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."
He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.
Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.
Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (Â£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.
He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.
"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.
"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."
In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world", external, saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".
After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.
He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse, external, saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird."
The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'
"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."
The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.
By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men, external.
"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.
Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.
Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.
With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.
But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.
Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.
"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times, external.
"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.
"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."
Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

6f1f9f63c782.text: By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-asia-reset-deals-in-manila-and-shenzhen-then-a-rare-nuclear-summit-with-xi-and-putin Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's Asia reset: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, then a rare nuclear summit with Xi and Putin Politics Nov 16, 2026 9:38 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump's departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days, even as a nationwide ground stop snarled air traffic and his Republican administration faced tough questions on its handling of the situation. WATCH: FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances' His trip to Asia, which begins in Manila then continues to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, gives Trump the opportunity to change the narrative from his domestic woes, including the air travel problems and fallout from the November midterm election where his party lost both chambers of Congress. The controversy over tech powerhouse and chipmaker Nvidia is also certain to hang over Trump's visit to China, despite efforts by administration officials to downplay the president's close ties to Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved. Trump had no plans to raise the issue with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet, said U.S. officials who briefed reporters anonymously about the president's Asia trip under ground rules set by the White House. WATCH: What China stands to gain from Nvidia's CEO's alleged affair with spy Huang accompanied Trump on Air Force One during the president's last trip to China in May, and he has been a sporadic presence around Trump at the White House while speaking to him frequently. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on artificial intelligence, and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition. Scrutiny of the Trump administration's actions as they relate to Nvidia has been growing, including on the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by the alleged Chinese spy with whom Huang had the affair. WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips Asked about the matter in an interview that aired Sunday with Fox News Channel anchor Larry Kudlow, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will "leave the internal workings of the Commerce Department to the Commerce Department. "I think what's more important here, Larry, is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions ... and at what level?" Bessent said. He added: "I think we're going to see answers." "Jensen Huang is an incredible innovator, but that does not abrogate their duties of compliance," Bessent said. Among the travelers on the Asia trip with Trump will be Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is shaping up to be a top investigative target of the incoming Democratic majority in Congress. WATCH: How Elon Musk gained so much power over U.S. security interests In the Philippines, Trump will meet with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing's aggression in the region. He plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, the White House said. Then he heads to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit — and at the end of the trip, the first-ever three-way talks with China's Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss nuclear stockpiles. Trump and U.S. officials have indicated that the meeting with Putin and Xi will focus on nuclear weapons and that topics of discussion would not include Russia's war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Still, the president has recently played up chances for a settlement to the conflict. READ MORE: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large prisoner exchange as talks end with no major breakthrough The three-way meeting will also put in the spotlight the ongoing U.S. war with Iran, a country which has often allied with China and Russia. The war has been widely blamed for the Republican Party's steep losses in the midterms, and while Trump has tried to play down the chances he will order a resumption of major strikes against Iran, he also has said he does not see the need for talks. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Monday that the trilateral talks would be of "groundbreaking significance" and that China aimed to have in-depth exchanges about safeguarding world peace and promoting stability. "Under the current circumstances, the three countries shoulder an important responsibility to work together in addressing global challenges," she said in a regular briefing in Beijing. Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe".
The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.
They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.
On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.
The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website.
Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".
Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.
The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media.
Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions.
One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.
Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."
Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions.
Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.
Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.
Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.
With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”
Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.
Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.
As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.
The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.
But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

French film star GÃ©rard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault, admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.
On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety.
"Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this convictionâ¦ I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.
It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands.
"Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as AmÃ©lie, who was at the court.
"There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.
In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence.
"For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence.
"I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel.
"Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of handâ¦ including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."
The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.
His new lawyers, Delphine Meillet and David-Olivier Kaminski, said that with his admission of guilt Depardieu wanted to "move on", adding that "basically, as he turns 78 years old, he is saying to himself that life is more beautiful than 10 days of court hearings".
In the original trial, Depardieu was said to have touched the two women on intimate parts of the body during the making of Les Volets Verts, which is a film about an ageing actor coming to terms with his declining powers.
He himself admitted to using vulgar language but denied being "a metro-train groper". However, he also said he did not consider touching a woman's buttocks to be an act of "sexual aggression".
The trial was the first time the star of films like Green Card and Cyrano de Bergerac appeared in court on sexual assault charges. Several other women have made similar allegations in the media.
A decision on whether an alleged rape case can come to trial is expected this month.

The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ãngel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.
His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.
Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.
The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.
His son, whose name is also Miguel Ãngel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."
Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.
Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.
Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.
Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.
Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.
But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Ãrbenz GuzmÃ¡n was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile.
At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".
The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from PÃ¨re Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo ArÃ©valo, was elected in 2023.
ArÃ©valo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world".
"He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said ArÃ©valo, whose father Juan JosÃ© appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older ArÃ©valo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

Speaking from the Bahrain capital Manama, which a few months earlier had been bombarded in Iranian attacks, Bob Diamond, chief executive of private equity firm Atlas Merchant Capital, says heâs still optimistic about the outlook for the Gulfâs future, the US economy, and the prospect to raise more capital to consolidate the banking industry around the world.
Panmure Liberum, a UK investment bank heâs invested in, is expanding into the Gulf. Wall Street investors increasingly see the region as a place to invest, not just a place to raise money, and the war isnât deterring that. âThis is a really serious economy,â he said.
Diamond has experience in the region spanning decades. His contacts in Abu Dhabi and Qatar helped secure a Â£11.8 billion bailout for Barclays during the Great Financial Crisis, enabling the bank to avoid a taxpayer-funded rescue. He left Barclays in 2012 in the wake of a scandal around its role in manipulating interbank rates, and has since reinvented himself as a private equity investor, backing bank consolidation deals and fintechs. He is also chairman of the advisory committee of the Export-Import Bank of the US and chairman of Abu Dhabiâs tokenization platform Finstreet.
Diamond also said that Bitcoin, the most well-known and biggest digital asset by market capitalization, is âirrelevantâ (though useful as a store of value untethered from governments) and that the future of finance is tokenization â an industry is being led by the US as well as the Middle East.
Q&A
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Matthew Martin: You just announced Panmure Liberum, the UK investment bank you own, is expanding into the Gulf â how do you think about the opportunities in the Gulf now, particularly with the conflict thatâs still going on?
Bob Diamond: I donât mean to be dismissive of the severity of the situation here for a second, with the invasion of Iran, but when youâre here, as you and I are today, it feels pretty normal. For people who have not spent time in this region, I donât think thereâs a recognition of how developed the economies are, how developed the leadership is.
And then Iâd say that since we started Atlas Merchant Capital just over 10 years ago, Iâve been as interested in investing Middle Eastern money in other parts of the world as I have been in how we can find ways to help develop business here on the ground.
I think thereâs just a tremendous opportunity in this region for an on-the-ground advisory and M&A business for middle-market and family-owned businesses, because, as we are seeing here, the entrepreneurial spirit is very, very strong in many of these countries.
Financial services here is a great example of an industry where the vast majority of banks are ultimately state-controlled. As governments need to redirect capital to other things in the wake of the war, is there an opportunity for private equity investors to come in and play more of a role in the financial services industry in the Gulf?
One hundred percent. But I think you hit on a key issue, which is that traditionally that state control made things more opaque, so you couldnât get outside investment because it was opaque. And two, it was intrusive and more focused on subsidized business. And you can see why, right? Because as the Middle East was growing, much of the commercial real estate, for example, had to be âif we build it, they will come.â So some of the unbelievable commercial real estate, whether itâs in Abu Dhabi or Dubai or Qatar, or the financial services center that was built in Riyadh, was done really with strategic impetus, if you will, as opposed to pure commercial activity.
And I think thatâs changing, because a lot of those initial strategic investments have been done. I think it was the same in the early days of the development of Singapore. You could say the same thing, that it was strategic investing, but if you go to Singapore today, itâs a very commercial city. You donât see commercial buildings being put up.
What impact do you see the conflict in the region having on how Wall Street sees the Gulf?
I think sometime around 2024, 2025, we hit an inflection point where the Middle East being seen purely as a source of funding for the Western world changed to âthis is a really serious economy.â Going forward the Gulf will be focused much more on inward investment, as well as outward investment. I think it probably happened already with Saudi Arabia, and theyâve been a little bit ahead of it. But I think itâs really true across the region.
But there are still significant pools of capital in this region â if you just look at the sovereign wealth funds, thatâs the best example but not the only example â for investment in good ideas wherever they happen to be.
Dubai and Abu Dhabi are both making this big play into fintech and tokenization. How much are you getting involved in that, and what do you see as the chances of centers in the region becoming hubs for this new asset class?
I feel very strongly. Bitcoinâs irrelevant. Itâs not that Bitcoin isnât going to go up or down, and Iâm not questioning whether Bitcoinâs going to have a significantly higher price or not. Iâm personally not an investor, but I have a number of close associates who believe strongly. My point is different. In its best version, Bitcoin is a store of value away from a government, much as gold is. And if it doubles or triples or quadruples in value, it doesnât have a single strategic implication for financial services. Itâs just made somebody money, and itâs a good store of value.
Compare and contrast that to stablecoins, basically making payments electronic institutionally for the major currencies around the world. The News
Africa has plenty of investors ready to finance much-needed electricity projects, but too few developers with the expertise and early funding to get them off the ground, the head of a UK government-backed power developer told Semafor. More than 40% of sub-Saharan Africans lack electricity, with private investment central to a World Bank and African Development Bank push to connect 300 million across the whole continent by 2030.
âPeople spend a lot of time talking about a lack of capital for infrastructure projects in Africa. There is not a lack of capital,â said Chris Flavin, chief executive of Gridworks, which develops and invests in electricity networks across Africa. The issue for him is that investors generally want to get involved once projects are ready for construction, leaving the four or five years of preparatory work harder to finance.
Gridworks, which has electricity projects in countries including Uganda and Mozambique, is set to become the majority shareholder in a planned $300 million power line linking Zambiaâs grid to DR Congoâs copper-mining region, under an agreement signed in October. Lenders have shown âvery strong interestâ in the line, Flavin said.
When it develops its own projects, though, Gridworks faces the same hurdles as others despite its UK backing, he added, from permits and environmental approvals to years of planning âbefore you even get close to the financing.â In DR Congo, for example, commercial banks will not lend at that stage, said Archip Lobo, co-founder of Nuru, a solar mini-grid operator in the countryâs east. âThey will take the risk on something that exists,â he told Semafor. Instead, Lobo highlighted the existence of state support for early development costs and World Bank Group insurance against political risks.
But the World Bankâs own evaluators are less sure capital is plentiful. They found in a recent review that private financing remained too limited to meet Africaâs electrification needs. The narrow pool of investors, such as development lendersâ private arms, government-sponsored funds, foundations, and impact funds âare unlikely to meet the scale of financing needed for electrification growth,â the group said.
Industrial advantage
Private power projects in Africa are easier to develop when they serve large industrial buyers, such as mines, rather than households and small businesses, Flavin said. A mine with a strong balance sheet and known electricity consumption gives developers a clear customer to design around. For projects aimed at individual customers âthe challenge is one of guaranteed demand.â
In southeastern DR Congo, CrossBoundary Energy, a Mauritius-based power producer, commissioned a 233-megawatt solar farm with battery storage in August to supply Kamoa-Kakula, a copper complex co-owned by Ivanhoe Mines. âKamoaâs books are very good,â Auguy Bakome, a project manager at the mine, told Semafor in an earlier interview. He said its expected 40-year operating life and a 15-year contract to buy the electricity helped reassure lenders.
Utilities must estimate consumption across tens of thousands of customers. Building networks to serve them is âat the much harder end of the spectrum, full stop,â Flavin said. Moyi Power, a Gridworks-backed utility planned for three cities in northern DR Congo, relies on donor grants for about a quarter of its $190 million first phase and is not expected to deliver electricity before 2029.
Notable
- Africaâs shortage of reliable power is stalling its industrialization, Bloomberg reported, citing World Bank data that put manufacturing at 11% of sub-Saharan Africaâs GDP, half East Asiaâs share.

The News
Zambiaâs majority state-owned mining and energy investor plans to borrow about $700 million by 2028 to expand its business, its CEO told Semafor, as Africaâs second-largest copper producer seeks a bigger share of the wealth from its minerals. The money, which ZCCM Investments Holdings has yet to secure, will help fund a $2.7 billion investment proposal it unveiled on Monday.
Over the next decade, the company looks to back new infrastructure including a coal-fired power plant in southern Zambia and to raise its stakes in copper mines, among them a project led by Bill Gates-backed Kobold Metals. âWe donât want to be a quiet minority shareholder,â CEO Kakenenwa Muyangwa said. He added that any changes would be negotiated on commercial terms, and that âinvestors who share the ambition will find us a committed long-term partner.â
ZCCM-IH holds stakes in mines run by other companies and earns much of its income from their dividends, which depend on what is left after the mines pay their costs and debts. âFor a country that owns a share of its mines, that is not good enough,â Muyangwa said. The company now aims to earn more from royalties, a share of a mineâs sales that is paid regardless of profit. Its only such arrangement, with Canadian miner First Quantumâs Kansanshi mine, will bring in more than $990 million over the next decade, the company forecasts. ZCCM-IH aims to add at least one more later this decade.
The investment company said it now owes $5 for every $100 of its own capital, down from about $66 in 2021. Muyangwa said a cleaner balance sheet had put ZCCM-IH in a strong position to fund its expansion.
Trading ambitions
ZCCM-IH also plans to negotiate with its mining partners to get a share of the copper produced at each mine, which it would then sell directly. That would give the company âa trading income on top of its investment incomeâ and build âthe skills to market Zambian metal from Zambia,â Muyangwa said.
The plan comes as state-backed companies across Africaâs copper belt seek a more influential role over the trade of the metal. In neighboring DR Congo, state miner GÃ©camines sells copper through a venture with Swiss trader Mercuria. Zambiaâs state-owned Industrial Development Corporation also has a trading venture with Mercuria, which last month named ZCCM-IH as a regional partner.
The goal is greater control over the money countries earn from their minerals, Ekpen Omonbude, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, told Semafor. As demand for critical minerals grows, governments are looking to take a more active role in their sale, an approach he said is more common in oil and gas than in mining.

7f44e40be2ca.text:
- Published
US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028.
In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind.
"I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is."
The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections.
People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision.
Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions.
He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November.
But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race.
Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates.
Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid.
The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all.
The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda.
Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy.
The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run.
In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump.
"There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said.
He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment".
Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session.
He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy.
"There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said.

ced3d5cccecf.text: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that Europe would have a seat at the table, but Ushakov said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

Singapore is pressing Trump administration officials for details on new rules designed to crack down on Chinaâs access to advanced US-made chips, and which pose a potential threat to the countryâs booming AI sector.
Josephine Teo, Singaporeâs minister for digital development and information, said Monday her government is âengaging with our US counterparts as to the scope of implementation.â
âI think more importantly, how we can facilitate trusted access to this very important AI infrastructure,â Teo said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World, noting she has spoken with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
The new US Commerce Department rules include closing a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access advanced US semiconductors via third-country data centers, which the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, at the center of the Nvidia scandal that took down CEO Jensen Huang, is accused of exploiting.
Singapore has also been added to a list of countries that faces export restrictions on advanced chips, a move US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had postponed repeatedly until his agency came under scrutiny in recent days.
âSingapore takes very seriously the upholding of the rule of law,â Teo said, noting that there are about 6,000 US companies in Singapore: âWe safeguard our integrity in the business environment and we do not condone anyoneâ¦ violating the laws of other countries.â
âIf they also violate our laws, they can be very certain that we will actively investigate and also hold them to account,â Teo said.
Teo declined to comment on her governmentâs claim that the US had been unhelpful in the city stateâs investigation of Megaspeed â whose former executive, Alice Huang, is accused of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset â but noted that Singaporeâs own investigation into the company predated its knowledge of an investigation by the US Bureau of Industry and Security.
âSuffice to say, investigations into Megaspeed are still continuing,â Teo said.
Teo said the environment in Singapore for AI companies would continue to remain favorable, and pointed out that firms including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind had deepened their presence in Singapore in recent months. âThere is positive momentum. Weâd like to keep it going.â
âI think we will try our best to understand the impact and help ensure that we continue to have trusted access to the critical infrastructure needed for legitimate businesses,â Teo said.

a90e538dfa61.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has joined a group of âbrilliantly intelligentâ corporate leaders who âjust lack wisdom,â Arianna Huffington said Monday.
Speaking at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World, Huffington called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment.
âWe see incredibly intelligent people all around who are incredibly deluded, incredibly destructive, and self-destructive,â said Huffington, the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavioral change tech company. âWe need to invest in making humans better.â
Speaking alongside Huffington on the panel, Willett Advisors CEO Steven Rattner said the idea of bringing Huang back as CEO is âridiculous.â Some in the tech industry are calling for Huang to come back, though the Nvidia board reportedly isnât considering it. Rattner said the comparison between Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to his post after an ouster in 2023, âdoesnât even come close to computing. You canât bring Jensen back.â
Both Huffington and Rattner agreed the tech industry needs to do a better job making a case for itself to a skeptical and anxious public.
âThe crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,â Rattner said, referencing the recent US midterm elections that were widely seen as a rebuke of tech. He said tech leaders face the same responsibility as politicians or public officials âto communicate and explain to people. And the tech industry just blew it.â
Huffington said that peopleâs anxieties and fears stem from how life â not just the economy â is changing. âThere was no effort to really tell a story that would touch peopleâs hearts and minds, that would explain how AI would benefit their lives.â
Rattner, who led the Obama administrationâs 2009 rescue of the auto industry, said the US government shouldnât take stakes in AI companies.
âWe did not want to have stakes in the auto companies. We had to have stakes in the auto companies because they needed our money and there was no other way to do it except putting equity in,â he said. âI think itâs a slippery slope and a murky bit of business when you start doing that.â

a8851e3ed78b.text:
The CEO of a major medical AI startup said on Monday that medical students should do paper exams and master the material, even if they also use AI.
âThe risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,â OpenEvidence CEO Daniel Nadler said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. He would advise students to âtrain classically, learn classically, learn the hard way, do paper exams, do paper tests, make sure you actually know it,â he told Semaforâs Mohammed Sergie.
Nadlerâs company aims to cover a niche within the medical business, synthesizing complex medical information with AI trained on millions of medical papers. The startup has hit a $15 billion valuation on the promise that AI can condense the complexities of the medical field into information palatable to physicians.
The threat of cognitive offloading, or deskilling, is real. Early studies have found that deferring work to AI can weaken neural networks, leading to lower cognitive performance. Nadler says the concern is especially pressing for younger generations, those who have grown up in academic environments with access to AI.
He noted that all of his companyâs engineers use âdozens and dozens of AI buddies.â
Benjamine Liu, the CEO of Formation Bio, which uses AI to accelerate drug development, also noted onstage on Monday that in the pharmaceutical industry âAI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams.â
Noting that the GLP-1 drugmakers âdid more revenue than OpenAI and Anthropic combined last year,â he told Sergie that âsome people underestimate how big pharma is.â
âWeâre early innings in these things that help you live longer and healthier â and in an area that our industry sometimes misses,â Liu said.

169201a7e678.text:
Anthropicâs IPO is âgood for the ecosystemâ and âgood for us,â Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI said Monday at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World, adding that the company was unconcerned with being second.
Retail investors are ready for access to frontier models, not just hyperscalers which come with âpros and cons,â she said.
After OpenAI closed a $122 billion fundraise in March this year, Friar said that the company was closing out a smaller fundraise at a $1.25 trillion valuation. But she suggested that the latest round was unplanned and âopportunistic,â and was prompted after a âvery well-respected, well-known publicationâ¦ announced we were fundraising, which we werenât.â
âThat caused a whole bunch of inbounds from investors, and so we said, okay, if we can be super fast and in kind of a six-week period, go in and out of the market, be done by the midterms, letâs do it because why not?â Friar said.
Friar also said that OpenAIâs advertising model has been very successful, garnering more than $1 billion in revenue in under 200 days â a record for the company.
Addressing the public resentment in the US over data centers, Friar said that for companies to regain trust, âyou have to show up in those communitiesâ and âbe accountable.â
She noted that in Georgia, where the company is hoping to build a 3.2 gigawatt data center, OpenAI has sponsored school lunches, a local park, and an AI summit for small businesses. But she acknowledged that OpenAI is still seeing the backlash to the AI buildout that was evident in the US midterm elections.Â
âPeople are getting way too bombarded by kind of the rage element to not feel that thereâs something they should be reacting to,â Friar said. âBut when you go talk to people in real life, and show up for them, you have a very different conversation, and I believe a very different outcome.â

4fbc1424cef9.text:
White House cyber director Sean Cairncross said Monday that a cyberattack was not behind the Trump administrationâs nationwide ground stop of air traffic or other outages reported on Monday, attributing the problems to upgrades of old technology.
âNo, this is not any sort of coordinated, nefarious cyberattack from a malicious actor,â Cairncross told Semafor. âWhat we are seeing, and frankly Iâd expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems.â
He said the US government is tracking all recent software outages in the last few days.
Cairncross told Semafor in an earlier interview that the Trump administration has no plans to release, or require compliance with, its voluntary framework for review of new advanced AI models â adding that frontier labs have cooperated.
âThe labs have been extremely good about being in communication with us and giving their new models for evaluation to be assessed,â Cairncross said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
Putting a strict regulatory regime in place âisnât going to work at the speed that we need,â he added.
Cairncross said that the administration did not release the full text of the framework, which was set in motion by a June executive order, to enable a âfrank conversationâ with AI companies. He did say he believed the White House will soon make âit much more clear how this is working in practice.â
The White House has taken a lighter-touch regulatory approach to the AI industry compared with Europe or the Biden administration; it has also taken steps to block states from stepping in.
On the question of cybersecurity, Cairncross was bullish on AIâs defense capabilities, which were âunimaginable even a short time ago,â he said.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, appearing on stage with Cairncross, pointed out that Russiaâs hacking capabilities have improved along with AI in the last year. Michal said the countryâs ultra-wired government has been increasingly under attack, blaming private actors, as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran.
When asked whether cyber attacks could be considered acts of war, Michal said he believes some could rise to the NATO definition of âattackâ covered by the allianceâs Article 5.
âItâs mainly a question about the consequences,â he said.

ca9fdc7ec044.text:
The CEO of fuel cell maker Bloom Energy said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World that heâs not worried about rising natural gas prices or political pushback to data centers, as the economy-wide scramble for electrons marks an âarchitectural shiftâ for the grid that will favor onsite power production.
Bloom, whose gas-fueled mini power plants are used by data centers, hospitals, retailers, and other big power consumers, has faced some headwinds recently: Its share price is down 20% in the past month thanks in part to economy-wide jitters about the pace of the AI buildout, and its flagship data center project in New Mexico has been held up by permitting issues.
Still, CEO KR Sridhar said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World on Monday, âI see nothing but a huge opportunity.â Power use continues to surge across the economy, and if the price of natural gas â Bloomâs crucial input â rises because of increased demand or trade disruptions like the war in Iran, âour value proposition gets even better,â Sridhar told Semaforâs Liz Rappaport, as the technology can operate more efficiently than conventional gas turbines.
Bloom is on a steep growth trajectory: Its net profit hit $250 million in the third quarter, up from a $23 million loss in the same period last year. The company is expanding its manufacturing base, and targeting projects in the Middle East and elsewhere, Sridhar said. Though he is eyeing projects abroad, the company will continue to invest in the US. âWe should not cede this opportunity to any other country, but from our perspective, we will be happy to sell our power to neighboring countries,â he said.
âNothing is NIMBY-proof,â he said, of backlash to data centers in the US. Still, âAI happens to be a catalyst pushing everything to the right very steeply.â

383394a77aba.text:
The News
Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mimed a coin flip on Monday night when asked if heâll support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer over his insurgent opponent, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.
It was a joke â but one that also showed how Democrats are wrestling with the decision.
âLeave it to the Democrats. We flip nine seats and the person who actually helps put it together and do all that, all of a sudden thereâs a revolt,â Hickenlooper said. He quickly made clear he didnât mean that as a Schumer endorsement: âI havenât picked a position. I do think itâs useful to go and look at: How could the caucus be better?â
If the first few days of the leadership race are any indication, itâs going to be a very long two weeks for Senate Democrats. Several declined to comment on Monday night after days of celebrating their big election wins, with one senator saying Schumerâs challenge is all reporters are asking about.
But thatâs because itâs such an unusual moment for the party: The vast majority of sitting Senate Democrats have never experienced a contested leadership race for the top job. And Van Hollenâs rebel campaign isnât following crushing losses â but instead a historic victory.
âNo one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer. Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anyone else in the caucus and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge,â said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. âThe voters are also demanding change.â
Kaine, who will chair the Budget Committee next year, also declined to publicly come out for or against Schumer.
Van Hollenâs pitch for change
Van Hollen is not exactly an obvious change agent: He previously chaired the partyâs campaign arms in both the House and Senate and has been in elected office since 1991. But he is seeking to draw bright contrasts with Schumer, pushing for a prohibition in the next spending bill on offensive weapons for the Iran war and highlighting Schumerâs opposition to the Obama era Iran nuclear deal.
And while Schumer has several times the public support of Van Hollen, most of the incoming 56 Democratic Caucus members next year have declined to publicly endorse either one. Van Hollen said he knows âfor a factâ some public reporting about senatorsâ support for Schumer is not true: âSome are voting for me and others are undecided on that list.â
âPeople are still listening. Theyâre very interested in having a debate,â Van Hollen said on Monday evening. One of his supporters, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said he thinks the Maryland Democrat has a real chance to defeat Schumer. Most Democrats still see Schumer as the heavy favorite given the election results, however.
Still, a number of other longtime Democratic senators who know Schumer well are keeping their powder dry. Asked about the race, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said only that heâs âlaser-focusedâ on his agenda next year leading the Finance Committee and pushing Medicare for All, a billionaireâs income tax and repealing tariffs.
âEverybody deserves to be heard and then our caucus will make a decision,â said Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who will chair the Appropriations Committee. âI have not declared anything,â
The next leader will decide when Murray or Wydenâs legislation will come to the Senate floor over the next two years â giving them incentive to stay neutral. And many Democrats are still digesting how to handle a secret ballot election that comes after the partyâs most commanding win since Barack Obama became president.
âEvery candidate should make their pitch. And Iâll hear out any candidate for leader,â said Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who obliterated his opponent in his reelection bid. âIâm grateful to everyone for their efforts, including Leader Schumer.â
Schumer has served as Democratic leader for a decade, during which time the partyâs activist base has soured on him; heâs also the architect of multiple Democratic majorities and made the most of a 50-seat Democratic majority during the first two years of Joe Bidenâs presidency. But no leader hangs on forever: both former Democratic Leader Harry Reid and former Republican Leader Mitch McConnell lost a handful of votes in their last leadership races, before stepping down from the job.
Schumerâs given no indication he would do that, but heâs up for reelection in 2028 and has a big decision ahead of him. And Van Hollen knows it.
âThatâs a decision for him,â he said of Schumerâs 2028 plans.
Room for Disagreement
Some Democrats said itâs healthy to have this debate after more than three decades without a real contested battle for the leadership race. âWeâre not afraid to have a discussion because weâre Democrats,â Kaine said. âWe like democracy.â
âIt just comes with the territory,â said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.
Burgessâs view
Van Hollenâs leadership challenge to Schumer has made things very awkward for Senate Democrats. The contest will supercharge the debate about the partyâs agenda in 2027 as well as how they handle the lame duck. And regardless of the outcome, itâll have long term consequences for the usually tight-knit caucus.

The leaders of the worldâs most advanced AI companies are helping drive an âunnaturally negativeâ narrative around the technology, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
In an interview with MIT Technology Reviewâs Mat Honan, Arora argued that the focus on AIâs risks is overshadowing its potential benefits of the fast-moving technology.
âI find it strange that sometimes the leaders of frontier [large language models] want to come up here and talk about the dark side of AI. Every technology has a dark side,â Arora said at the event, adding that the negative narrative has âbeen driven by some of the people who should be espousing the benefits.â
Arora described AI as a âtransformational technologyâ with âthe potential of uplifting a huge amount of humanityâ and âdemocratiz[ing] intelligence.â
âA villager sitting in India or anywhere in the world will have the ability to not just read 10 websites, but have them summarized and have the best intelligence available to them,â he said.
Arora also challenged concerns that growing domestic resistance to data center construction could slow innovation, arguing that constraints on computing capacity would instead accelerate efforts to make the technology more efficient.
âScarcity breeds innovation,â Arora said. âIf you say thereâs only so many data centers that can be built, think about the amount of companies that are going to come back and say, wait, Iâve got this compression technology which makes tokens more efficient.â
But Arora also acknowledged that AIâs growing capabilities are inevitably also intensifying cybersecurity risks by making it easier to uncover vulnerabilities in software.
âAll the bad software weâve written for the last 50 years as humans, is now going to be found out,â he said, warning that as more vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited, the higher the risk of systems being forced offline as companies scramble to patch longstanding weaknesses.
âI donât think thereâs a panacea. I donât think thereâs a quick solve. I just think weâre gonna power through all of these and grind ourselves through them,â he said.
