Sisak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-appeals-to-state-and-federal-courts-to-erase-hush-money-criminal-conviction Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money criminal conviction Politics Nov 16, 2026 7:48 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court is weighing whether it can — or should — intervene in President Donald Trump's hush money case now that a New York State appellate court has heard arguments in his quest to erase the historic conviction. A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday spent more than an hour questioning Trump's lawyer and a state prosecutor about the president's latest bid to shift the case from state court to federal court, where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds. There was no immediate decision. The sides were in court for the second time in 11 days as Trump pursues a two-pronged legal strategy in an attempt to get the May 2024 verdict thrown out. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels. READ MORE: Trump loses again in bid to erase his hush money conviction Along with his federal court fight, the Republican president is also waging a traditional appeal through New York's state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule. Regardless of the outcome, Trump will forever be associated with the case, which went to trial as he was campaigning for his return to the White House. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment. Now, with little over two years left in his presidency, he is steadfast in trying to rid himself of the dubious distinction of being the first U.S. president convicted of a crime. Trump's lawyer says case could go to the Supreme Court Trump's lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., urged the 2nd Circuit judges on Monday to issue an order as soon as possible — even before writing their full decision — to take control of the case and stop the Appellate Division's deliberations. Without federal court intervention, Trump "will likely have to wait years" for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court, Giuffra said in a letter previewing his argument. But Judge John M. Walker Jr., who was appointed to the appeals court by his cousin, President George H.W. Bush, and Chief Judge Raymond J. Lohier Jr., who was appointed by President Barack Obama, weren't so sure. "How does that work?" Walker asked. "I mean, assuming we were to agree with you, there's been an argument in the Appellate Division. Briefs have been filed in the Appellate Division. Will those briefs be refiled by everybody here?" Federal law doesn't spell out precisely how such a move would play out. Giuffra suggested the case would first go to a federal district court judge, who would adopt the state court verdict, before going to the 2nd Circuit for arguments and a decision on dismissal on presidential immunity grounds. The briefs, he said, would remain the same — albeit with different covers. "You're asking us to embrace an entire procedural mechanism that I don't see anywhere authorized by Congress," Lohier said. "We think it is authorized," Giuffra said, calling a provision of the law that allows such post-verdict transfer petitions "a safety valve that's intended to protect against exactly the gamesmanship that's gone on here." A federal judge declined Trump's transfer bid 3 times Trump asked the 2nd Circuit to step in after a federal judge in August ruled against the president for a third time. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, wrote in his decision that "paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity." Trump first sought to move the case to federal court weeks after he was indicted in March 2023. He tried again after his conviction and the Supreme Court's July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can't be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can't use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal. Giuffra argued to both the state and federal appellate panels that prosecutors used the type of official acts evidence that was later barred by the Supreme Court's immunity ruling, including testimony about his Oval Office conversations, workflow and social media posts. Giuffra also took issue with the prosecution's description of the hush money payment as an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act, arguing that such allegations belong in federal court, not state court. After Trump appealed Hellerstein's second denial, the 2nd Circuit ordered the judge to reconsider, finding that he had failed to weigh "important issues relevant" to the president's request to move the case. That panel, which also included Lohier, said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties. Steven Wu, chief of the appeals division at the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, urged the 2nd Circuit panel to uphold Hellerstein's ruling and leave the case in state court. Even if Trump were to prevail, he argued, the state appeals court would still be free to rule. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 3c7fccd5ae28.text: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October. A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals. The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in. But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation. "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal. "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year." "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it. Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress. But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda. "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios. "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added. "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

AI agents are nowhere near having the âcontextâ to outperform skilled humans, Glean CEO Arvind Jain said Monday.
âWhen you deploy AI agents, and you actually point them to the right data and knowledge that they need to do their work, they still come and act more like Day 1 employees,â Jain told the editor-in-chief of The Verge, Nilay Patel, at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. âThatâs the gap that needs to close before we can come and talk about fancy things like job elimination.â
Jain, who co-founded the AI platform Glean in 2019, said ânobodyâs anywhere closeâ to building AI systems capable of replacing experienced workers. Glean, he said, is meant to bring âtacit knowledgeâ and experience with a company to its internal AI systems, to combat that âDay 1 employeeâ problem.
Despite AIâs limitations, Jain also said companies are under âenormous pressureâ to adopt it. That may be one reason, he said, for recent high-level technological disruptions, like the outages this week reported by banks and airlines.
âSometimes businesses didnât get time to actually set the right foundationâ before rolling out AI tools, Jain said.
Jain also predicted a future in which around 90% of work can be done by open-source and non-frontier AI models, though the remaining â10% of the tasks will actually still consume the majority of your AI spend.â

64d764896883.text: By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/judge-sets-march-retrial-date-for-lindsay-clancy-in-deaths-of-her-3-children Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge sets March retrial date for Lindsay Clancy in deaths of her 3 children Nation Nov 16, 2026 7:23 PM EST PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy's retrial for late March after prosecutors signaled that — at least for now — they intend to prosecute her again on first-degree murder charges in the killings of her three young children. Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed. READ MORE: Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence While the Plymouth County district attorney hasn't indicated publicly whether his office will pursue the same charges in a second trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told the judge during Monday's hearing that prosecutors were "ready to pick a jury trial date." Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he took that to mean that prosecutors intended to go ahead with a first-degree murder case, as a lesser charge would allow Clancy to waive her right to have a jury. "The die has been cast," Reddington told Judge William Sullivan. "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments." Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Sullivan set the retrial for March 29. The decision to schedule Clancy's second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy. Attorneys are scheduled to return to court Dec. 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family's Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can afflict mothers after childbirth. Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Parts of northern England and southern Scotland are set to get an early taste of winter as hill snow moves in on Tuesday.
A Met Office yellow warning for snow is valid until midday Tuesday with 5-15cm expected at some locations above 300-400m.
Major routes like the A74(M), A66 and M62 could all have problems with transport disruption.
Some railways are also likely to be affected with longer journey times for train services.
Cold health alerts are also in place, external for northern England issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
What's causing the snow?
A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. As this rain reaches northern England it will encounter a reservoir of colder and drier air.
Some of the rain will evaporate in this drier air, which will cool the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.
Eventually rain will start to turn to snow, initially over higher hills in the Pennines, moving to lower hills with time. As the precipitation moves northwards and eastwards, the snow will spread to the Cumbrian hills and into Scotland's Southern Uplands.
The snow will come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to powerlines and tree branches.
The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and powerlines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.
How long will the snow last?
Some snow may accumulate down to 100m elevation or so, with around 1-5cm possible.
Any snow will probably be quite short-lived, turning back to rain by 09:00 in most parts.
Cold outbreaks of rain will be left across northern areas of the UK through Tuesday afternoon with some hill fog and a chilly wind.
Meanwhile the south will have sunshine and blustery showers but it will also turn milder with temperatures up to 14C.
Rain and showers will continue to impact Northern Ireland, England and Wales for the next few days.
There will still be some rain in Scotland on Wednesday but then high pressure will take over with sunnier weather returning.
This drier, sunnier weather will then push southwards across most of the UK by the end of the week with cold air returning, along with some overnight frosts and a few coastal showers.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

09f5966c22f3.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Astrid Suárez, Associated Press By — Luis Andres Henao, Associated Press Luis Andres Henao, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-bids-hasta-luego-to-peru-as-he-wraps-up-marathon-south-america-trip Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope bids 'hasta luego' to Peru as he wraps up marathon South America trip World Nov 16, 2026 7:09 PM EST LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an "hasta luego," after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery. READ MORE: Pope crosses Peru in the finale of a trip home to visit flock high in Andes and deep in Amazon During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended. The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public. A trip and pontificate modeled on a missionary saint For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his "patria" or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship. "It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter," Leo said at the end of Mass as many in the crowd knelt on the dirt ground to receive his final blessing. "I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family," he said. Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo. Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous members and overseeing the translation of church teachings so they could understand. Following his example, Leo traveled across Peru to where the Catholic hierarchy rarely goes to minister to his flock, going high up in the Andes mountains and deep into the Amazon rainforest and points in between. On his final full day in Peru on Sunday, Leo went from his former diocese of Chiclayo on the north Pacific coast to the southeastern Andean city of Cusco, to the northeastern Amazonian city of Pucallpa and back to Lima on the coast. The climatic and altitude changes alone were exhausting — from hot, humid Chiclayo to chilly and rainy Cusco (at an oxygen-challenging altitude of 3,400 meters or about 11,150 feet) to the steaming heat of the Pucallpa rainforest and back to the gray humidity of Lima. It was a daylong lesson in what it means to be a shepherd. But it also served to say "So there!" to the nay-sayers, including some in the Vatican who had questioned whether Leo would have to change the course of his pontificate given his lung cancer diagnosis. On Monday, Leo proceeded with his program as planned and made clear he wasn't saying "adiós" or goodbye forever to Peru. Speaking to the crowd outside the Vatican residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip. "Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!" he said. At the home for the elderly in Callao, where Leo visited with residents, Leo bid farewell again saying "hasta pronto, hasta luego," another way of saying "see you soon." Callao Mayor César Pérez told The Associated Press that Father Roberto, as he is known to the Peruvian people, would drive approximately 12 hours from Chiclayo in northern Peru to Callao during the pandemic because he wanted to ensure the well-being of older residents. Leo delivered food and other supplies to the home but didn't enter the facility in order to protect the residents from the virus, Pérez said. A visit that was questioned but went ahead The Peru stop capped a visit that began on Nov. 6 in Uruguay and proceeded on to Argentina, the homeland of Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, who never returned during his pontificate. The trip itself was in doubt after Leo underwent lung cancer surgery Oct. 13 in Rome. But Leo said as the visit began that he had "no doubt" that he would make it. Rosa María Flores, who was attending Leo's final Mass, was glad he did. She said the most important thing about the pope's visit was that he brought faith to the people of his homeland of Peru. "We have so much crime, so many deaths; we're in great need of peace, reconciliation and faith," she said. "I know that he's pouring blessings on Peru and that things will get better for all of us." Some people at the Mass complained they couldn't hear the pope because the giant TV screens didn't work. Others begged firefighters to spray them with water to cool off, and the firefighters obliged. Paying homage to his inspiration One of the most meaningful visits for Leo was to the sanctuary of Mogrovejo in the city of Zaña in the diocese of Chiclayo. Leo revealed that he had come there the night before he was ordained a bishop to pray, so important to him was the saint who died there after falling ill during one of his own miss

9f06b1abca42.text: Three days after air travel was halted in the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11, the focus has turned to how the air traffic control network can be fixed. The Trump administration is calling for tens of billions of dollars to pay for improvements, but Democrats are questioning that price tag, saying billions have already been approved for an FAA overhaul. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: Three days after the federal government brought air travel nationwide to a standstill, attention is shifting to what it will take to fix the nation's air traffic control system. Amna Nawaz: Investigators are still digging into what went wrong, and now a funding fight is brewing. The Trump administration is calling for tens of billions of dollars to pay for air traffic control improvements. Democrats are questioning that price tag, saying billions have already been approved for an FAA overhaul. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, begins our coverage. Liz Landers: Planes are back in the skies tonight, and air travel is slowly returning to normal. Ashley Lynn Qua, Air Traveler: I'm the only one that's currently not delayed. Fingers crossed, but I got here three hours early. Liz Landers: After being ground to a halt nationwide for more than four hours last Friday, creating an entire weekend of travel headaches. Jim Clifton, Delayed Air Traveler: We wound up with cancellation, rescheduled, cancellation. Tired, ready to go home and crawl in the bed and sleep for a week. Liz Landers: The Trump administration is now pointing the finger at a government contractor that was replacing aging copper wire communication lines to fiber at a single FAA facility in Southern Arkansas. A network router, there overloaded communication systems that air traffic controllers use to guide pilots, with thousands of data pings every few seconds. That then may have led a network router in Texas to do the same. Sean Duffy, U.S. Transportation Secretary: This was a remote facility, in Arkansas, and we didn't anticipate that this could take down the system, which is why it was done during the day. Well, we're going to review all the our whole procedures on when we do this work, how we do this work, so the system doesn't go down. President Donald Trump: Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack. Liz Landers: And there's more blame being placed on outdated equipment and the age of air traffic control systems altogether. President Donald Trump: I don't take any responsibility. They did a great job, Secretary Duffy. They acted incredibly. Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt, no crashes, no nothing. And, I mean, the only responsibility should be, for 40 years, they should have done this with a system that's probably, on average, 50 years old. Liz Landers: Secretary Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion to upgrade the FAA's air traffic systems, but Democrats are demanding answers about the billions already approved to do that job. Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT): My first question would be, well, what about that other $12.5 million (sic)... Margaret Brennan, CBS News: Yes. Rep. Jim Himes: ... that's sitting in your bank account right now? How about if you spend that before we -- we put more money in that bank account? Sean Duffy: So, actually, whoever's saying that, they have to actually read the bill that gave me the money. I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s. But there's no money for that. Liz Landers: Democrats on the House Transportation Committee say most of the $12.5 billion appropriated last year still hasn't been spent. Secretary Duffy said he planned to send a breakdown to lawmakers as soon as today, detailing what his $50 billion ask would pay for. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Liz Landers.

3076f7982bab.text:
Warren Tidwell is glad the election is over.
Tidwell, a community organizer, recognizes there was a sea change on election night.
“They say it was a blue wave,” Tidwell said. “Or a blue tsunami.”
But he’s tired of the water metaphors.
For weeks, Tidwell had been working to help organize disaster relief across the rural Alabama counties that stretch atop the Florida panhandle. Because of the rains and winds of Hurricane Isaias, which hit Alabama last month, he’s seen enough water damage for a lifetime. So for him, the analogies fall flat.
And for the residents he’s been helping, the election wasn’t a political game, he said. It was a cry for help.
In Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, which includes many of the impacted counties, voters bucked state Republicans’ attempt to oust U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democratic incumbent they had drawn out of his own district earlier this year. That move came after President Donald Trump called for redistricting in red states, and the Supreme Court ruled that the Voting Rights Act does not require the creation of majority-minority congressional districts to facilitate the election of minority voters’ candidates of choice.
Figures, running in the new, heavily Republican district, outperformed all expectations, defeating his Trump-endorsed opponent, Rhett Marques, by more than 7 points. Had those new boundaries been in effect during the 2024 presidential election, Donald Trump would have beaten Kamala Harris by 15 points, 57 percent to 42 percent.
“Where is FEMA?”
On Oct. 9, Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Florida Gulf coast around 8:30 p.m. local time, cutting its way across the middle of Alabama, eventually killing nine people across three states and causing billions of dollars in damage.
On Oct. 24, all of Alabama’s congressional delegation—Republicans and Democrats— signed a letter supporting Gov. Kay Ivey’s request to Trump for a major disaster declaration for 23 counties in the southern part of the state, including much of the second district. They have received no reply.
Instead, on Oct. 27, Trump issued a major disaster declaration for the 15 Florida counties in the path of the storm. Escambia County, Florida, residents would benefit from a major disaster declaration; residents of neighboring Escambia County, Alabama, still have no word whether they will get help.
Everywhere Tidwell has travelled across the impacted counties in south Alabama, residents still struggling to meet their basic needs have asked him the same question: “Where is FEMA?”
Tidwell, who serves as executive director of the Alabama Center for Rural Organizing and Systemic Solutions, said many voters likely had that question in mind on election day. But disaster relief shouldn’t be about political affiliation, he said.
“If someone asks me who these people voted for, I’ll scream,” he said. “These people need help, not a campaign promise.”
Pastor Timothy Williams, a resident of the historically Black Shiloh community in Coffee County, said voters living in the district were already tired of high prices and low wages before the hurricane. In its wake, Williams said, neighbors have had to rely on each other, not the federal government, to recover from the storm.
“We haven’t seen much of any federal response,” Williams said. “The hurricane split light poles. It took trees. It damaged people’s roofs.”
Williams’ family evacuated to a local motel during the storm instead of hunkering down in their home, which has repeatedly faced flooding since a 2018 highway expansion.
Andrea Eckelman, a political science professor at the University of Montevallo, Alabama’s public liberal arts college, said that issues like disaster relief can compel voters to the polls for a very good reason.
“That’s the point at which it all starts to feel personal,” Eckelman said. “You may be able to explain away high prices for a while, but you can’t explain away why the family whose home has been destroyed isn’t getting help.”
Sources familiar with Ivey and Trump’s relationship told Inside Climate News that Trump’s delayed decision on a major disaster declaration for Alabama in the wake of Isaias stems from his icy relationship with the state’s governor, which began with the denial of Trump’s request to hold a political rally in 2021 onboard the U.S.S. Alabama, a battleship docked in Mobile Bay. Ivey denied any involvement in the decision to reject Trump’s request at the time.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied that Trump’s decisions regarding disaster relief are motivated by politics.
“The President responds to each request for Federal assistance under the Stafford Act with great care and consideration, ensuring American tax dollars are used appropriately and efficiently by the states to supplement—not substitute, their obligation to respond to and recover from disasters,” Bis wrote. “There is no politicization to the President’s decisions on disaster relief.”
In an interview Monday, Rep. Figures said that he hopes the president isn’t playing politics with disaster relief decisions but that he wouldn’t be surprised.
“Nothing would surprise me with this president and how petty [the White House] can be in terms of decisions they make—even decisions as basic as getting disaster relief to impacted communities,” Figures said.
Figures’ first speech on the House floor in 2025 urged federal relief for California in the wake of the state’s historic wildfires.
“I still don’t know that they’ve received adequate aid like they would have gotten under a normal presidency, Democrat or Republican,” he said.
As he fed his fussy one-year-old—his “fourth and final” child—Figures told Inside Climate News that Alabama’s congressional delegation and Gov. Ivey have done everything they can to secure a major disaster declaration.
“One would think that we’d be able to get a response quickly and go ahead and get resources down to the people who actually need it, but unfortunately that hasn’t happe

583b86906ca6.text: To discuss what went wrong to cause Friday's nationwide ground stop, and the funding fight that is brewing in Washington, Amna Nawaz sat down with aviation correspondent Miles O'Brien and congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins. Amna Nawaz: For more now, we turn to aviation correspondent Miles O'Brien and congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins. So, Miles, let's start with you. You have been reporting on this since Friday, speaking with your contacts. Help us understand more about what happened and what you make of the official explanations for what went wrong. Miles O'Brien: Amna, the whole thing is kind of stunning, that one simple router could bring down the system in the way it did. But, basically, a crew with the contractor L3Harris was installing a new router, which was part of the overall effort to put in fiber-optic cable in the system, part of the modernization effort. Evidently, that router was not configured properly, and so it sent out broadcast messages, thousands of requests for information. They call them pings, thousands every second. And it's like somebody yelling nonstop in a room and nobody else can be heard. And that's what caused the network to break down; 17 of 20 en route air traffic control centers were affected with static and potentially inaccurate information. And so, when you don't know, and when clarity means life-and-death situations, out of an abundance of caution, they issued that ground stop. But aviation, Amna, is built on redundancy. And the fact that this could happen, this one box in one place could cause this, really speaks to a much bigger systemic problem, a systems engineering problem, which needs to be addressed. Amna Nawaz: Lisa, meanwhile, you have been looking into the funding piece of this. We have heard Secretary Duffy say repeatedly it's about a lack of funding. Is that what your reporting has shown you? Lisa Desjardins: I'm waiting for responses from the administration to my questions, but based on my research and speaking with my sources, no, it this is not about congressional funding. It is true that our FAA and our system needs more funding for some things, but the modernization effort, President Trump has gotten what he's asked for. Let's look at these requests when I went back through them. In the past two years, President Trump's budgets have requested some $5.5 billion to modernize FAA facilities and engineering, including that copper wiring. Congress has funded far more than that, $14.4 billion in two different bills. And, instead, in my research, it turns out, in September, some of the holdup of this funding is from the president's own OMB, which has put a pause on $5 billion of modernization funding. It cannot be spent until next year. I did ask for comment and context on this. But it shows that there is money flowing. Something else that shows us is the map of these repairs. The FAA has this map on its Web site of all the modernization efforts going on. That certainly speaks to the fact that there is current funding flowing. Amna Nawaz: So, Lisa, the fact that Secretary Duffy is now requesting another $30 billion to $50 billion more, what would that be for? Lisa Desjardins: Right. It's the right question. And one thing I wanted to find out is, has this program to exchange fiber-optics in for the copper wire, is that fully funded? So I looked back at what the request has been. Here's what President Trump requested initially for this in his budget last year. He asked for $1 billion -- that's it -- for this transferred from copper to fiber-optics. So then the question is, Secretary Duffy, what is he talking about when he says $30 billion or $50 billion? There is a proposal in Congress for $30 billion for the FAA. That is called Modern Skies. But here's what's in it, $10 billion of it for air traffic control. Most of that, actually, though, is not for this kind of fiber-optics switch. There's another 10 billion for terminals at three airports, $10 billion more for control towers, more infrastructure. All in all, basically, this $30 billion right now is really not for this same modernization project. It's for other things that might be necessary. But Secretary Duffy at best is conflating things. Amna Nawaz: So, Miles, there's some other new concerns being raised here, referencing back to a GAO report, a Government Accountability Office report, in September that was warning these kinds of upgrades need to be paced properly. They need to be staffed properly. There was concern that the FAA plans weren't specific enough. Do we know more about that, if those concerns were ignored or overlooked here? Miles O'Brien: Not a pretty picture, Amna. And as Congress and all of us consider throwing more money at this problem, we should think about how it is currently being spent, including that box problem on Friday the 13th and how that happened. The GAO discovered a modernization campaign that has no real central strategy. There are, Amna, nearly 12,000 individual project schedules without it all being integrated together. Couple that with the fact that the FAA has had systems engineering expertise degraded steadily over the cat past decade or so. And then throw in the DOGE cuts, a couple of years ago, additional work force cuts to the technical and engineering enterprises at the FAA. If you're really serious about modernizing, why would those things be cut? So the FAA really needs to rebuild its engineering ethos, its brain trust from the inside out. Amna Nawaz: Lisa, meanwhile, you have been talking to your contacts on Capitol Hill. What's the reaction to last week's nationwide ground stop been? Lisa Desjardins: Quite a lot happening. Secretary Duffy actually has been on the phone lines. I have confirmed that he spoke to Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries tonight. He is planning to speak to all Senate Republicans at their lunch tomorrow. I know they have a lot of questions from him, especially about not just why he is blaming Congr

5530537bb35a.text: In our news wrap Monday, President Trump left for Asia, where he'll meet regional leaders, followed by talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that North Korea is providing Russia with ballistic missiles and customers at some of the country's largest banks reported difficulty accessing their accounts online. Geoff Bennett: In the day's other headlines: President Trump left for Asia today, where he will meet with regional leaders in the Philippines, followed by talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin later this week. Speaking to reporters as he left the White House this morning, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would discuss the Iran war and denuclearization. They're due to meet in the southern city of Shenzhen on Thursday for what will be their first ever trilateral summit. President Trump says he will also bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, telling reporters that he thinks Putin is softening his stance towards the war. President Donald Trump: I think he's backing down a little bit. I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly. I think he's backing down. I think he'd like to -- frankly, I think he'd like to see it finish. Geoff Bennett: Mr. Trump also said that he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un during his time in China, though no further details have been provided. Meantime, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned today that North Korea is providing Russia with ballistic missiles, and he called on Europe to boost its support in response. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President (through interpreter): Ukraine also needs clear parity so that we can respond to the Russian threat on equal terms. Geoff Bennett: During his evening address, Zelenskyy also said that Ukrainian officials spoke with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner again today on prospects for ending the war. Ukraine has scaled up its aerial attacks in recent months. Russia said today it intercepted more than 1,300 drones, making it Ukraine's biggest aerial assault of the war. The U.S. Supreme Court is declining to hear a challenge to Maryland's ban on guns in so-called sensitive places. The decision leaves in place a block on firearms in places like health care facilities, schools, and public transportation. And it comes as the justices prepare to hear a separate case on state laws banning AR-15s and other semiautomatic firearms. In another decision today, the High Court rejected the Trump administration's effort to cancel research funding at the University of California. The justices left in place a lower court ruling that the administration violated researchers' free speech rights by terminating grants over objections to diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Lindsay Clancy will be tried for a second time in the killings of her three young children, with a judge in Massachusetts setting a trial date for late March. Her first murder trial ended in a mistrial in September after a lone holdout prevented the jury from reaching a unanimous decision. Clancy has been charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her lawyers have argued she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis when she carried out the killings in 2023 and cannot be held criminally responsible. Customers at some of the country's largest banks reported difficulty accessing their accounts online today. According to the Web site Downdetector, users reported problems at Bank of America, Chase, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo, among others. The Associated Press is reporting that a technical issue at J.P. Morgan Chase was initially to blame, and that then affected other banks. In a statement, Chase says the problem is not the result of a cyberattack. The disruption follows a major outage at Microsoft last week that affected services like Teams and Outlook. In entertainment news, Robert Pattinson is trading Batman's cape for James Bond's tuxedo. The 40-year-old British actor was named as the next 0007 in a social media post, ending years of speculation over who would succeed Daniel Craig. Pattinson, who first rose to fame in the "Twilight" films, becomes the seventh actor to play Bond, adding another iconic franchise to a resume that already includes roles in "Batman," "Harry Potter," and "Dune." Filming on the next James Bond movie is expected to start next year. And British singer songwriter Raye leads the field of 2027 Grammy nominations. Raye earned 11 nominations, including for record, song, and album of the year. That ties a record for female artists set by Beyonce, who now has a staggering 100 career Grammy nominations. The classically trained Spanish singer Rosalia earned nine nominations, while Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers, and newcomer Ella Langley all tied with seven. The 2027 Grammys take place in February. On Wall Street today, stocks crumbled to start the week, as Nvidia led another sell-off in tech shares. The Dow Jones industrial average dropped more than 700 points. The Nasdaq plunged near nearly 2.5 percent. The S&P 500 fell for its third straight session. And the oldest known survivor of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor has died. Freeman Johnson was just 21 years old serving aboard the USS St. Louis when Japanese forces attacked on December 7, 1941. In an interview with the Associated Press earlier this year, Johnson recalled being below deck unaware of the attack as it unfolded. He was among some 87,000 American military personnel stationed on Oahu that day. With his passing, fewer than a dozen known survivors of the attack remain. Freeman Johnson was 106 years old.

b81275929fb9.text: United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes. Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop . What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer. "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com . Thanks for bearing with us!" The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem. United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights." "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said. About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website. United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

19c13e69f57a.text: The Trump administration announced new rules today to further restrict China’s access to advanced chips for the use of AI. It comes as questions are mounting about how the Commerce Department allowed loopholes for chip exports. The rule puts new restrictions on overseas data centers and is designed to counter possible smuggling. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Liza Tobin. Amna Nawaz: The Trump administration announced new rules today to further restrict China's access to advanced chips for the use of AI. It comes as questions are mounting about how the Commerce Department allowed loopholes for chip exports, including for the most advanced ones known as Blackwell. The rule puts new restrictions on overseas data centers so that China cannot access advanced computing power remotely. And it's designed to counter possible smuggling by putting new curbs on Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. Just before he left for his trip to China, President Trump told reporters he was not opposed to having former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company, and he was asked about the risks of their relationship. President Donald Trump: Jensen, as you know, wanted to sell to China. And the only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics, our aviation equipment. He wasn't allowed to sell them Blackwell or any of that, no. But, no, it's a different approach, just a different approach. We're heading to China. And I don't think you want to insult China just before you get there. Amna Nawaz: To help us sort through all of this, I'm joined now by Liza Tobin. She's the former China director for the National Security Council in the first Trump and Biden administrations and currently managing director at Garnaut Global. That's a geopolitical risk advisory firm. Liza, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for being with us. Liza Tobin: Thanks for having me, Amna. Amna Nawaz: So let's just look at that new rule that was issued this morning. What exactly is its practical impact? Does it close the loopholes that it's intended to? Liza Tobin: Yes, this is a really important rule, and it's a long time coming. So, as you explained at the top, the U.S. and China are in a race to lead in AI.And the key variable there is compute, or these advanced AI chips that are primarily designed by Nvidia and made at TSMC in Taiwan. And so, after the Biden administration back in 2022 and 2023 restricted the export of these chips to China directly, there -- this sort of shadow trade developed where Chinese AI developers started accessing them remotely in places like Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore. So that's essentially a gray area. It was technically legal, and there's been growing pressure from national security professionals and from the Congress to close this loophole. And the Commerce Department just this morning has put out a rule to do just that. Amna Nawaz: How do you look at this, though? Is this a matter of an administration trying to save face or is this going to have a real effect? Liza Tobin: Yes, so, clearly, President Trump is on his way to Beijing. He's been anticipating this meeting with Xi Jinping for a long time. And so he's not throwing Jensen Huang or his commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, under the bus or anything like that. But he has been clear for a number of months now that his policy is it's all right to sell China the so-called H200 chip, which is this more older generation, but still very good AI processor, but he said no Blackwells to China. Up until recently, Blackwells were Nvidia's most advanced chips. So he's been clear about that. And so for months and months, there has been this gap between what he said the policy was and what China was able to do remotely by accessing these chips kind of through the back door in these other countries. So, today, the Commerce Department closed that gap. And what's interesting is, of course, that there's kind of a disagreement playing out in public, where most of the president's Cabinet members, Secretary Bessent, the trade representative, Jamieson Greer, you had the director of national intelligence, Clayton, and many others who are all on one side clearly advising the president, you have to put out a rule. And so that's what actually happened today. And the secretary of commerce, Howard Lutnick, was kind of the lone man left out who was wanting to keep this loophole open. Amna Nawaz: Liza, can I just underscore something here in terms of what made its way to China? Because we heard the president say there that the chips that made it to China were largely obsolete, that they did not put national security at risk, essentially. Do we know that to be true? Liza Tobin: No, I think the president has probably gotten some bad briefings. We know that Jensen Huang for a long time had a lot of access to the president. He was essentially acting like the president's chief technology officer. And what he told the president last year essentially was that these H200s were kind of not that great of a chip. And it's just not the case. They actually are really good chips. They're far superior to anything that the Chinese can fabricate themselves at Huawei, at SMIC, at their chipmaking facilities in China. So even though they're not Nvidia's most cutting-edge chips, they are good chips and they are advancing China's AI ambitions. Nonetheless, that's where the president drew the line. He said, H200s OK, Blackwell chips not OK. And we know that there's a lot of evidence that there have been these shell companies like Megaspeed, the company run by this woman Alice Huang, has been facilitating the diversion of these chips, the smuggling of Blackwells and other advanced chips into China directly or into these other countries. Amna Nawaz: Alice Huang, of course, who Jensen Huang had admitted to having an affair with. Liza, you mentioned Lutnick being on the other side of other administration officials on thi

56c641a36a21.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/united-airlines-says-it-resolved-a-technology-issue-that-delayed-departing-flights Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter United Airlines says it resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights Nation Nov 16, 2026 6:36 PM EST United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop. Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. The airlines also said there was "no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue." READ MORE: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media. It resolved the issue about 1 1/2 hours after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers. United did not immediately provide details about which of the airlines systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to United's system that helps them determine a plane's final weight to ensure it can safely take off. A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking. The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 418 delayed flights late Monday afternoon. The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days. Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem. On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored. 13cc11d87de9.text: NPR’s Tamara Keith and Amy Walter of the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter join Geoff Bennett to discuss the latest political news, including President Trump's trip to Asia, his planned meetings with the leaders of China and Russia, what the summit might accomplish, Trump blaming Biden for the FAA's problems and the battle over Democratic leadership in Congress. Geoff Bennett: President Trump kicked off his trip to Asia today ahead of a planned meeting with the leaders of China and Russia later this week. But what the summit might accomplish remains unclear. And that's where we start tonight with our Politics Monday duo. That's Amy Walter of The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter and Tamara Keith of NPR. It's great to see you both. Tamara Keith: Good to be here. Geoff Bennett: So President Trump is on his way to Asia. He's seeking economic deals and nuclear talks with Russia and China. Tam, China says it's not going to participate in these denuclearization talks, and the war in Ukraine may not fully be on the agenda. So what's the president hoping to accomplish here? Tamara Keith: Yes, I mean, he likes meeting face-to-face with his fellow leaders. And he will get the image that he wants, which will be Trump and Xi and Putin all together, these three global powers. In some ways, that's all he wants. Often the president doesn't come into these meetings with a very clear agenda. He was asked repeatedly today about things. Will you bring this up? And he's: Well, I may talk to she about Nvidia. Or he wants to talk about Ukraine and Iran and denuclearization and economic issues, but it's not clear that there are any sort of deliverables or specific end goals, because so much of the way President Trump does foreign policy is about his gut and about his feeling for the leaders. And so whatever the goals of the people around the president going into these meetings, different outcomes may come out, or there may be no notable outcomes at all. Geoff Bennett: And in administrations past, if there are going to be no deliverables, you don't take the meeting, right? So, like, for President Trump, what's the political value of a summit like this? Amy Walter: I think the political value is exactly us Tam laid out, which is, it's more about the optics than almost anything else. I mean, there is something about a lame-duck president who has just lost midterm elections, not particularly popular at home, going abroad to show strength. Other presidents have done similar things, and so standing with these other leaders, showing basically, hey, I'm still the president of the United States of America, I can still do things regardless of what the actual outcome is. Geoff Bennett: Meantime, you have got President Trump. He's blaming the Biden administration for the problems plaguing the FAA. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, says the agency needs more money. Democrats have already -- they're pointing to money that was already appropriated that hasn't been spent. What's actually standing in the way of Democrats and Republicans working together to fix these issues, Tam? Tamara Keith: Democrats are not the only ones pointing out that there was a lot of money already appropriated to the FAA that isn't getting spent. Senator John Thune has also noted that. And so I think that this meeting that's going to happen, this lunch meeting with Republicans and Secretary Duffy, will be important in Duffy trying to resolve concerns and potentially move towards convincing Republicans that they should actually get on board with his requests, which ballooned from $30 billion to $50 billion basically overnight. I don't know what it will take to get them to work together. Obviously, there are millions of inconvenienced travelers who are upset who want solutions. I think that we're going to see hearings. We're going to -- that there will be a lot more investigating of exactly what happened and why the money that's been appropriated hasn't been spent in a cohesive way. Amy Walter: And I think that's the issue here too. I mean, we have talked a lot over the course of these last two years about Congress sort of being sidelined and the empowered president and executive branch. And the breakdown has also been on appropriations, right, these pocket rescissions basically saying, well, I know that Congress said we have to spend this money, but we really don't want to spend it. So there's no trust between -- even before we turn the page in 2027 to a Democratic-controlled Congress. This breakdown between Congress and the president, it actually matters in terms of not just what gets -- what members of Congress want to spend, but then whether the administration actually spends it on the things they said it should go to. Geoff Bennett: Well, as we turn the page to 2027, I can't believe it's almost upon us. Amy Walter: I almost said '28, so be careful. (LAUGHTER) Amy Walter: That's where our heads are already. Geoff Bennett: Yes. Well, we have got this battle over Senate Democratic leadership that is heating up. You have got Senator Chris Van Hollen. He's now challenging Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats, who Schumer has done that for nearly a decade. Here's Van Hollen yesterday talking with our friend over at CNN Dana Bash. SEN. CHRIS VAN HOLLEN (D-MD): This is not about one person or any one individual. This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven't fully hired the Democrats. They have given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual, not going back to the status quo. Geoff Bennett: So Van Hollen is presenting himself as the candidate of change. You have a number of progressive senators and new senators-elect who are backing him. How compelling is his argument that he represents a break from business as usual? Tamara Keith: It's a challenge for a 67-year-old career politician

Air Force bets on hybrid-electric aircraft for transport
Electra Defense’s nine-seat aircraft builds on existing development and aims to take on special operations missions.
The Air Force is pitching in nearly $5 million to help a Virginia-based aerospace company bring a 9-seat hybrid-electric airplane to flight—and to evaluate its potential use in combat.
A $4.7 million other transaction agreement contract from AFWERX will help Electra develop its EL9 prototype aircraft, building on the company’s existing EL2 two-seat prototype.
The EL9 is a small aircraft, comparable to a Cessna Caravan or Pilatus PC-12. Its size, combined with the ability to take off and land in just 150 feet, could make it good to use for special operations.
“The USAF has always been interested in what new technology can bring to the battlefield, and the new contract will let it test what an ultra-[short take off and landing] aircraft can do in service,” said Douglas Royce, senior aerospace and power systems analyst for Forecast International. “The contract isn’t a signal that the USAF is ready to acquire this type of aircraft, but the vulnerability of traditional air bases to missile attack may encourage the use of distributed operations in combat zones. Operating an ultra-STOL platform from short or improvised runways may be a part of that concept.”
“The special forces use would make sense because having a nine-passenger aircraft that can fly in and fly out of very short runways or roads would be useful for the way they operate. The more traditional transport missions would be handled by larger aircraft. But these tests may also spur other ideas once they have one in hand,” Royce said.
The Air Force’s interest in electric aircraft garnered Congressional support in the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act, which formalized the Air Force’s Agility Prime efforts to develop hybrid and electric vertical-takeoff-and-landing aircraft with commercial industry. AFWERX received $4.96 million for the “electrification of fixed wing aircraft” that year. Last week, the Air Force raised the funding ceiling of its operational testing contract with Joby Aviation, which makes autonomous eVTOL aircraft.
Under the AFWERX contract, Electra would need to verify its hybrid-electric propulsion, and conduct ground testing and acoustic flight testing of the EL9 prototype. The latter would show whether the aircraft could do “battery-only low-signature ingress and egress for special operations missions,” the company wrote in the release.
“We're starting to move into the design and development of the EL9. A lot of the work up to this point has been the development of the technology in general. So blown lift, hybrid electric propulsion, etc.,” Donn Yates, Electra Defense’s vice president and general manager, told Defense One. “Then there's what we call the operational analysis, specifically targeted at how an aircraft like the EL9 would do agile combat employment operations in contested theaters for contested logistics...We've never been asked to do that before, ever. So they're funding us to go do operational analysis.”
To do that, Electra has teamed with Lockheed Martin Skunk Works to analyze how the EL9 aircraft “would help enable contested logistics operations in the Pacific,” Yates said.
The plan is to fly the EL9 by early 2029, which then “begins the certification process” and brings the aircraft closer to flying in military exercises.
Yates also said the plane is being designed for possible uncrewed operation.
“Because we're marketing to commercial customers first, our plane is piloted. Now, the cool thing about our plane, and our company, is that it has DNA and roots in Aurora Flight Sciences, [which] was doing autonomy when autonomy wasn't cool–-and nobody wanted to talk about it—20 years ago,” Yates said.
Compared to the more traditional build of a Cessna Caravan, which uses mechanical flight controls, EL9’s design is “all digital flight controls, so you can do autonomous behaviors and fly an aircraft without a pilot much easier,” Yates said. “And so, even though we're not in an autonomy play up front, I think you'll hear some announcements in the coming months about work that we're doing…with specific customers towards making the aircraft, what we call, optionally piloted.”
Electra has completed multiple demonstrations of its two-seater aircraft to show off its blown-lift, a mechanism that allows the aircraft to generate lift at slower speeds by using electric motors to blow air over the wings, and hybrid electric propulsion technologies. The most recent one was landing the aircraft at the Downtown Skyport in New York City.
“That New York City event was massive because people started to go, ‘Oh, you could take off from barges in the Pacific or various locations.’ And they're starting to really grasp the future of what the technology could do,” Yates said.
As the company preps the EL9 for flight, it’s also writing code to “plug into simulations in war games, which I would argue is actually even more compelling than actually doing an exercise. Because that's where you're plugging into the entire contested logistics apparatus.”
That could help commanders and troops know how to use a technology, even before seeing it perform in a military exercise.
“Another reason why this contract allows us in that operational analysis piece that I talked about, the validation of using our model into these things will be significant,” Yates said.
In 2023, the company received a potentially $85 million strategic funding increase award from AFWERX, which combines government and private money, for development of a full-scale preproduction aircraft, including test flights and demonstrations of “the potential of Ultra-STOL aircraft and hybrid-electric propulsion to support runway-independent distributed military operations and mobile power generation.”
