- Published
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

b16d704e72ab.text: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

93bdc8eb0df6.text: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100 billion a year on information technology. Roughly 80% goes to keeping old systems alive. Eight of the 11 systems most in need of replacement run on dying languages like COBOL . The people who can read, write and fix them are retiring. The debt: We paid $1.052 trillion in interest last fiscal year. That's more than we spent on defense. The Congressional Budget Office sees the interest doubling to $2.1 trillion in 2036 . Every dollar of interest is a dollar that can't fix another crisis on this list. The retirement cliff: Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in 2032. Current law then cuts benefits by 22%, automatically. Medicare's hospital fund follows in 2033 . We have known those dates for decades, and they've been creeping up. Now they're just a few years away. The shriveled arsenal: Rebuilding the advanced weapons we've burned through in the Iran war will take years . Back in May, a paper from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that replacing some interceptors used heavily in the war, including Patriot and THAAD anti-missile systems, would take three years. The minerals: China controls 91% of the world's rare-earth refining capacity, giving the other superpower a chokehold on vital ingredients of AI. We're one trade war away from slowing AI and the entire economy. The bottom line: When choosing and rating leaders in harrowing times, put a premium on competence. We'll need it. Go deeper : The chain-reaction era.

6b256a6ce083.text: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Elon Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question. Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips. The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to The Wall Street Journal. In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives . Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic. Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers. In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO. After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package , shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award. Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable. The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy. But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward. Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence. The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal. OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal. Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct. "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said. Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg. The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.

e20dd7a20ce3.text: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other changes beyond changing the eligibility age. More than a dozen Senate Democrats have introduced legislation capping Medicare out-of-pocket spending at $5,000 a year. House Democrats' health care working group called for both a $5,000 out-of-pocket cap and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits within the first 100 hours of taking the House majority. Between the lines: More sweeping proposals for a single-payer system would result in a Medicare program without premiums or patient cost-sharing. It would instead fund care with taxpayer dollars. Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket. This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan. That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes. What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all. Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes. They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency. Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

8f9f0823954d.text: Look past the White House renovations , the proposed arch and the golf course : President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace. Why it matters: " Build that wall " helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished. State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029. There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10. The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data. But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms. Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention. "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands." Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there. The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border. "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would make more sense to have the wall in," Flores said. The General Land Office already reprimanded CBP and one of the border wall contractors for unauthorized construction in a cease-and-desist letter this July. Between the lines: Trump faces two main fronts of legal fights. Injunctions: More than a half dozen lawsuits are challenging the border wall in West Texas alone, building on legal fights elsewhere on the border and in Washington. Eminent domain: If local private landowner resistance continues, the federal government will also have to file individual eminent domain cases for each plot of land across the border. It has already filed some of these cases, including one against a church in New Mexico. Zoom out: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference this summer that he was planning for a physical wall from "the Pacific to the Gulf of America this time next year." CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott gave an extended deadline to the end of 2027. Based on data shared by CBP, there would need to be a rapid increase in construction tempo to make this possible. What they're saying: Flores plans to tell administration officials to ease their aggressive timeline. "Let's be a little bit more careful because you know this is gonna stand there for a long time. Let's understand those ramifications a little bit more. But that is not to say that I'm not willing to explore all legal options at my disposal to make sure I am defending the best interests of Texas," he said. The other side: Art Del Cueto, a former Border Patrol agent and adviser at the immigration restriction group FAIR, argues that the border wall needs to stick to the original plan. "Now you've heard other individuals saying, 'Well, maybe we don't need it where you have natural barriers,' and that's understandable. But when you don't build in those areas, what it's going to do is it's going to create a funnel," Del Cueto said.

The Iran war will loom over President Donald Trumpâs sitdown with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week.
A senior US official said that the president plans to discuss the ongoing conflict in the trilateral meeting, which comes as Trump has signaled dwindling interest in a peace deal with Tehran.
Last week, Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to turn away from negotiations with Iran. Earlier reports that Vance was considering face-to-face talks with an Iranian security official were incorrect, a source familiar with the situation told Semafor. Trumpâs post aimed to make clear that the administration doesnât need a meeting or a deal, the source said.
Still, the war continues to weigh on the administration and multiple sources say the US president would not be opposed to an agreement, if he views it as positive for the US; the source familiar with the situation argued that so far, Iran has not negotiated in good faith.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries starts his path to the speakership this week on smooth footing.
Heâs not expected to face any serious opposition within the Democratic Caucus â and while progressive activists have protested him, progressive lawmakers are heartened by his recent pledges to expand Medicare and take steps towards universal healthcare (just donât call it Medicare for All).

84ce1146103b.text: Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found. Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold. " There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios. "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat." The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of. Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades. Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains. State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race. Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024. The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35) and Mexican and Central American ones (D+3 to D+44). The intrigue: Outside of Tampa, democratic socialist Ashley Herrmann flipped state House District 69. Zoom in: The swing was particularly noticeable in the Cuban American core of Miami-Dade. In precincts where 75% or more of the voter base is Cuban, voters favored Nixon slightly more than they did Jolly, data show. Nixon lost Hialeah by 31 points. Demings lost it by 59 in 2022, and Mucarsel-Powell by 53 in 2024. She lost Westchester by 34 points and Tamiami by 33, down from 55 and 54 in 2022. Between the lines: Jolly outperformed Nixon statewide, but only because he had stronger support among white voters and in the most Jewish precincts of Miami-Dade, Palm Beach and Broward counties. The left-wing Nixon held her own with Hispanic voters, though the party's Hispanic statewide nominees did better. In Hispanic-majority precincts, Nixon ran slightly ahead of moderate governor nominee Jolly (losing them by 2.8 points to his 3.2) but behind attorney general nominee José Javier Rodríguez, CFO nominee Annette Taddeo and agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins. By Axios' estimates, Nixon ran about 3 points ahead of Jolly among Black and Hispanic voters and about 4 points behind him among white voters. The results could mean the anti-communist and anti-socialist attacks against Nixon resonated less this year — the result of Trump's immigration efforts, Smith said. "The sentiments are still there, but it'll be interesting to see if [the results] were a wholesale move away from the Republican Party for those who turned out to vote or a backlash against the overzealous anti-immigration efforts by the Trump administration," he said. Yes, but: The results still don't have "the full picture" of who actually voted on Election Day, Democratic strategist Steve Schale told Axios Monday. They don't show if some Cubans found Nixon or Jolly's comments appealing versus other Cubans simply not showing up to vote, he said. An Axios analysis found ballots cast in Miami-Dade precincts where most voters were born in Cuba fell 3% from 2022, while they rose 7% countywide. The bottom line: For Schale, Democrats must focus on the "gap," or what it will take to lose a Hispanic precinct by 20 points instead of 30.

Will President Trump meet Kim Jong Un?

ff99fa484e81.text: President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious. Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios. Substance aside, Western diplomats worry about the optics of Trump appearing alongside two emboldened strongmen. On Monday, Trump also floated a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?" But other topics will get attention, too, Trump went on to say. "We'll talk about Iran. We have Iran in very good shape, but we'll talk about Iran a little bit," he said. The president also said "we'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine." His comments came after U.S. officials stressed in a call with reporters on Friday that the summit would not deal with the war in Ukraine. Chinese officials said the same thing. Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine. Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat. Some of them raised concerns about what Trump might say about the war in Ukraine, the diplomat said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among the more vocal during the private session. He then went out and spoke about it publicly. "Our message to the U.S. before Trump meets Putin is: No surprises, please," Merz said. Ukrainian officials expressed similar worries. Japanese officials also privately relayed concerns to U.S. counterparts about the message the summit might project about Washington's stance on Taiwan or Asia more broadly, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. A potential public meeting between Trump and Kim Jong Un would be even more concerning for Japan. The intrigue: European diplomats said U.S. officials tried to downplay the summit and lower expectations about any substantive results. But many of the U.S. allies are nervous that the meeting will project an image of the three leaders scheming to carve up the earth into spheres of influence. Some of them invoked "Yalta II" — referring to the 1945 summit between the U.S., Great Britain and the Soviet Union that helped shape post-war Europe. State of play: On the same day Trump meets with Xi and Putin, his envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to be in Berlin with senior officials from Ukraine, Germany, France, the UK, Italy, Poland, the EU and NATO, according to two sources. The purpose is to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi the following week. On Monday, Kushner and Witkoff held a virtual meeting with the representatives of the different entities. "We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years. It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe," Kushner wrote on X. The other side: Witkoff and Kushner also spoke on Monday with Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the peace process. The White House said Putin had agreed to allow European representatives to join the negotiations with Ukraine and to launch a parallel track of talks regarding a Europe-Russia security deal. But Ushakov said no such agreement had been reached.

05e2b3bb0004.text:
Jael Samano’s recent move from Illinois to Wisconsin after college changed a lot of things in her life.
It brought a new job as an environmental consultant and a new housing situation — living on her own for the first time.
Those were expected changes. But it wasn’t until she saw her therapist, shortly before moving, that she realized how relocating out of state would also change her healthcare. She’d have to find new providers and learn a new health insurance system through her employer.
When it comes to finding mental and physical health providers, “I’ve definitely started to realize that it’s a little bit more important than I initially thought,” she said. “I feel so adult-y saying it, but it’s definitely at the top of my list right now.”
Moving to a new state can change the insurance options and even the kind of healthcare you have access to.
The QTip:
Before you move, find out what healthcare access you might gain — or lose — in your new state.
Here’s what to keep in mind before you make a move across state lines, especially if you are under 30:
Check Your Insurance Options, Including Medicaid
If you won’t have insurance through work or school, you can go to healthcare.gov to see what’s available in your new state. Moving is a “qualifying life event,” so you can sign up for a new Affordable Care Act plan even outside open enrollment season.
But keep in mind: Medicaid eligibility in particular varies by state. The government-run health coverage provides free or low-cost care to people with lower incomes or disabilities. In 40 states and Washington, D.C., Medicaid covers unmarried people making up to $22,000 a year. But in other states that haven’t expanded Medicaid under Obamacare — including Texas, Tennessee, and Florida — it is extremely hard to qualify for Medicaid if you are single and don’t have children. (KFF’s Medicaid fact sheets break it down by state.)
“Medicaid can be an important source of coverage for people in transition,” said Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of the Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. “If you need Medicaid as a source of coverage, you should not move to states that have not adopted the Affordable Care Act’s Medicaid expansion.”
Also, federal work requirements for Medicaid take effect in most states in 2027, which means that many people will have more paperwork to keep Medicaid coverage.
Staying on Mom’s or Dad’s Health Plan Can Be an Option
If you are a young adult and on a parent’s health insurance plan, you can usually keep that coverage until the end of the year in which you turn 26, no matter where you move. But if you plan on keeping insurance through a parent, you may have a limited network of providers in a new state.
A limited number of states have also extended the age limit beyond 26. In Florida, for example, if you meet certain criteria, you can stay on a parent’s health plan until age 30, but you have to remain a resident of Florida or be a student. Several states also allow you to stay on a parent’s health plan past age 26 if you have a disability.
Healthcare Access Varies, Too
The healthcare you can legally access can be different from state to state, too.
For example, 40 states allow residents to buy marijuana for medicinal purposes. (About two dozen allow it for recreational use.) Most others allow CBD usage, although Idaho and Kansas have banned marijuana in all forms, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Abortion access also varies by state. Thirteen states have banned abortion altogether; six others have cutoffs in the first trimester, according to KFF. Even if you don’t think you’ll ever choose abortion care, restrictions have kept some women from getting medical help with miscarriages.
“If you’re moving to a new state and you’re considering making this kind of change, it’s important to research and know what your options are before you get there, not once you get there and you can’t make changes,” said Alina Salganicoff, director of the Women’s Health Policy Program at KFF.
People and Policy
You might be able to see a remote provider, such as a therapist, after you move. Some states recognize providers licensed elsewhere, usually through multistate licensure compacts or telehealth registries. But in many cases, a provider has to be licensed in the state where the patient or client is located. Ask your providers before you move whether they’ll be able to keep offering care remotely.
Emily Siner at Nashville Public Radio contributed to this report.
HealthQ is a health series from reporters Cara Anthony and Blake Farmer, approachable guides to an unapproachable healthcare system. It’s a collaboration between Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

41e0514b7c41.text:
‘A Hard Time’ as Federal Cuts Hobble Efforts To Stop Overdoses From Tainted Drugs
GREENVILLE, N.C. — When the federal funding ran dry, Diannee Carden Glenn’s options were few.
Carden Glenn is the director of ekiM for Change, a volunteer-run public health organization that works to prevent overdoses in Greenville and surrounding rural communities. For much of the past decade, she relied on funding from the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to buy drug test strips, used to check for contaminants in the street-drug supply.
But in April, the federal agency sent out a “Dear Colleague” letter announcing that organizations like hers could no longer use its money to buy test strips for fentanyl, xylazine, medetomidine, or other substances that heighten the risk of overdose, particularly when the user is unaware of what they’re consuming.
Carden Glenn’s options?
“Well, I’m 81 years old, and I get Social Security,” she said, “so I use my Social Security. And I’m lucky to have a husband who can support me.” She also has other retirement income; she allocates that to ekiM’s work as well. Occasionally, she receives a donation. The federal funding was a little more than $15,000 a year.
Carden Glenn’s small organization is part of the “harm reduction” movement, which aims to help people who use drugs stay safe. Opponents argue that distributing test strips and similar supplies abets drug use and detracts from abstinence-based recovery. Proponents counter that checking street drugs for contaminants is a proven way to prevent overdoses, particularly with so many unknown drugs now in the supply. While fentanyl is ubiquitous, front-line workers are also commonly discovering that drugs sold on the streets unexpectedly contain methamphetamine and an increasing number of ultrapotent synthetic drugs, including carfentanil, medetomidine, and nitazenes.
Research has indicated that people who use test strips are more likely to engage with other harm reduction services and strategies, such as carrying naloxone and not using drugs alone.
In North Carolina, the federal agency was the state opioid response program’s exclusive funding source for fentanyl and xylazine test strips, which were then distributed to organizations across the state. These cuts are part of a more than $300 million reduction in federal funding for overdose prevention and treatment initiatives nationally.
North Carolina is among the states that permit such groups to use a variety of drug-checking tools. Carden Glenn’s organization typically hands out test strips for fentanyl, xylazine, and medetomidine. The strips can cost $1 or more apiece, depending on the type. Giving away several hundred a week adds up.
Test strips are one in a spectrum of tools that are being utilized throughout the state.
Each Friday afternoon, 100 miles west of Greenville, North Carolina Harm Reduction Coalition team members arrive at Elizabeth Street United Methodist Church near downtown Durham with a toaster-oven-sized contraption called a Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy machine. The device allows for more thorough examination than test strips, providing insight into the varied, sometimes startling contents of drugs brought in by the people who use them or by their friends, family, or advocates.
Jennifer Carroll is an associate professor of anthropology at North Carolina State University who partners with the Harm Reduction Coalition to evaluate testing results from such equipment. The university received funding from the North Carolina Collaboratory to enable this work. The utility of the technology excites her; each new drug sample presents a mystery.
Those who visit the testing site range from regular to occasional users. Often, they have no clue what might be found in a sample. “It just feels nice being able to offer this to people, and for them to have the power of having that knowledge,” Carroll said.
“We see quinine, lidocaine, tetracaine,” she said while seated behind the testing machine on a Friday afternoon in January. “We see tranquilizers like xylazine and medetomidine. We occasionally see gabapentin show up, but it’s not common. We occasionally see heroin.”
The machine isn’t perfect, she said. For example, it might miss traces of medetomidine in cocaine that a test strip would detect. So the staffers keep strips on hand.
For more comprehensive testing, the team sends samples to the Street Drug Analysis Lab at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, known more commonly as “Nab’s Lab,” in recognition of Nabarun Dasgupta, the lab’s director and recipient of a 2025 MacArthur Fellowship “genius grant.”
Dasgupta and his team use an instrument that provides more thorough analysis, offering confirmation of the chemical formula of a sample. Since the lab’s launch in 2022, they’ve detected some 500 unique substances in the drug supply. From rural Edgecombe County, for example: levamisole, a medication primarily prescribed to treat worm infestation in animals. From Asheville: the industrial chemical BTMPS, used to protect plastics from ultraviolet exposure.
Pearson Ripley with the Steady Collective, a harm reduction organization in Asheville, said keeping up with the flow of adulterants in the drug supply is probably the foremost challenge today for those doing this work. For a time, the biggest problem was the emergence of fentanyl. But people have learned to adjust to its effects, he said. Now it’s the unknown complexity of the supply.
Look at graphs charting the composition of street-drug samples, Ripley said, “and it’s just, bam, stepping up every single year in the number of substances found in a supply.”
Thus, those on the front lines say, the urgent need for easily accessible drug testing.
Carroll emphasized the critical role street-drug suppliers can play in drug-checking initiatives.

Trial by Fire: Third in a series about the impacts of wildfire litigation.
The small fire slowly licked its way through a dense growth of pine trees in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of northern New Mexico. A team of federal employees moved in tandem with the flames, dropping more fire from drip torches to clear out the small trees, deadwood, scrub and grasses that could fuel a runaway blaze in the future. Everything seemed to be going to plan.
But come afternoon, strong winds swept into the burn area. Powerful gusts carried the carefully planned fire beyond the control line intended to contain it. By 5 p.m. on April 6, 2022, the U.S. Forest Service reported the burn had escaped its control and declared it a wildfire.
The Hermit’s Peak Fire would eventually merge with another prescribed burn that had survived the winter as a “sleeper” fire in nearby Calf Canyon. In January, the Forest Service had burned piles of tree trunks and limbs left over from previous forest-thinning operations. But embers from the pile burn had smoldered beneath the winter snow and the fire reemerged in the spring.
By the time the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire finally came under control in August 2022, the once-modest prescribed burns intended to reduce the potential for megafires in New Mexico had become the largest wildfire in the state’s history.
The colossal fire swept across more than 340,000 acres and destroyed more than 900 structures in San Miguel, Mora and Taos counties. Torrential rain in the fire’s burn scar spawned a flash flood that killed three people.
More than four years later, the fire’s memory has barely faded for those who witnessed the towering walls of flame. Outrage, too, has endured. How did a government-sanctioned project go so, so wrong?
“There’s a lot of trauma,” said Brian Colón, an attorney with Singleton Schreiber who is representing victims in a lawsuit against the federal government. “People that have looked out over their acreage for years now look out and see a burn scar or worse. … They are reminded every day of that time when they had to evacuate because they saw a roaring fire coming down the hill. That doesn’t go away quickly.”
Foresters, firefighters and land managers say prescribed burns are a critical tool to not only reduce the threat of catastrophic wildfires, but also boost ecosystem resilience. Yet they also warn that a small number of those burns will inevitably escape containment. That’s concerning for prescribed fire practitioners as wildfire litigation has exploded over the past decade, with ignition alone often equaling culpability in courts—regardless of the weather, climate and fuel conditions that influenced the fire’s behaviour.
Lawsuits that have held utility companies accountable for billions of dollars, experts say, have also set a precedent for wildfires from other ignition sources.
Out of Control
Many landscapes in the American West are naturally adapted to fire. Indigenous peoples used intentional burning for millennia to manage forests, grasslands, wildlife and crops. But throughout the early 20th century, U.S. policies sought to prevent all wildfires, allowing an unprecedented amount of fuel to build up in America’s woodlands that could drive far more intense blazes than occurred historically.
By the 1960s, the federal government was beginning to recognize that carefully burning off dead trees, dry brush, leaf litter and grasses could help to control future fires—preventing the worst of the worst. The 2000 National Fire Plan and 2003 Healthy Forests Restoration Act encoded what has come to be called prescribed burning into national strategies to combat wildfires.
Since then, millions of acres have been treated with prescribed burns across the U.S. Some are handled through pile burning—bonfires of heaped-up logs and brush—and others with broadcast burning, which allows fire to travel over a defined but much broader area of still-standing vegetation.
Several studies have quantified the benefits of low-intensity prescribed fire. Recent research from Stanford University found that prescribed burns conducted from the fall of 2018 through the spring of 2020 helped to reduce wildfire severity during the severe 2020 fire season by 16 percent across the Western U.S. compared to areas left untreated. A 2023 study found that low-intensity fires, like prescribed burns, reduced the risk of a high-intensity wildfire by about 60 percent in the fire-prone forests of California.
Most prescribed burns are conducted without incident. The U.S. Forest Service conducts about 4,500 prescribed burns every year, treating an average of 1.3 million acres. More than 99.9 percent of those do not escape the planned burn area, an agency spokesperson said.
Proper procedure dictates that burns are only carried out when weather conditions—wind, humidity, fuel and soil moisture—are within safe ranges for burning and will minimize the impact of smoke on nearby communities. Fire crews and contingency plans must be in place to contain the fire and respond if it escapes.
But every now and then, things don’t go as planned.
An investigation into the New Mexico escape by the Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, found that fire managers had followed a burn plan within approved limits, but a later analysis of weather and vegetation conditions found the “prescribed fire was burning under much drier conditions than they understood.”
Prescribed fire proponents have argued that even with such escapes, prescribed burning is far less risky than doing nothing.
“The controlled risk of conducting prescribed burns under our rigorous plans is significantly lower when compared to the threat of uncontrolled wildfires,” a Forest Service spokesperson told Inside Climate News.
The challenge is the burns that best target reducing future fire losses are often located in areas near people.

2180048a87fa.text:
Almost a decade after a compromise between the Bureau of Land Management, conservationists and local governments safeguarded about 90 percent of the Roan Plateau in Western Colorado from gas drilling, those federal protections are being unraveled in the Trump administration’s push to open more public lands for resource extraction.
The Bureau of Land Management first proposed permits for oil and gas development on the plateau in 2007, spawning years of protests and lawsuits from environmental groups as well as hunters and anglers. In 2008, the BLM auctioned 55,186 acres of the iconic plateau for fossil fuel extraction, earning more than $114 million. At the time, it was the most revenue raised from a single lease sale in the contiguous United States.
But in 2012, a U.S. District Court judge in Denver ruled the agency hadn’t followed proper protocol in developing the leasing plan and ordered that it be updated after the BLM conducted additional analysis of air quality impacts and considered an alternate plan, the “Community Alternative.” After two more years of litigation, the plaintiffs and the BLM reached a settlement in 2014 that canceled all but two leases on top of the plateau.
Those protections are now in doubt. The second Trump administration’s push to increase resource extraction on public lands has reopened the possibility of development on lands that were previously protected. This December, the Bureau of Land Management will offer four parcels atop the Roan as part of the quarterly statewide lease sales mandated by 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
For Coloradans, if the hard-won safeguards on the Roan aren’t durable, what is?
“There was such broad consensus on the ground in this local community to protect this very special place,” said Chris Winter, a natural resources and environmental lawyer who runs the University of Colorado Law School’s Getches-Wilkinson Center for Natural Resources, Energy, and the Environment. “And then the administration can come in and just override that local consensus. I think that should concern everybody across the West.”
But not everybody on and around the Roan Plateau is opposed to more drilling there.
“There’s nobody out here who lives out here who wants to ruin the land,” said Wade Haerle, Executive Director of Club 20, a Western Slope advocacy organization that promotes resource development as essential for area economies. “We have been in support of leasing it as soon as practical … and we firmly believe that hunting and fishing, and oil and gas, [are all appropriate uses of] public lands, and they can coexist together.”
East/West Divide
The Roan Plateau rises 3,500 feet above the Colorado River Valley between De Beque and Rifle on Colorado’s Western Slope. It sits atop the southern margin of the Piceance Basin, one of the most heavily drilled natural gas fields in the West; the federal land at the center of the fight covers some 73,600 acres.
The western top of the plateau is privately owned and already industrialized, pockmarked with gas pads linked by dusty doubletrack roads that branch across the mesa like dendrites. On this side, the Roan is scrub-oak brown near its base with scattered stands of aspen and fir toward its rim, where the beige pads and road cuts break up the green.
The public land just to the east stands in sharp contrast, with emerald-green alpine meadows, aspen and Douglas fir giving way to Gambel oak on the lower slopes.
Mule deer and elk browse on the trees as they migrate across the plateau. In the Roan’s deep folds run streams the state has designated as “Outstanding Waters,” among them East Fork Parachute Creek, where genetically pure Colorado River cutthroat trout spawn within the boundaries of the parcels now proposed for leasing.
Giving Industry Leverage on Public Lands
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in the summer of 2025, transformed the leasing of federal open space from a discretionary process in which agencies had more leeway to balance multiple uses for public lands into a mandatory proceeding that gives industry more sway. Now, lease sales are required quarterly in each of nine producing states, and once industry nominates a parcel that a management plan leaves open to leasing, land agencies no longer have the latitude to hold it back from a sale. Each quarterly sale must offer at least half of the available nominated parcels, and nominated land must be made available within 18 months. If a sale is canceled, delayed, or deferred, the BLM must hold a replacement sale in the same fiscal year.
The Department of Interior said the bill bars the BLM from adding restrictions beyond those already included in resource management plans.
So new leases on the Roan would carry the stipulations that are baked into the management plan written in 2016, such as requiring extraction techniques with a smaller surface footprint, limiting the timing of extraction operations to protect seasonal high-traffic migration windows and controlling surface use to place any potential development under strict conditions set by the BLM. However, the original stipulations cannot be revised, even as land managers and wildlife experts say the plan is already outdated and needs to incorporate updated science and more stakeholder input.
New science, including a 2017 study documenting the negative impacts of energy development on ungulates, cannot be incorporated into new stipulations. Neither can new protections requested by land managers, such as occupancy protections that allow companies to lease and extract minerals while prohibiting surface infrastructure. Colorado Parks and Wildlife requested similar protections at Tuttle Ranch in Moffat County during a June 2026 lease sale.”The BLM only offers leases that conform to local resource management plans,” an agency spokesperson told Inside Climate News in an email.

More than Â£160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of Â£161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
'Road map for remediation'
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.
Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.
The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.
All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.
In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.
The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".
On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".
"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."
Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".
The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.
Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.
When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.
They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.
Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.
Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.
Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.
Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.
In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".
"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.
"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."
Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".
"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.
In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

The Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak on Tuesday night, giving UK sky gazers their best chance to see it this year.
The celestial spectacle runs until 30 November, but the greatest activity is expected on the night of Tuesday 17 November, into the early hours of Wednesday.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second, meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
How to spot the Leonids
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.
Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
What will the weather be like on Tuesday night?
Viewing conditions could be particularly good around the peak. The Moon will set at around 23:30 GMT on Tuesday, meaning its reflected light is less likely to spoil the view in the hours after midnight.
The best chance of seeing the Leonids will be in the far north of Scotland, including Orkney and Shetland, where cloud is expected to be well broken with only a small chance of a passing shower.
Parts of Northern Ireland, Wales, the Midlands and southern England will also have clear spells at times but there will be periods of cloudier weather and some splashes of rain.
In Northern Ireland, the Midlands and North Wales, the best chance of clear breaks will be earlier in the night.
Much of Scotland away from the far north, and northern England, will have limited opportunities. A few places may see the odd gap in the cloud but for most it will be cloudy and damp.
You can read the monthly outlook for our thoughts on the weather for the rest of the month.
You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.

Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.
They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.
Police in the Peel region of Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (Â£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.
The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.
The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.
The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".
The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.
Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.
"Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.
Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.
Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks.
"Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.
Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.
In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.
They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.
South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.
Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.
In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.
In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.
"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."
"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."
The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."
Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.
The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.
With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.
BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.
Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.
A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.
While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios
Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.
The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.
Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.
Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.
Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.
Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".
Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.
Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring
