Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.
But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.
Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.
BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.
This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.
How did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?
Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.
A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".
But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.
"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.
How does voting work in Alaska?
Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.
"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.
On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:
- Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.
- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent
There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.
As of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote.
In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.
What does ranked-choice voting data show so far?
Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".
Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.
We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.
A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.
"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."
Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright

Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.
Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.
He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.
He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.
Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".
"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.
Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.
Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.
Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".
Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.
The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage, a network failure that grounded all US flights, and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".
Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.
Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.
Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".
The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.
The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.
Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.
Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.
US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.
Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.
Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.
As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.
Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".
That issue resolved within a few hours.
The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.
The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.
The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.
On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.
The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.
Additional reporting by Max Matza.

As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.
"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.
One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.
"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.
Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.
"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.
Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.
Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.
Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.
Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.
It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.
Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.
The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.
"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.
As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.
"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."
Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.
She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.
- Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, external
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.
The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.
One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.
He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.
The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.
Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.
But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.
The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.
In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.
Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been doneâ¦ I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".
She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.
She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".
In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".
Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.
They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.
Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.
"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.
With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; Â£500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.
That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.
'We've saved thousands'
They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with â Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.
In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.
The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.
Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".
While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.
Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.
It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.
It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".
"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."
Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.
While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.
"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.
Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.
'We have house meetings'
Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.
While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.
She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."
They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.
"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.
In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.
For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.
Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.
Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.
"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.
The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".
British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.
Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.
He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.
Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."
But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.
And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.
It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.
"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.
"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

21729ee21b74.text: Donald Trump Jr. signaled that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem in an interview during Axios' annual BFD summit in New York. Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it is not reinstating ousted founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Collette Kress said Nvidia's "roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater".
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (Â£86.9bn), with shares in the company recovering some recent losses in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday Huang, said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a possible spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones told investors on Tuesday.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worry that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

d638519e93ce.text: Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation. Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit. Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier. S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion. The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion. The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke. The stock was up 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday. It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history. She didn't mention Huang on Tuesday in the earnings report but touted Nvidia's role as "an exceptional technology leader" and said sales of the company's new, advanced Vera Rubin chips are "off to an explosive start." "Our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater," she said. What we're watching: Whether Nvidia discloses any additional details about its CEO search or other investigations on its earnings call. WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Huang posted a public letter Tuesday saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO. Newly appointed Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on Tuesday afternoon's earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation "and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders. What's next: Tech analyst Gene Munster said on X that the Nvidia earnings call Tuesday is "the most anticipated conference call of all time, and the one we'll likely get the least information from." Editor's note: This story was updated to include comments from Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones made on the company's earnings call.

0f76514fda6d.text: By — Maria Ramirez Uribe Maria Ramirez Uribe Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/can-the-u-s-regain-its-measles-elimination-status-heres-what-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Can the U.S. regain its measles elimination status? Here's what to know Health Nov 17, 2026 4:44 PM EST The U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status for the first time in 26 years, an international health organization determined Tuesday. With more than 5,400 cases and six deaths reported in 2026 so far, the status loss is an indication that measles spread in the U.S. is now considered endemic. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. When measles is considered "eliminated" in a country, that doesn't mean there are zero measles cases. It measures whether there are large outbreaks or continuous transmission for 12 months or more. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 43 outbreaks, which it defines as three or more related cases, this year. WATCH: What's behind the growing measles outbreak and how the Trump administration is responding "For most citizens of the United States, the loss of that formal status probably doesn't have much meaning," said William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins University. "What is much more important for citizens of the United States is that there are a lot of measles, so people are at risk of acquiring measles." Aubree Gordon, an infectious disease epidemiologist at the University of Michigan, agreed. Beyond the loss of the designation itself, "we are losing ground against a disease that we know how to prevent," she said. "While the loss of elimination status has no formal penalties, it represents a reversal of decades of public health progress." Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Measles in the U.S. was first declared eliminated in 2000 by an independent commission of experts from the Pan American Health Organization, PAHO, when the country recorded 85 cases. The major public health accomplishment was "made possible by widespread vaccination," Gordon said. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, or MMR vaccine, are 97% effective at preventing measles, according to the CDC. PAHO met from Nov. 10 to 13 to vote on the United States' and other countries' statuses. Bolivia and Mexico also lost their measles elimination status on Tuesday. Canada lost its measles status last year, as part of a 2025 review that found the Americas had lost its status. "This marks a historic setback for the Americas, which had previously been the first region in the world to eliminate measles twice," the group's report said. The loss of the elimination status for the U.S. doesn't come as a surprise. Measles cases have been rising since 2025 as vaccination rates among kindergarteners have dropped while non-medical vaccine exemptions have risen. WATCH: 'It's close to bulletproof,' doctor says of MMR vaccine as measles cases rise "This is a natural consequence of being unable to mount an effective response to growing misinformation and disinformation related to the MMR and other vaccines," said Amira Roess, professor of global health and epidemiology at George Mason University. Here's what to know about the measles and the United States' elimination status. What is measles and how can you prevent it? The measles is a preventable, highly contagious virus that spreads through the air. It can cause a fever, rash, dry cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. For many people, the disease will last about 10 days and doesn't cause further problems. But for people who are unvaccinated, including infants and people whose immune systems are weakened, the disease can be serious. Some people can develop pneumonia and encephalitis, which can lead to death. READ MORE: Babies too young for MMR vaccine become 'sitting ducks' in measles outbreaks The virus can also damage the immune system's memory of previous infections, Gordon said. This can leave "people more susceptible to other illnesses for months to years after they recover from measles." People who are pregnant are also at high risk, and they can pass the virus on to their baby. A preliminary analysis published in The New England Journal of Medicine Evidence found that from Jan. 1, 2025, to Sept. 28, 2026, there were 112 confirmed cases of measles during pregnancy, and 13 cases of congenital measles — when the disease is passed to the child during pregnancy. WATCH: Pennsylvania doctor urges vaccination as measles outbreak grows The best way to prevent measles is through vaccination, according to the CDC. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. People should pay attention to public health alerts about measles cases, particularly if they are immunocompromised or care for someone who is, Roess said. Those who think they may have measles should contact their doctor before going into a healthcare facility to prevent exposing others, Gordon said. Why did the U.S. lose its elimination status? Fewer people being vaccinated is at the core of the increase in measles cases in the U.S., experts told PBS News. "Measles is extraordinarily contagious, so even relatively small gaps in population immunity can allow substantial outbreaks," Gordon said. WATCH: Measles cases surged in 2025 as vaccination rates dropped Moss compared measles outbreaks to wildfires. When a forest fire starts, it produces sparks that land outside of the area where the fire started. In measles cases, the sparks are people who are infected. In places with a high coverage of vaccinated people, the sparks are unlikely to lead to an outbreak. But if people who have measles are in or travel to an area that doesn't have enough vaccinated people, it is likely to spread quickly. READ MORE: A p

b5539ed45aa7.text: By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/ex-ceo-jensen-huang-signals-interest-in-returning-to-nvidia-after-resigning-amid-scandal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ex-CEO Jensen Huang signals interest in returning to Nvidia after resigning amid scandal Economy Nov 17, 2026 4:40 PM EST Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signaled interest Tuesday in returning to lead the computer chip company in his first public statement since he resigned last week following revelations of an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. READ MORE: Trump backs campaign to reinstate Huang as CEO of Nvidia Some tech industry figures, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, have called for the reinstatement of Huang, a high-profile booster for the artificial intelligence industry who oversaw Nvidia's development as the key provider of chips driving advanced AI models. President Donald Trump, a Huang ally who has spoken with him frequently, has also endorsed the comeback bid. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in a social media post. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Huang acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life but said that he's received an "outpouring" of support from employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Huang's statement. On Monday, a person familiar with the board's thinking who insisted on anonymity to discuss it told The Associated Press that the board was not currently considering Huang's return. READ MORE: The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit The Santa Clara, California-based company was scheduled to release quarterly earnings later Tuesday. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is expected to speak with Wall Street analysts on the earnings call for the first time since being named interim CEO. A petition drive seeks Huang's return A "Stand with Jensen" petition set up last week has gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters. The petition calls on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeds or until there's "compelling evidence" that his departure is in the company's best interests. "We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," the organizers said in an open letter. "We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy." WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips Trump suggested Monday that the ex-CEO could return, saying Huang "learned a big lesson" and that he "would certainly not mind" if he was reinstated. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia, apparently ousted by the board after revelations that he had extramarital affairs, both with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being an intelligence asset for Beijing and with a senior executive who reported to him. The businesswoman Huang was seeing who reportedly had links to Chinese intelligence was an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International, a company being investigated by the U.S. for allegedly violating U.S. export controls by illegally diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Chinese companies. Huang faces questioning by Congress Also Tuesday, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips. Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2. "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight of China and intelligence issues. "The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the lawmakers said, referring to the People's Republic of China. Meanwhile, Nvidia said it's creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following the revelations about Huang. Nvidia's advanced chips are in high demand because they're essential for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China. Trump said it was "good" that Nvidia had created the new oversight committee. "Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," Trump said shortly after arriving Tuesday evening in the Philippine capital of Manila, where he participated in a photo opportunity with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea." Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Kevin Freking in Washington and Josh Boak in Shenzhen, China, contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Price, Associated Press By — Jim Gomez, Associated Press Jim Gomez, Associated Press By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/trump-arrives-in-philippines-to-kick-off-asia-trip-with-economic-deals-and-talks-with-allies Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip with economic deals and talks with allies World Nov 17, 2026 4:23 PM EST MANILA, Philippines (AP) — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he met with regional partners, sought to formalize a trade deal and get a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry. Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un. READ MORE: Trump's Asia reset: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, then a rare nuclear summit with Xi and Putin The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News But Trump could not escape all the controversies still swirling in the U.S. Reporters asked him about the recent service outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and online banking with JPMorgan Chase. The president played down the problems that caused mass flight cancellations and disrupted workdays. "It's life," Trump said. "When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine." The president was also asked about a CNN report that Iran was putting together plans to attack Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapons. "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said, adding, "I hope it's not. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy." Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit Trump's first hours in the Philippines included all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, such as a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals. After landing in Manila, Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan, that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific, for the first time since he returned to the White House last year. "We're all friends," Trump said. "It's a lot easier that way." The president announced that the Quad would conduct an exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft and launch an accelerator to speed the development of artificial intelligence. Trump signed a trade statement with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats. The president said that he was looking forward "to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks." The joint statement included details that were posted more than a year ago by the U.S. government. Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing American autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs. Trump said Tuesday that Thailand would buy $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products. As part of the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump participated in what was billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders. They finalized a set of principles to tackle online scams, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said. Leaders at the dinner were also expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety. Washington has rejected China's expansive claim to the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack. Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S. They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby. "The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press. Nearly 23,000 police personnel and other law enforcers, including SWAT teams, were deployed to secure the ASEAN summit. fe9baa296284.text: By — Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/the-long-wait-is-almost-over-heres-what-to-know-about-the-upcoming-release-of-grand-theft-auto-vi Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The long wait is almost over. Here's what to know about the upcoming release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Arts Nov 17, 2026 4:22 PM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — "Grand Theft Auto" has never been much for following the rules. Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment. READ MORE: Grand Theft Auto maker buys FarmVille company in $12.7 billion deal Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, "Grand Theft Auto VI" is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Nov. 19 with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists. For longtime fans, "GTA VI" is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here's what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release. Why is 'Grand Theft Auto' such a big deal? The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes. The release of "Grand Theft Auto III" in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings. Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars. Ubisoft's Assassin's Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo's "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild" later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems. For "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas" and "Grand Theft Auto V," Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences. That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women. But controversy did not stop the franchise's commercial rise. According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Its online multiplayer component, "Grand Theft Auto Online," has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases. When can players start playing 'GTA VI'? "Grand Theft Auto VI" will become playable at midnight local time on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, according to Rockstar Games. That means players can begin playing at 12 a.m. in their respective time zones. In the United States, the game unlocks at midnight Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific time as Nov. 19 begins in each region. READ MORE: From Golden Retrievers to 'Grand Theft Auto' -- 10 exports you didn't know were Scottish Players who preordered the game digitally can already preload it, allowing the game files to be downloaded before launch. Preloading does not provide early access. How closely is Vice City based on Miami? "Grand Theft Auto VI" returns players to Vice City, Rockstar Games' fictional version of Miami and South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area's history and architecture. Rockstar has promised its largest and most detailed open-world experience yet. A woman poses for a photo while sitting on a "Vice Beach" sign ahead of the release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI in Miami Beach, Florida, Nov. 16, 2026. Photo by Eva Marie Uzcategui/ Reuters Miami is also leaning into its fictional alter ego ahead of the release. Miami-Dade County struck a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant "Welcome to Vice City" display atop the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center, while Miami and Miami Beach have launched their own promotions tied to the game. The Heat will also wear black-and-pink "Vice City" jerseys on the eve of the release. Not everyone has embraced the connection. Some South Florida officials have criticized using public resources to promote a franchise known for crime and violence, while supporters argue the campaign allows the region to capitalize on the enormous attention surrounding the game. What's the story behind 'Grand Theft Auto VI'? This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar's fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises. At the center are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path. Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida

8082b8e3489a.text: The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed. The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections. The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition. The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers. Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause. What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement . "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them." Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so. "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed." They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned. The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23. The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands. "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said. By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter. Just 69 are operational. Go deeper: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

Sens. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., and Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., are introducing a new, far-reaching hemp regulatory bill that could smooth over a major point of contention in the government funding negotiations, according to details shared first with Semafor.
The bipartisan proposal would bar sales of consumable hemp products to people under 21, ban âgas stationâ marijuana products derived from hemp and copycat advertising for those products, and also restrict synthetic cannabis products from China.
The bill would also require hemp products be produced in the US, preserve access to CBD products, and empower the FDA to inspect hemp facilities. The timing of the compromise is crucial: A new federal definition of hemp goes into effect on Dec. 11 â the same day as the government funding deadline â and without action could upend the industry in the US.
Internal Republican disagreements over the issue complicated the last funding bill. Sheehy has made solving the hemp issue within his party a major priority; heâs holding a hemp roundtable on Tuesday afternoon with veterans to discuss the issue.
In a statement, the Montana Republican said the compromise with Klobuchar will put âevery bad actor in the hemp space out of business and keep intoxicating [productsout of the hands of children,â while shielding farmers, cancer patients, and veterans from criminal penalties.
Klobuchar, who will leave the Senate in January after being elected governor of Minnesota, touted her stateâs hemp industry and warned that the âlooming federal ban on hemp products is threatening farmers, brewers, small businesses, and consumers across Minnesota and the country.â
A coalition of veterans groups is also asking congressional leaders to support the bill, according to a letter shared with Semafor. Republican Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., is a leading opponent of delaying the new hemp definition deadline and is gearing up for another push ahead of the December funding deadline. Sheehy and Klobucharâs bill would go into effect on Dec. 11 if passed.

Data center builders must adapt to AI pushback, SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang said on Tuesday at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach âdisrupts the communities less,â he told Semaforâs Liz Rappaport.
AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria.
Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be âmuch more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,â Liang said. Still, he said, itâs good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now.
âTo distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem â itâs not a bad way to do it,â he said.
Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that âcompute constraintâ in the near term is a real possibility.

Europe must enact more innovation-friendly regulation if it wants to compete in the AI race, Germanyâs director-general for digital policy and economic affairs at the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization said Tuesday.
There are âa lot of things we need to do to catch up in the race,â Marco-Alexander Breit said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World. âOne of these is actually having a more innovation-friendly regulatory framework, especially in Brussels.â Germany also needs to âstep upâ its capacities and capabilities, he told Semaforâs Mohammed Sergie, adding that the country hopes to quadruple its data center capacity by 2030.
Steve Jurvetson, managing director and founder of Future Ventures, who joined Breit on stage, went further, saying Europe is âtrapped in a sort of regulatory doom loopâ that smothers innovation. Jurvetson said âregulation is the elephant in the roomâ that âis stifling European innovation at every step of the way.â
While Breit pushed back, saying, âitâs not all doom and gloom in Europe,â he acknowledged that red tape and regulation needed to be cut, arguing that change would ensure European AI leaders âdonât need to leave Europe to work on AI and change the world and make a lot of money.â
Breit said he agreed with the vast majority of the EU AI Act, for example, but continued on to say that âit actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world,â he said. âSo it actually hurts our economy, even more than people maybe think in Silicon Valley that it hurts the US companies.â
Speaking earlier at Silicon Valley & The World, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak also criticized the EU AI Act, saying âtrying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.â Still, Sunak said he supports some regulation, because despite being bullish on new AI technologies, âthey bring new risks with them.â

A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.
Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.
Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".
"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.
"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."
In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.
But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.
Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
