River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.
River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital".
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.
River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.
"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved last year.
"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."
An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

7cd52d71e1a9.text: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else. Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone. "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change. A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut. Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News . If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime. The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress. Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared. But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy. "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey. State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities. A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather. Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer. Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year. Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick: An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity. A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood. Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring. And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change . Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed. By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly. Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place. Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems. How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police. This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data. Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments. Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab. Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification. Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts. The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035. Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic. In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises. Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said. Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year. Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders

79c92c5d8e8b.text: Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week. Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen. Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking. To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have just as much to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as they do with slop software. Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented. Driving the news: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday. United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages. Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones. Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks. United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment. Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking. Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed. That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say. AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible. What they're saying : Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios. "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says. "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology." "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right." By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios. However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five. The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame. "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI." Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked. That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover. The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected. When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns. Go deeper: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool

277427ad45b6.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press By — Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/400-largest-u-s-data-centers-produced-more-carbon-dioxide-in-a-year-than-denmark-study-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 400 largest U.S. data centers produced more carbon dioxide in a year than Denmark, study finds Nation Nov 17, 2026 3:31 PM EST The 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday. READ MORE: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead Meanwhile, negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary pledge Monday for companies and countries to power the world's data centers with clean energy and be more open about their power and water consumption and emissions. "We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse." The pledge also calls for focusing the power of artificial intelligence on solving the so-far intractable problem of climate change and reflects burgeoning concerns about AI's ever-expanding environmental footprint. The political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites. The explosion of new and planned data centers also has prompted a push for new sources of power generation that has the biggest tech companies failing to reach their climate goals, with their electricity consumption rising 240% between 2022 and 2025, according to a new report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation. Study quantifies how much big data centers pollute Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centers between May 2024 and April 2025 using available data and modeling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity use by the centers produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to a study in Monday's Nature Sustainability. More than half their 82 terawatt hours of electricity use — enough to power nearly 7 million homes for a year — came from fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found. The emissions estimate is two to three times what previous studies had shown, said study senior author Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor. "It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country," Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centers make that quantity more worrisome for the future. "We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions." Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday's study made sense and reached realistic conclusions, finding the use of modeling reasonable because companies aren't open about power consumption and pollution. "We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure," said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn't part of the study. "Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centers, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity." A voluntary pledge proposed at climate talks The "Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge," launched by U.N. climate talks host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centers should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems. The pledge also calls for AI systems to be designed and managed responsibly, using environmental standards and reusing or recycling infrastructure and hardware. It says the environmental impacts of data centers should be assessed and shared and signatories should support using artificial intelligence as a climate solution. COP31 President Murat Kurum has said world leaders at the talks must openly discuss AI's growing energy consumption and start setting the terms. AI produces pollution but also offers hope One of the biggest climate fighters, former U.S. Vice President Al Gore, said while it is essential that data centers are powered by carbon-free energy, he is less concerned about the emissions from AI than others. And he is hopeful that its computing power can find novel ways of fighting climate change. READ MORE: To make AI morally good, tech companies are turning to religion. But some experts say it isn't that simple In an Associated Press interview, Gore quoted a study by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern who predicted by 2030 "we will see 6 to 9% reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy." Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association said, "AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centers face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centers, but the fears may be overblown." But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical. US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.
A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.
Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with US partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese.
"Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said.
"We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added.
Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components.
The US is hoping to draw more countries here into its "Pax Silica" tech and AI ecosystem, and away from China.
But China's huge influence in this region cannot easily be challenged, and certainly not in the few hours Trump is in the Philippines.
Later on Tuesday, Trump signed a trade deal with Thailand alongside the country's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year.
Trump then joined South East Asia leaders at a dinner, telling those gathered: "This is one of the world's most vibrant and productive regions filled with the tremendous potential."
After an overnight stay in Manila, the US president will fly to Shenzhen in China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Asked if he would also be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, Trump said: "If it's available, I would".

13feb81f079f.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/van-hollens-bid-to-replace-schumer-puts-pressure-on-democrats-to-take-sides Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Van Hollen's bid to replace Schumer puts pressure on Democrats to take sides Politics Nov 17, 2026 2:52 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats elect their leader every two years behind closed doors and on a secret ballot. But this year's race has burst into the public eye as Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen mounts an insurgent bid against New York incumbent Chuck Schumer. The Dec. 1 contest has put Senate Democrats on edge and has forced what could become an ugly fight immediately after major victories in the midterm elections. It has also put the more moderate incoming Democrats in a tough spot, forced to take sides in a leadership race before they are even sworn into office. Schumer, who recruited several of those moderate Democrats who helped win the majority, has said he has the votes to be reelected, and around 15 of the 55 elected Democrats in next year's caucus have said publicly that they will support him. Four Democratic senators have said they will support Van Hollen. Everyone else is staying quiet for now. "Leave it to the Democrats," said Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper, who flipped an imaginary coin when asked by reporters on Monday how he will vote. "We flipped nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that, and all of a sudden, there's a revolt." Van Hollen, who is backed by progressive groups, says it's time for new leadership after Schumer's nearly decade-long tenure. While the two men align on most issues, Van Hollen says Democrats need to more aggressively push to end the Iran war and potentially even shut down the government next month, if necessary, to stop the flow of war funding. "To deliver, we need new leadership," Van Hollen says. "This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call." Van Hollen is making his argument to the public as Schumer mostly keeps quiet and holds private conversations with the senators who will decide his fate. Schumer shared his agenda for the next Congress in a caucus luncheon last week, laying out a plan to try to quickly pass legislation on healthcare and tariffs and to launch multiple investigations into President Donald Trump's Republican administration. "I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said in a statement. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people." A public campaign for an insider's job The unusually public race — the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades — comes when Schumer has drawn intense criticism from the party's base. Some voters and progressive groups called for his removal in 2025 after he voted with Republicans to keep the government open and as they called for stronger opposition to Israel's war in Gaza. Still, many in the caucus see the role not as a national figurehead but as an inside operator who can navigate intraparty politics and the 100-member Senate's arcane rules to pass legislation they like and block legislation they don't. "I want to hear from any candidate what their vision is for the floor and managing the caucus," said Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was just reelected. He said he hasn't committed to either Schumer or Van Hollen. Party leaders also spend much of their time fundraising and recruiting candidates — a particular interest for Schumer, who has been directly or indirectly in charge of the Senate Democrats' campaign arm for two decades. Most Democrats don't want to reveal their vote Returning to Washington on Monday for the first time since Van Hollen entered the race, most Democrats would not answer questions about who they would support. That included prominent progressives like Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin appeared last week at a press conference with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, as he declared that he would not support Schumer. Two days later, Sanders immediately endorsed Van Hollen when he entered the race, but Slotkin has not. "I'm not saying anything," she told reporters on Monday. WATCH: Does Van Hollen have enough support to beat Schumer in Senate leadership race? Others like Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine defended Schumer while saying that they are still open to Van Hollen or someone else. "Chuck delivered an amazing win," said Kaine. "Chuck knows Trump, and that will be really, really important going forward." Still, Kaine said, "The voters are demanding change, so we have to figure that out as a caucus, and we're going to be able to. We're not afraid to have a discussion." Freshmen put on the spot The eight incoming freshmen Democratic senators — nine if Mary Peltola wins the Alaska Senate race, which has still not been called — are set to alter the caucus next year. But only two have said how they will vote in the leadership election. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, both of whom were backed by progressive groups in their campaigns, say they support Van Hollen. Schumer supported both of their opponents in their primaries, though he eventually put $67 million into El-Sayed's competitive race. El-Sayed said Tuesday that he likes Schumer and will work alongside him if he wins. But he said he thinks Van Hollen is the best person to take on affordability challenges and liberal priorities like Medicare for All. 42a4cea607c7.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/the-symbol-of-the-occupation-ukraine-destroys-span-of-kerch-bridge-linking-russia-with-crimea Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'The symbol of the occupation': Ukraine destroys span of Kerch Bridge linking Russia with Crimea World Nov 17, 2026 2:40 PM EST KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the vital Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, calling it an "unprecedented" operation as Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day. Zelenskyy portrayed the bridge operation as a masterstroke following a weekslong effort by Ukrainian forces to gradually wear down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with a barrage of missiles and drones overnight. Zelenskyy didn't detail the damage, but the Ukrainian General Staff said that an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but with a damaged arch. Russia's Investigative Committee, the nation's top criminal investigation agency, said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage but didn't elaborate. The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and for supporting troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory to Ukrainians. "The symbol of the occupation has cracked," the Ukrainian General Staff said in a statement. Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people. A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week. Missiles delivered the final blow in the 7-stage operation The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media. Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said. Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Precision-guided Flamingo missiles delivered the final blow, he said. READ MORE: Ukraine's drone chief says push to cripple Russia in Crimea is just getting started Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military published videos showing what they said were the attacks and subsequent damage to the bridge, with part of the deck in the water and a fallen arch. The Associated Press wasn't able to verify the images. The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic across the bridge was halted but rail traffic was restored by Tuesday afternoon. He didn't mention any damage. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that "there is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before." Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day. There were significant power outages Tuesday in three Ukrainian regions, he said. "We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said. U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels with Ukraine's Western backers, said the Kerch Bridge strike was "another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine's absolute determination to defend itself against Russian aggression." The United Kingdom announced £240 million ($317 million) in air defense support for Ukraine this winter, including more than 1,000 short-range missiles and more than a dozen radars. Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday. That was a day after Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war. Ukraine also attacks industrial areas deep inside Russia Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the southern Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones in the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, officials said. 5df7d8f5f45d.text: President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats. The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption. Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it." "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added . Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not." Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack. Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C. CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless." Read more about dirty bombs below. What is a dirty bomb? How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says. How dangerous is a dirty bomb? The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission . The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled. "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says. The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC. Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast. What would happen if one exploded in Washington? Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats. The Department of Homeland Security 's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors. DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks. The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials. Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site. The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off. Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says. Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says. Has a dirty bomb ever been used? No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports , though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts. The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia. In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice . The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized. The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

b5a29fbebacd.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/faa-stops-installation-of-routers-it-linked-to-national-ground-stop Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FAA stops installation of routers it linked to national ground stop Nation Updated on Nov 17, 2026 2:54 PM EST — Published on Nov 17, 2026 2:22 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Aviation Administration has paused installing routers linked to last week's ground stop that caused chaos for travelers, the agency said Tuesday. The move comes amid growing scrutiny over the nation's air traffic control system and as the Trump administration is making a new request for $50 billion to improve air travel. Democrats in the Senate are demanding that the administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for the nationwide grounding of all planes and upheaval at the nation's airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration. FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas. The FAA has said that another router installed three weeks earlier in Amarillo, Texas, also went haywire. The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA's telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation. The ground stop was needed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, after the new router that L3Harris installed in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. The FAA said that "excessive data" was flooding the system "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds." That deluge created instability with "aircraft communications and radar feeds," the agency said. For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday's trouble. READ MORE: Debunking social media posts that claim a 90-day blackout will start Nov. 17 The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris. A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, told ABC News that the company believes the routers were working properly when the ground stop occurred. The company did not immediately respond to inquiries from The Associated Press. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly," the company said in its statement. Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee said they believe that only 400 out of more than 3,600 new routers have been installed. "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues," the Democrats said in a letter sent to Duffy. Upgrading the nation's air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. The problems with aging equipment at the FAA date back decades and past efforts to modernize the system have come up short. Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades, saying again Monday that much more is needed. The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers outlining its request for $50.1 billion to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports. The request calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation's air traffic control system. Similar amounts would go toward boosting airport infrastructure, replacing or refurbishing terminals at high-impact hubs, constructing five new traffic control centers and improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers. "Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient," states the letter, which was obtained by The Associated Press. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize much of the key infrastructure that more than 45,000 flights a day rely on to reach their destinations safely. The funds were earmarked for replacing outdated technologies such as copper wires, floppy discs and radars built in the 1980s, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction projects. The rest of the world is looking at the AI arms race between the US and China with âsome kind of alarm,â the UNâs top tech envoy said Tuesday.
Other countries âdonât want their agency taken away with this attention just on this competition between two players,â Amandeep Singh Gill, the Under-Secretary-General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies of the United Nations, said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
âThe rest of the world wants to build up its own models, its own infrastructure.â
Gill told Semaforâs Mohammed Sergie that while other countries are not trying to compete with frontier labs in the US and China, they still want to innovate.
âSo this also translates to some alarm in terms of guardrails, because if you have a race, then you tend to ignore the rules,â Gill said, adding that recent incidents around AI safety have sparked concerns among several countries that âshortcuts are being taken.â
Building out Africaâs AI infrastructure
Gill also emphasized the importance of addressing Africaâs AI shortfall, saying more capacity needs to be built to bridge the AI divide and guarantee the continent access to emerging technologies.
Gill said a country like Ethiopia, with a population above 130 million, needs significantly more GPUs. âYou need a massive infusion of capacity, but capacity alone is not enough,â he added. Connectivity and energy availability are necessary, too.
Investing in African AI would be âcreating a market,â Gill said, and could improve AIâs reputation by showing how it can be used to improve water scarcity, public health, and public services issues.
âItâs easy to say AI will solve cancer, but if you can point to these useful applications that work at societal scale, then it reinforces the case on the beneficial side of AI,â Gill added.

32339ed383a9.text: By — Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Rebecca Santana, Associated Press By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/mullin-defends-use-of-government-plane-to-attend-football-game-after-ground-stop Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mullin defends use of government plane to attend football game after ground stop Nation Updated on Nov 17, 2026 2:42 PM EST — Published on Nov 17, 2026 2:07 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop that caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country. Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the game a day after all planes were grounded. Mullin's flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as flights were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options. Mullin's flight comes as the ground stop is garnering increasing scrutiny, with Democrats in the Senate demanding that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it was pausing the installation of the routers that were linked to the ground stop. Asked on CNBC whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes. "We would have never went if the airways weren't completely open," he said on CNBC. "They'd been completely open for 21 hours." He added: "We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn't open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time." Mullin took over as DHS secretary earlier this year from Kristi Noem, whose tenure was rocked by scandal over spending at the department, as well as an aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. Mullin vowed to serve as a steady hand for the department and keep it out of the headlines. The Department of Homeland Security said Mullin was required by law to travel on a government plane. It said in a statement that he pays personally for any flight unrelated to government work. "Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," it said. The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop. The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports. The stoppage resulted in thousands of canceled flights and massive disruptions at airports across the nation ahead of the busy Thanksgiving holiday. President Donald Trump's administration has said the air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia. WATCH: Trump administration seeks to deflect responsibility for nationwide ground stop He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country's airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden. "I don't take any responsibility" for Friday's ground stop, Trump said. "What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," the president said. He later noted: "Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing." Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements. Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pennsylvania. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 1b11b29c4d2e.text: Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware. Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat. Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy. Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices. KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker. KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added. The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns. Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said. That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people. AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said. By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data . In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours. Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news or planned events impersonated a globally recognized brand, according to KnowBe4. The bottom line: Palma recommends taking a closer look at any unexpected email that appears to reference breaking news, even if the headline seems familiar.

Canada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as it grapples with US tariffs on the sector.
Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution.
But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Donald Trump.
While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.
If Canadian auto workers are "not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.
"Canada's going to move forward either way," he said.
He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.
Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.
In January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles, external (EVs) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector.
American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.
At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.
The move was a significant break from the US, which tariffs Chinese EVs heavily to protect domestic manufacturing.
Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned the prime minister against cosying up to China in a post on X, external.
"Are u really threatening to play China off the US? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."
His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.
Chinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for market access.
Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China, external. He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese EVs in Canada by early 2027.
These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.
Stellantis, a multinational car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.
The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs.
The sale has led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported, external, citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.
The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. In a letter to Carney, he warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled at the Brampton plant.
China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.
Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American industry could be eroded.
"We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.
Carney noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week.
Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.
Progress has been made in negotiations, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.

61e166a93df2.text: By — David Rising, Associated Press David Rising, Associated Press By — Amir-Hussein Radjy, Associated Press Amir-Hussein Radjy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-fires-at-u-s-facility-in-bahrain-as-tehran-resumes-strikes-on-arab-neighbors Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iran fires at U.S. facility in Bahrain as Tehran resumes strikes on Arab neighbors World Nov 17, 2026 1:53 PM EST CAIRO (AP) — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom in the Persian Gulf after a roughly two-month lull in fighting. After issuing an alert about the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military said there was no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel. The attacks have brought condemnations from the region, while analysts say that Tehran's growing economic pressures and stalled peace negotiations are raising the risk of renewed escalation. Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28. U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time. Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market. Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press. Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X. "In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation." US expands its Middle East naval presence With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war. The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies. The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region. Iran says it's responding to US attacks Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done. The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating. READ MORE: Third U.S. aircraft carrier in Middle East as Trump keeps options open in Iran war "Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement. Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability. Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar. In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement. Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies. "Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet." Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it. Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy. Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic p

8368cc447b45.text: By — Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/retail-spending-slowed-in-october-as-high-prices-gave-shoppers-pause Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Retail spending slowed in October as high prices gave shoppers pause Economy Nov 17, 2026 1:28 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to pull back on a variety of purchases from cars to clothing and furniture, even their hobbies, ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday. Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month after spiking 30.3% in September. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1%. Overall retail sales were pulled down by a decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Motor vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6% drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3% increase in September. Excluding auto-related stores, retail sales rose 0.6%. Adjusting for higher prices, consumer spending was "negative," according to Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, according to data released last week, hotter than expected. "The cautious consumer is back," Long wrote Tuesday. "October retail sales were tepid. Budgets are tight for many households." She noted the drop in gas prices in November will help free up some much-needed cash this holiday season, but middle-class and moderate-income households are "feeling the strain." Yet even with a recent decline in gas prices, a gallon still costs nearly 20% more than at this time last year. Business was down at clothing stores and furniture and home furnishing retailers last month, according to the report. Sporting goods, musical instruments, books and hobby stores also saw sales decline. Such retailers had performed strongly through the spring and summer as consumers treated themselves to little splurges, Long noted. One of the bright spots was online retailers, which saw a boost from a two-day Amazon Prime Day event, which took place in early October. That sector was up 1.2%. WATCH: How companies are using AI to make you spend more money The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn't include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category — restaurants — registered a 0.2% increase. Still, the so-called control group—which excludes food services, autos, building materials and gas station sales and is used to calculate economic growth—rose a solid 0.6%. Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4%, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data. Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics. Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped. Companies like Kohl's and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing. Target said it's offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are $20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at $5 and under. Kohl's has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise. Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable. "More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they're handling them well," said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion. Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said. That signals that "consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays," he added. Stephen Lebovitz, CEO of CBL Properties, a Chattanooga, Tennessee, mall owner, remains optimistic about the holiday shopping season, noting that higher gas prices haven't derailed business. He believes that a solid job market is still propping up spending among its middle-class customers. Malls have also been helped by a resurgence in business at movie theaters, fueled by Generation Z shoppers. "People are working and earning, and they're still spending," he said. The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".
"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".
Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
'New approach'
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel, which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.
But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.
The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.
The company's board is investigating his conduct, which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.
The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.
Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.
The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life".
Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal.
Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".
"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.
Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.
Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.
Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.
On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.
While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive Â£1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.
Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.
Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.
Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.
During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.
Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.
Earthshot Prize 2026 - full list of winners
- Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land
- Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries
- Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters
- Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution
- Fix Our Climate: Ãrsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind
The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.
Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor.
As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women.
The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev.
Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists.
As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun."
The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar.
