Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-and-canada-expand-tariff-relief-while-relations-with-the-u-s-are-strained Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China and Canada expand tariff relief while relations with the U.S. are strained World Nov 17, 2026 6:20 PM EST SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The leaders of China and Canada agreed Tuesday on additional tariff cuts as they pledged for deeper ties and Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States. READ MORE: U.S. and China release product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties. Carney's office said in a statement that the new measures extend and expand an earlier agreement between the countries. Under the agreement, China will provide additional tariff relief on Canadian exports worth around 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million), including frozen pork cuts, fish and seafood. In return, Canada will extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years. The meeting between the leaders came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry. "Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity," said Xi. "This is the right choice." Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is "greater predictability and stability" in their relationship. "The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems," he said. Carney added that his country is ahead of schedule in its plan to increase exports to China by 50% by the end of the decade. Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 6cf874e5b096.text: What secrets might a 194-year-old tortoise have for humans when it comes to living longer? William Brangham examines the remarkable life of Jonathan. Amna Nawaz: Finally tonight, what secrets might 194-year-old tortoise have for humans when it comes to living longer? Geoff Bennett: William Brangham examines the remarkable life of a much-loved tortoise. William Brangham: It's lunchtime for Jonathan. Man: And he gets the freshest produce. William Brangham: Jonathan is perhaps the most famous resident of the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he's lived for most of his 194 years. Dr. Stephen Clark, Kallel Foundation: And he was born before the telegraph was invented. He was born before the lightbulb was invented. He was born before the telephone was invented. When Abraham Lincoln died, he was 33 years old. William Brangham: Remarkably, after nearly two centuries, Jonathan remains in relatively good health, says neurologist and longevity expert Dr. Stephen Clark. Clark recently led an examination of the earth's oldest living land animal. Dr. Stephen Clark: He is blind. He has cataracts in both eyes, but he's very mobile, and still has a very good appetite, and is very social still. So, we expect he could live quite some more time, for sure. William Brangham: How did you land on the idea of -- that Jonathan would be a useful subject to study? Dr. Stephen Clark: Well, first of all, Jonathan's kind of accessible. So a lot of the long-lived species, like the bowhead whale and the Greenland shark, are kind of difficult to get to. And so knowing Jonathan was on the island was critical, and we could get access to him. And then we wanted to get a blood draw, but the island is very protective of Jonathan because he's very famous on the island. And so they wouldn't allow us to do a blood draw, so we had to do a buckle scrape of his -- of the inside of his mouth. So that's how we got the samples initially is, we actually did a buckle scrape of his mouth. William Brangham: Giant tortoises can live 150 years or more on average, but few reliable historical or medical records about them exist, and many of them outlive the researcher studying them. And what is it, practically speaking, that you're hoping to glean from Jonathan that could be applicable to humans and longevity? Dr. Stephen Clark: Yes, so that what really Jonathan represented is the first time we were able to really look at a difference between two different individuals over 200 years. So we compared him to a 5-year-old tortoise. The secret we have sort of identified with him is, he seems to have somehow been able to keep his mitochondria very young. And the mitochondria are sort of like the powerhouses of the cell. They provide the energy for the cell. They also provide energy for all the repair that's done for the genome. And so by keeping his mitochondria young, we think it's allowed him to repair his genome over 190 years. And so that was really the kind of surprising finding that we found with Jonathan. William Brangham: Do you think that this research and all the other research that is ongoing in this field, do you think we are on the cusp of extending human life in a meaningful way? Dr. Stephen Clark: So there have been predictions about what the maximum lifespan is for humans, and those predictions have ranged from 115 years old to 122 years old. I'm a believer and the nonprofit that I work with is a believer that we can increase current health lifespan at least closer to that. Going beyond that, I think it's going to require a lot more knowledge about the biology of aging. But I think the increasing average health span and lifespan to around 100, I think, is very doable in the near future. William Brangham: In their study published in "Science" this fall, Clark and his colleagues wrote -- quote -- "These investigations have deepened our understanding of gene markers that potentially slow aging and inhibit cancer in these species." In the meantime, one easy lesson from Jonathan... Man: He does love his carrots. William Brangham: ... slow down and enjoy a good meal in the sun. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham. Geoff Bennett: The secret to a long life, taking it slow. Amna Nawaz: Ba-dum-bum.

cd81011a0f9c.text: Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward. Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital . What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said on at the end of conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this." She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added. In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds . Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world." CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each ose by more than 10% in after-hours trading. Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly. Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said. The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make." Catch-up quick: Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence. She was also a major Nvidia customer and helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country. On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones through cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang . "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said. The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.

Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.

e856d44f265b.text: By — Laura Ungar, Associated Press Laura Ungar, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/doctors-are-raising-concerns-about-u-s-babies-born-with-measles Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Doctors are raising concerns about U.S. babies born with measles Health Nov 17, 2026 5:52 PM EST For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles. Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns. READ MORE: Can the U.S. regain its measles elimination status? Here's what to know From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday. "This is a brand new phenomenon," said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. The condition's emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus's spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it's had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases. "We're now seeing levels of measles that we haven't seen in 30 years," said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' infectious diseases committee. "When you have measles under control," congenital measles doesn't happen. The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn't get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community "are important to prevent measles and related complications." CDC scientists authored the alert. Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania's health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation. A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles. "What's happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back," Osterholm said. "Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth. MMR can't be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications. Congenital measles can seriously harm babies If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there's a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says. READ MORE: U.S. and Mexico officially lose measles-elimination status Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. "That's something that sadly we're learning more about," he said. Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots. This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas. "We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that's gonna take some doing," Ratner said. "It's going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it's an important thing for us to do." AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York. The Associated Press' health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism

Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police had filed documents requesting that Markle be charged on Monday.
Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material, from storage units Markle rented.
Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.
Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had asked prosecutors to charge Markle with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

c130833e0467.text: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. But Democrats are also expressing skeptcism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't." The intrigue : Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab. "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters. "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said. "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

Rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.
At the time, “one of the big questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” says Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”
One key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s important for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.
Pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.
“As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals says. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”
Experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.

3b512e5d8837.text:
Public health is invisible — until it’s not.
It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” says Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”
But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”
In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.
Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.
Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.
Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.
Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.
“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.
The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.
Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”
A preventable outbreak
On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.
About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.
Measles’ improbable comeback
As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.
Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.
The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.
In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.
Fading protection from measles, mumps and rubella
During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

- Published
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
Dario Amodei
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.
Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Daniela Amodei
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked eachother, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.
Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.
His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left Toronto University early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish
Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

e35b8f4cb2d0.text: Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive. Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost. This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab. The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year. State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data. There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic. That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year. The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits. He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving. Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less. How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied. EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals. There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year. The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes. "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run," he writes.

Africaâs richest man, who originally built up his conglomerate in cement and sugar before developing the continentâs largest oil refinery, said the proposed partnership with the government had the potential to create more than 50,000 jobs in Ghana, the worldâs second-largest cocoa producer.
In a separate development, the Dangote Refinery said it plans to increase its initial public offering by nearly a third, to $2.1 billion, after it was heavily oversubscribed, Reuters reported. 33381f78cd1e.text: Hakeem Jeffries could soon become America's first Black House speaker, even as Black lawmakers confront rising threats to their power in D.C. Why it matters: Proposed committee term limits and another round of redistricting could weaken Black lawmakers' influence they spent decades building. By the numbers: The number of Black lawmakers in the 120th Congress will be stable from the 119th, based on results so far. The House will likely seat 59 Black voting members, down from 61, according to the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies . All four Black House Republicans are departing, while Black Democrats have gained two seats. Black membership in the U.S. Senate will rise from five to a record seven, including Sens.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi and Juliana Stratton of Illinois . Zoom in: Democrats are in the middle of a sometimes messy generational power transfer, with younger lawmakers challenging more senior members for committee chairmanships. Those chairmanships have long helped Congressional Black Caucus members exercise power beyond their numbers. "For CBC members, the power is seniority," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) told Politico in 2014. "I've been around a while. ... Some wisdom, at least, is important to what we're going through right now," Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, 81, (D-N.J.) told Axios in 2025. Sticking point: Democrats are considering a four-term limit for committee leaders , starting after the 2028 elections, that could eventually force three veteran Black Democrats to step aside as committee leaders. Bennie Thompson, 78, of Mississippi, leads Democrats on Homeland Security. Bobby Scott, 79, of Virginia, leads Democrats on Education and Workforce. He faces a challenge from Connecticut Rep. Jahana Hayes, 53. Maxine Waters, 88, of California, leads Democrats on Financial Services. She faces a challenge from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54. Zoom out: A Democratic wave helped Black incumbents survive redistricting this year, but that level of support may not be repeated in future elections. The Supreme Court's April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais narrowed protections against maps that watered down the Voting Rights Act, potentially exposing more Black-held districts to redistricting. Texas' new maps pushed veteran Democrat Al Green into a primary against another Black incumbent. Green lost. His heavily redrawn former district elected Latina Democrat Leticia Gutierrez. Black Democrats Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina won in redrawn districts. Louisiana's 6th District heads to a December runoff. Between the lines: Hispanic Democrats are also gaining influence, with their numbers in Congress reaching new highs. California Rep. Pete Aguilar, a Hispanic Democrat, appears headed for majority whip, a top party leadership job. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus expects 55 members, including senators and Puerto Rico's nonvoting resident commissioner — its largest membership since its 1976 founding. Yes, but: Hispanic gains don't necessarily come at Black lawmakers' expense. Hispanic Democrats on Financial Services have backed Waters , showing how the two groups can work together as their members seek more influence. Younger lawmakers say term limits could open doors for the next generation of Black and Hispanic leaders.

The colossal $40 billion financing that Apollo is lining up for SpaceX could hit markets as early as this week, but it wonât be hitting their balance sheet, according to people familiar with the matter.
The financing will go into an SPV, or special-purpose vehicle, allowing SpaceX to keep it off its own balance sheet and instead rent GPUs from its subsidiary. Apollo will be lending close to $20 billion of the deal upfront and then syndicating it or selling it to other investors later.
Other companies, including Meta, have utilized this kind of financial workarounds to keep debt off their bottom lines. It also allows the companies to keep their ratings elevated.
Portions of the seven-part deal could be sold to investors as early as this week. The arrangement includes an array of pricing âÂ the bulk of which, $35.5 billion, will price at 8.3% and 7.75%, Semafor reported earlier.
Other, riskier parts of the deal will price even higher, at a blended rate that could exceed 9%, but will account for less than $3 billion of the overall financing.
Pricing for debt related to data centers and artificial intelligence has gotten more expensive for borrowers as investors get choosier about where they put their money and fret over the growing debt loads at companies in the AI buildout.
Apollo declined to comment. SpaceX didnât respond to a request for comment.

Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.
The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.
After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.
Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.
However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.
A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.
It was not clear on Wednesday what form separate Trump-Putin talks would take, though a Kremlin spokesperson indicated short informal talks may happen without large delegations in the room.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.
Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.
Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".
In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.
Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".
Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.
The south-east Chinese city the Apec summit is being held in is a booming area for manufacturing and advanced tech.
It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.
Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.
Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.
Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

49576f8bd190.text:
Google is trying to prove that AI wonât replace artists.
The tech giant has rolled out a suite of generative AI music features over the past year, including Flow Music â a tool it acquired in February when it bought the startup ProducerAI â which allows users to create songs from a single prompt, in the same style as AI music giants like Suno and Udio. But the companyâs pitch to artists is that its technology can also act like a tool in their creative process, not unlike Auto-Tune or MIDI.
To prove it, Google launched Flow Music Sessions earlier this year, an artist residency program for those curious about integrating the technology into their creative processes. Residents work in Spaces, a Flow Music feature carried over from ProducerAI that allows artists to vibe code their own tools and plugins.
The fusion of art with artificial intelligence makes some artists queasy, and it has since ChatGPT launched in 2022. But, Google has long found ways into the creator economy from different angles. It grew YouTube, today a juggernaut video-sharing site rivaling cable, largely by giving platforms to independent creators. Now, itâs betting that artists wary of AI can be won over in the same way: on their own terms.
For artists in Googleâs Flow Music residency, that distinction is important. âI draw creative fuel and energy and joy from making things myself,â Avanti Singh, a sound designer and resident at Flow Music, told Semafor. âIâm not particularly interested in prompting an entire song to be created because the most fun part for me is writing lyrics and singing and collaborating.â
Instead, artists in the program vibe code to bolster the creative process, cutting down on the most tedious production steps. Mike Costanzo, a producer in the residency, built a âperfect kickâ plugin in Spaces that he says cuts down the time it takes to find an apt kick drum for a song. He picks a genre, taps a musical key to tune the drum, and the plugin handles the rest.
Google has come under fire for its AI music generation. A group of independent musicians and songwriters filed a lawsuit against Google in March, alleging the tech giant trained its music model Lyria 3 on copyrighted recordings from YouTube without permission or compensation. Google Flow now runs on newer versions of that model. Google has moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that music uploaded to YouTube is already broadly licensed for AI training in accepting the platformâs terms of service.

The News
The recent dip in AI company valuations isnât concerning to one of the Gulfâs biggest investors in the space because it could allow stronger businesses to emerge and give the industry time to win over public opinion, Qatar Investment Authorityâs CEO said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
The $580 billion sovereign wealth fund invests for future generations, a time horizon that can absorb volatility while the industryâs winners emerge. âA quarter of a blip or a year of correction doesnât really mean much for us as a long-term investor,â Mohammed Al-Sowaidi said. âWe have a super cycle of innovation happening now. Itâs a big revolution, it has to have its ups and downs.â
A possible downturn could deliver productivity gains across industries, according to Al-Sowaidi. Companies that succeed will become more distinct and focused, which makes assessing their business models somewhat easier. The potential of AI in areas such as manufacturing, drug discovery, and other applications that could improve lives and expand the economy as reasons for confidence in the technology.
QIA has committed to invest $500 billion in the US over the next decade. That plan hasnât changed, despite the US-Iran warâs effect on the country: Qatarâs energy infrastructure was struck by Iran, and LNG exports are a fraction of normal flows. Still, QIA has remained acquisitive this year, and Al-Sowaidi said âno dividend has been given out to the government,â which is funding itself with other reserves.
Q&A
These responses were condensed and edited for clarity.
QIA backs Anthropic. Did you seek additional shares in the IPO?
Weâve been early backers of Anthropic. We believed back then that this could be a very good, new form of enterprise solution. We did submit and in a couple of days weâll see how the results are. It canât be more interesting from a timing perspective. Itâs a large business and theyâve demonstrated great execution.
Has Qatar been able to secure the advanced AI chips it needs from the US?
From a Qatar perspective, we are very well integrated into the United States. Most of the applications we have are US applications from an AI stack point of view. Weâre very well integrated with the financial system in the US, with the Treasury Department. So we had no struggle really getting this executed.
Do you plan to invest more in US tech?
Over the past 12 years, weâve been doubling down on technology in the US. We have an office in New York, where we doubled the operation to about 40 people, and theyâre frequent visitors to the West Coast.
A lot of great ideas come from San Francisco and from the leading technology companies. Weâve been focusing on artificial intelligence and applications and frontier labs and infrastructure plays. I think itâs just the beginning of a large cycle of super innovation.

An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.
The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).
Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading".
SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.
The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.
The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.
Daera has two months to respond.
Ongoing investigation
The ongoing investigation began in 2024.
A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.
In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.
"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.
"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.
"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."
And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.
Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.
"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.
"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.
"We hope today's OEP report will be the catalyst needed."
Failures and recommendations
The decision notice is the latest step in the OEP's investigation.
It identifies failures and recommends what actions Daera should now take to fix them.
It says Daera has failed to classify and update SPAs, has not put measures in place to protect declining birds, and has not carried out a required review of habitats.
Recommendations include addressing outstanding recommendations "where they remain ecologically relevant" from a review of SPAs, carried out in Northern Ireland in 2001.
Where they cannot be implemented, it says "transparent, ornithological reasons" must be published.
Daera is also advised to identify the causes of declines and put in place resourced plans and effective measures to maintain or restore wild bird populations and the habitats they depend on.
And it says "the overdue habitat sufficiency review" must be carried out "as soon as practicably possible", to identify gaps in habitat provision and the action needed to address them.

Fitchâs downgrade of the Africa Export-Import Bank in June 2025 sparked a furious debate about the assessments of multilateral development banks by global rating agencies. Then in February, Moodyâs proposed changes to its methodology for assessing these types of banks.
The revisions, applied since July, introduced a potential two-notch downgrade if a bank does not have large, highly rated, and non-borrowing shareholders. This could make it difficult for African-owned development banks to secure higher ratings without bringing in non-African shareholders, effectively forcing these lenders to surrender part of their ownership and control.
Credit ratings are intended to provide an independent assessment of an institutionâs capacity and willingness to repay its obligations. In the case of assessments of multilateral banks, rating methodologies have a bias towards non-African shareholders. In effect suggesting that African governments, irrespective of their demonstrated financial commitments, cannot provide sufficient capital to the institutions they have established.
The nationality of shareholders may be relevant to risk analysis, but it should not become a substitute for examining fundamentals. If the institution has strong risk management and governance structures, adequate capitalization, quality assets, and high liquidity, where the shareholders come from should be less important. Foreign investment and diversity of shareholding are valuable, but they should be a strategic choice for the institutions themselves rather than a condition implicitly imposed by the architecture of credit assessment.
A more fundamental issue is the difference between paid-in capital that shareholders have actually contributed and callable capital that they have promised to provide if there is a need. Afreximbank is a good example. Shareholdersâ funds stand at approximately $9 billion, while its net income increased by 30% in the first half of 2026. The commitment of African shareholders is also significant. According to the bankâs leadership, African governments contributed approximately $2.6 billion in additional paid-in capital by the end of 2025. A further $526 million had been paid or committed in cash contributions in 2026. In addition, shareholders have committed substantial callable capital. This is another important layer of protection for creditors.
But Moodyâs new methodology still places more value on callable capital from foreign highly rated shareholders than substantial paid-in capital from African shareholders. A more balanced assessment should recognize capital contributions and other tangible financial commitments regardless of the creditworthiness of shareholders.
Todayâs rating methodologies characterize geographical concentration and an exclusive focus on the African business environment as indicators of high risk. This creates a further structural disadvantage for African-owned multilateral development banks whose mandates require them to serve African economies. To secure higher credit ratings, these institutions need to reduce lending to the very economies they were established to support. This will diminish their role and purpose.
Rating agencies should not be expected to overlook weaknesses in African governance, capital adequacy, liquidity or risk management. Independence and analytical integrity remain essential to the credibility of the ratings industry.
To maintain this, three changes are necessary.
First, ratings should be accurate and consistent in their assessments. African institutions should not be penalized simply because their shareholders are African and operate in Africa. Nationality should not be a proxy for financial capacity and willingness to pay.
Second, African governments must continue to support their institutions with capital and affirm their legal commitments established through their agreements and treaties: This pushes rating agencies to assess multilateral banks based on their legal and operational merits.
Lastly, African countries must strengthen cooperation among their multilateral financial institutions, deepen domestic capital markets, and support the development of independent African credit rating capacity. Greater competition and analytical diversity will improve the quality of credit assessments, provided all agencies maintain rigorous standards.
Africa cannot build its own strong multilateral financial institutions if the price of recognition is surrendering the ownership and control to foreign shareholders.

The Democratic Republic of Congoâs Ebola outbreak is spiralling, with the disease spreading at a record pace despite a surge in funding. Rampant misinformation, widespread violence, and a lack of medical equipment have aided the spread of the Bundibugyo strain, which is now Africaâs biggest-ever Ebola outbreak by geographic reach.
A lack of treatments or vaccines has also meant that the current outbreak is more fatal than ever: Around 50% of those who are infected die, the highest-ever mortality rate for Ebola. Although authorities are seeking more funding, more than $700 million remains unaccounted for by the DRC, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, while frontline workers have gone unpaid for months.

Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.
In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.
"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:
- Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa â the match before Bancroft was caught
- Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers â Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
- Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
- When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
- Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".
Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.
Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.
The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.
Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.
A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."
A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.
"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.
"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.
"It was not just the three of us â Steve Smith, David Warner and I â who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.
"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.
"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."
Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.
The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.
"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.
"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.
"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.
"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.
"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."
Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.

"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.

It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.
Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.
Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".
Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.
A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.
Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.
"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"
Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.
They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.
Steve followed his dad into the fire service in 1978 and his first posting was in Wrexham, where he was among the first responders to the lagoon fire.
Jilska said he was checked at hospital after falling in, then given a tetanus injection before being sent home.
"What is a tetanus injection going to do for him?" said the retired nurse. "It was a disaster waiting to happen. A time bomb waiting to go off, as far as I'm concerned."
The couple moved to Melbourne in Australia, then in 1994 Steve was diagnosed with stage four cancer â small cell carcinoma - and given weeks to live.
He died three days after the couple's 17th wedding anniversary. Their children were aged six and 10.
The Llwyneinion site was a dumping ground for chemicals suspected to have included cancer-causing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) from chemical giant Monsanto.
Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels of PCBs in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.
Buried with Michael Sheen
What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales.
PCBs were once widely used in things like lipsticks and white goods - and were liked for being non-flammable and hard to break down.
But today they are seen as the first "forever chemicals" which are building up in the environment, threatening wildlife and human health.
The Llwyneinion lagoon was purchased by the then Clwyd County Council for just Â£1 in May 1980.
Andy Moore spent the day bringing in foam to help firefighters smother the fire at the former dump - and saw Steve fall in.
Andy, who was also stationed at Wrexham, said firefighters were not equipped to face the chemicals in the lagoon.
"There was no request for chemical PPE, we were basically fighting that fire in our normal tunics, drips and helmets," said Andy, now 70.
"I was walking around that fire ground in a shirt and tie - I've always been concerned about what it could have done to me.
"I was diagnosed a year ago with skin cancer.
"Whether I can relate that back to this specific incident I don't know but there's too many coincidences - I talk to my colleagues and we've had a lot of our guys who have died young specifically of cancers."
Jim MacGrane was also a firefighter at Wrexham at that time and his wife suffered a miscarriage in the period after the fire.
"There were six wives that we can recall had miscarriages within 12 to 15 months of that incident," said Jim, now 71.
"It was highlighted by one of the guys on the station who said, 'that's not coincidence. There's something not right there'."
Mark Jones and his father Ken both attended the fire and Ken later died of lymph and brain cancer in 2011.
"Out of the 60 people that attended that fire a significant number had cancers or passed away with cancer," said Mark, now 68.
"I'd be keen to participate in some blood testing to see if there was any link because it's only recently we found out about the PCBs in the vicinity.
"We were fairly well looked after health-wise when we were in the service, we used to have an annual health check. Unfortunately once you've finished the service that doesn't continue."
Prof Anna Stec, one of the UK's leading experts on fire chemistry and toxicity, warned it would be challenging to prove a firefighter's exposure to particular chemicals during their career had led to health issues later in life.
"It's very difficult to link specific chemicals to health disorders and it requires a multi-disciplinary approach where we're looking at residents' exposure, their lifestyle, and so on," said the University of Leicester professor.
"With firefighters it's even harder," she added, as they can be exposed to "a cocktail of toxic substances" throughout their careers.
But Stec said there should be more research into what happened at Llwyneinion.
