Need range time? The Army now has an online reservation system
Officials say industry’s wait times for weapons testing has already plunged.
The Army wants its new reservation system to reduce the wait for test-range time from more than a year to no more than 30 days. Since it launched in August, according to the commander of Test and Evaluation Command, they’re averaging 33.
Companies wanting to test a weapon can submit a proposal with dates and a preferred range, and within 24 hours, a “concierge” will call back to schedule a time.
“There's a perception that testing takes too long to get onto ranges, and at places like White Sands Missile Range—that's booked out. It may take a while to get on,” Maj. Gen. Pat Gaydon said Tuesday at an AUSA event near Washington, D.C. “But that's not the only range, and I think there's a misperception that that's where everyone needs to go to do their testing.”
The Army has opened up Dugway Proving Ground, Utah; the West Cibola Range at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona; Camp Grayling, Michigan; Camp Shelby, Mississippi; Camp Atterbury, Indiana; and an international range near Tan-Tan, Morocco, for its quick-turnaround reservation system.
The permissive test range construct has also pushed the Army to fast-track invitations to its own events. Covenant Industries was testing a missile in Morocco 14 days after getting a call from the Army this fall, according to their president, Abby Denberg.
“When companies are invited to participate in exercises, those invitations usually come about a year out,” she said. “So the final planning conference for exercises is usually about six months before the exercise. There's a few issues with that. First and foremost is that startups are changing every week, every two weeks, every three weeks, and so locking configurations six months out can hamper your ability to bring the latest and greatest technology to those exercises.”
The flexibility also allows companies to test their systems early and often.
“It was all about…recognizing that they needed a place where they could fly, fail, fix, fly again, and do that sort of iteration, and scheduling a one-week test window a year or 18 months out doesn't offer that,” Gaydon said. “So what we're trying to offer is…that they can almost test once a week or one week a month, those sorts of things.”
That is particularly helpful for unmanned systems that rely on artificial-intelligence models, said Nathan Diller, president of Mach Industries.
“What it allows us is very rapid closure on those models, to make sure that you can start to build trust in the models sooner,” he said.
And, dovetailing with the Army’s Continuous Transformation philosophy, companies can get soldier feedback early on, “getting the system into the hands of end-users, allowing them to kind of test your concept of employment and concept of operations, and come back to you and give you that feedback,” Denberg said.
The program has opened up opportunities for some of the Pentagon’s highest priorities.
“If you're in the drone business, the counter-drone business, the long-range fires, or the low-cost interceptor business, you can only do so much on your own before you probably need to come onto one of our ranges,” Gaydon said. “If you own the whole kill chain and drone/counter-drone, the FAA will not allow you to shoot down your own drone in airspace that is in ours. If you want to test how your drone operates or your missile operates in a contested electronic electromagnetic spectrum environment, it's hard to do that on a private range, to get those sorts of authorities.”
The Army is also offering companies a kind of initial evaluation that they can use to build confidence in their product.
“We will offer industry a memorandum that said you came, operated in this environment, and you can use that with program offices or however you want,” Gaydon said.
So far, the test-range reservation system has gotten 156 requests, he said. More than 60 percent of them are being or have been scheduled.
“We've completed 15 tests to date,” he said. “We have 14 more ready, and have about 93 that we're actively working to get on the range.”

8693ecf8483a.text:
Major AI platforms generated viable plans for terrorist attacks, GAO finds
Safety guardrails on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok failed to prevent federal investigators from developing detailed plans.
Four of the most widely used artificial intelligence platforms generated viable plans for attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure and mass-casualty events during covert government testing, despite safeguards designed to prevent their misuse.
According to a Government Accountability Office report published Wednesday, investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok in spring 2026. They found that all four platforms provided information that could help malicious actors plan and carry out attacks.
In each case, the investigators were able to circumvent the platforms’ safety guardrails by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques.
“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work. And I think that’s the story here,” Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity at GAO, said in a podcast interview published alongside the report.
The platforms generated information for two types of attacks: constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device designed to cause mass casualties, and targeting the electrical grid to cause economic damage. The platforms provided details including specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods.
Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate an attack. GAO investigators then worked with experts to verify that the information could be used to carry out the attacks.
The platforms initially deployed safeguards, including refusing requests, removing information or suspending accounts. However, investigators ultimately found ways around those protections.
“These products are not fully in the control of the companies that are operating them,” Walsh said.
“We looked at four of the most powerful companies in the world — Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — and we found that the product that they're selling is potentially dangerous,” he added.
The report does not indicate which platforms provided information for each attack scenario. GAO said it intentionally withheld the specific models and techniques used to circumvent safeguards to prevent malicious actors from recreating the tests.
“Officials from the companies generally stated that their companies will continue to improve the safety of their platforms,” the report says.
The federal watchdog also acknowledged that its findings reflect a point-in-time assessment and do not represent “a statistically significant sample.”
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who requested the investigation, said the findings underscore the need for Congress to take action on AI safety.
“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan said in a statement Wednesday. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”
“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” she added.
Hassan, who is set to become chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in the next Congress, said AI safety legislation will be an early priority for the panel. She said one of the panel’s first hearings in the new year will focus on the risks AI poses to homeland security and critical infrastructure.
Hassan said the committee will “prioritize developing legislation to address these threats,” adding that she is exploring solutions such as requiring more rigorous safety testing before AI platforms publicly release models.
GAO did not issue recommendations in the report, which examined third-party products rather than its typical examination of federal agencies. Instead, GAO said it sought to highlight the risks for lawmakers and bring attention to safety concerns.

7ad96b94554d.text:
Senate grills acting Navy secretary on Iran war costs, extended deployments
Democrats in particular bristled at Hung Cao’s characterization of unsuccessful suicide attempts as “mitigations.”
The White House’s pick to lead the Navy didn’t have clear answers Tuesday when lawmakers pressed him about ballooning Iran war costs, the resulting toll on troops deployed to the region, and the service’s overall readiness during a Senate confirmation hearing.
Hung Cao, a retired Navy captain who has been the service’s acting secretary since April, said the Iran war was a “strain” on resources, but failed to provide the detailed answers sought by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
“I do not know the daily cost, ma'am…I know the rough costs, how much it's costing us so far,” he told the Senate Armed Services Committee, later adding that it was around $30 billion after Warren quoted estimates of about $32.5 million a day.
Cao also didn’t have an answer when asked how much damage Iranian strikes had caused to the U.S. Naval Base in Bahrain. “We're still making all the assessments because it's a non-permissive area for us to go.” U.S. troops are still in Bahrain; some came under fire yesterday during Iran’s latest strike on radar facilities there.
Warren pointed to a Wall Street Journal report estimating $400 million to “construct buildings of the same types as those damaged at NSA Bahrain.”
Similar testy back-and-forth scenarios repeated throughout the nearly three-hour hearing. Senators on both sides of the aisle prodded Cao over the Trump administration’s exclusion of Democrats from meetings pertaining to national security and the Iran war.
Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said such partisan behavior puts defense funding in jeopardy because “it limits us to basically using Republican votes only,” Rounds said. “Pretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that if they're not even invited in to hear the information in the first place.”
And Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., suggested the Iran war's added costs were “holding up” naval modernization efforts and “the important improvements that we all want to make long term for our military.”
Cao, who was confirmed as the Navy’s undersecretary before being named acting secretary, promised not to have partisan briefings and to communicate with Congress.
As have other Pentagon leaders, Cao urged lawmakers to pass the administration’s proposed $350 billion reconciliation bill atop the regular, if still historically large, trillion-dollar defense appropriations bill for the fiscal year that started more than two months ago. He said that many Navy programs, including buying up to 35 landing ship mediums, depend on the reconciliation bill.
“That is also predicated on us having a $1.45 trillion dollar budget…because a lot of the LSMs, the extra LSMs, are in the reconciliation,” he said.
Cao’s reluctance to take stances that challenge or contradict public statements from the White House or Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth also drew ire from some Democrats.
When Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., asked if he “urged” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to end the Iran war, Cao said it is “not within my purview to do that,” adding that his “stance on our readiness and the strain it takes on our sailors” is known.
Duckworth said she would not vote for him.
The hearing ended after a fiery exchange with Sen. Kristen Gillibrand, D-N.Y., over Cao’s attempt to frame to sailor suicide attempts as “mitigations.”
Gillibrand said Cao was “minimizing” sailors’ mental health “strain” amid extended deployments and poor living conditions aboard the Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. Cao denied the accusation, and brought up his own experience in uniform. The exchange took a turn when Cao refused to back down from his assertion that the Navy has sufficient processes to address sailors’ mental health challenges when deployed.
“You see it as eight suicide attempts. I see it as eight suicides mitigations because of the the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists. Normally, most carrier strike groups, when they deploy, have about one or two suicides. This is well before Epic Fury,” Cao said earlier in the hearing, when Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., first asked about sailors’ welfare on the USS Abraham Lincoln. “Unfortunately, this is the fight we're dealing with right now. We had zero actual suicides on board the Abraham Lincoln.”
Cao previously called news reports of substandard living conditions aboard the Lincoln “dishonest.”
“I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand said, mentioning one incident when a sailor jumped overboard and was subsequently punished for it.
Cao disagreed: “I have done many deployments—Iraq, Afghanistan, Somalia. I have been in places [where] we get two MREs a day and five bottles of water. That's what I got. And, you know, talk about no showers or anything else. I understand what our sailors and Marines are going through, and I put mental health as a top of my concern.”
And then he doubled down on the service preventing suicides by putting “mental health resiliency providers as well as chaplains on board.”
Gillibrand retorted: “It's inadequate.”
Then Cao quipped: “Then that’s why we need the $1.45 trillion.”

ff776c31ccfe.text:
- Published
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (Â£760m).
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
Early nominations
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.
It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.
The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.
The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.
Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.
There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."
It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.
Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

849efd209ddc.text: President Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during the trilateral summit in China, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The meeting in Shenzhen will take place as Trump is making another push for a breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Also on Thursday, Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet in Berlin with Ukrainian and European officials to work on security guarantees for Ukraine as well as a postwar Europe-Russia security architecture. They want to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi planned for next week. The big picture: The Trump-Putin meeting will take place on the sidelines of the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The summit wasn't intended to deal with Ukraine, but U.S. allies are bracing for Trump to make unexpected public statements that serve the interests of Russia and China. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios.

c69b12ec7034.text: By — Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/grand-theft-auto-vi-arrives-with-enormous-hype-and-expectations-after-13-year-wait Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations after 13-year wait Arts Nov 18, 2026 12:13 PM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment's biggest releases is finally here. "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon. READ MORE: The long wait is almost over. Here's what to know about the upcoming release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI' The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, meaning players in Asia and other regions can start playing hours before its U.S. release. New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached. "The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented," said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. "That's more than a quarter of the average household's data usage in an entire month, all in one go." In the capital, Wellington, players stayed up to be among the first to try "Grand Theft Auto VI." Among them was Adam Simmons, 50, a director of photography who launched the game in his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low to avoid waking his wife and daughters. READ MORE: 6 best video games of 2025, according to this expert "The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," he said after half an hour of shooting, car theft and jokes about Florida. "You really feel like you are in a world," he added. "The places and how they're put together feel right." Simmons moved to New Zealand from Portland, Oregon, five months ago — a decision he joked had been influenced by the prospect of playing "Grand Theft Auto" before his friends. He praised the game's emotional connection with its characters and said he expected its expansive world to offer hours of play long after he finished the story. By 1 a.m., he reluctantly admitted he should go to bed, though he expected to put in plenty of hours in the coming days. "I have my own company that I have to run," he said. "So I'm the boss, but also I'm just going to lose sales because a video game came out." Game returns to Vice City after 13 years The "Grand Theft Auto" franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. At the center of "GTA VI" are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar's fictionalized version of Florida. Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from "Grand Theft Auto V," which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area's history and architecture. Miami embraces its fictional alter ego Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game's arrival as a marketing opportunity. Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant "Welcome to Vice City" display atop the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game's release. The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity. Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding "GTA VI" gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight. In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game's soundtrack. Years of hype arrive at launch day Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation. Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.
With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."
The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground â accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.
The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.
They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.
Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.
Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.
But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work â with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.
Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."
His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.
Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.
Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.
But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.
But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio PiÃ±a said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.
But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. PiÃ±a said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
PiÃ±a said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.
Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.
The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."
On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".
It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.
But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".
The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.
Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.
He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.
The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".
But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.
The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.
"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.
Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January 2017.
At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.
In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.
Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.)
First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.
Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.
Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.
Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.
They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

e887e961d389.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-nominate-hakeem-jeffries-to-become-house-speaker-a-historic-first Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to become House speaker, a historic first Politics Nov 18, 2026 10:55 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation's first Black American with the gavel. Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January. READ MORE: Here are some of the House seats that Democrats didn't expect to win — but did He ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media posts have been flooding the offices of Democrats and the newly elected, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Ahead of Wednesday's vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members in what will be their large majority. "I embrace those conversations," he said. READ MORE: House Republicans pick Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed. Jeffries will face a separate roll call of the whole House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. Skeptics question whether leaders are up to the job Wednesday's vote was the first of their careers for dozens of members-elect, before they're even sworn into office in January. With one of the biggest incoming majorities in decades, Jeffries will have room to spare. Rep.-elect Brad Lander of New York announced he would support Jeffries when he launched his campaign for Congress. Rep.-elect Randy Villegas of California has said he was supporting whoever would help him best deliver for his Central Valley district. WATCH: Pelosi reflects on historic career and predicts 'big victory' for Democrats Returning Rep. Emily Randall of Washington said she heard questions about House leadership during town halls in her district and had been watching direct messages stream into her Instagram feed about the leadership election. So she decided to start dialing them back. "People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the House," she said, referring to the Vermont independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. "Technically yes, and it would be probably difficult." (It's true that the House can elect anyone speaker, but it's unlikely to be Sanders because he already has his day job in the Senate.) On one call, Randall said, she listened to the constituent's concerns and then replied, "Truthfully, not like blowing smoke, whoever is our speaker — and I think it is going to be Hakeem Jeffries, and I am supporting Hakeem Jeffries for speaker — I think we will accomplish a lot of the things that he was asking us to." Lawmakers pointed to the livestream that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York did trying to explain the role of the speaker. "There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries," Ocasio-Cortez said at the Capitol. "I think that everyone is far more concerned what that leadership means, what is it promising." First leaders of a post-Pelosi era Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders of the post-Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time. When Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California decided to step aside from leadership in 2022 after the party's electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era. Pelosi, No. 2 Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina had often moved together, rising, and then stepping back, from their long-held positions. A similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House "are quite different." She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others. "His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction," Ansari said. "It is more productive to focus on preparing on what we're going to do in the majority and what we need and want to get done in those first 100 days," she said. Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who pulled off a stunning victory in a redrawn district favoring the Republican candidate, said before the vote that he'd be supporting Jeffries. "It's not even like a complex question," he said about Jeffries, who he said "led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation." "I'm not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.
Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.
The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.
Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in SuÃ¨vres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.
She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".
Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother â tested in an unrelated case â matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.
The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.
During the trial, prosecutor AnaÃ¯s Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.
The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.
French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.
El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.
Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (Â£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (Â£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will be profitable.
The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Crucial test for AI
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price.
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Rapid rise
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".
With additional reporting by Rachel Clun and Osmond Chia

The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

(AP) — Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion. READ MORE: Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of AI's existential risk to humanity The higher-than-anticipated pricing signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble. Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totaling $81 billion put Anthropic's IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June. The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, offering 825 million shares that will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT." Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. "This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it's a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors," said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co. The company's rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year. IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector's massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei. The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock, 956,351,354 of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 of which are being sold by certain selling stockholders. AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all lost more money than they've made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector. Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months. READ MORE: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction. Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Investors will have less control in Anthropic's unusual structure The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners. Usually that means making profits and growing the business. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal: "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (Â£144.8m).
The sale of ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (Â£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

303dc1c63a7c.text: By — John Raby, Associated Press John Raby, Associated Press By — Cody Jackson, Associated Press Cody Jackson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/rainfall-supercharged-by-el-nino-causes-road-flooding-synagogue-roof-collapse-in-south-florida Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rainfall supercharged by El Niño causes road flooding, synagogue roof collapse in South Florida Nation Nov 18, 2026 7:46 PM EST PLANTATION, Fla. (AP) — A slow-moving storm system dumped heavy rains that prompted an emergency declaration Wednesday in South Florida where the roof of a synagogue collapsed and cars were submerged along roads, authorities said. READ MORE: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse? On the West Coast, heavy rain and high winds grounded planes at San Francisco's airport, disrupted ferry service and flooded roads in Napa County and other wine country areas north of the city. Preliminary figures for Florida showed 15.3 inches (39 centimeters) of rain fell in a 24-hour period ending Wednesday in parts of Broward County, the National Weather Service said. The threat was expected to last through Friday along Florida's Atlantic Coast with additional rainfall amounts of 12 inches (30 centimeters) possible, the weather service said. The Florida Division of Emergency Management said in an advisory Tuesday night that "potentially catastrophic" amounts of rainfall could cause flash flooding, life-threatening rip tides and expected minor beach erosion due to high surf. On top of all that, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, a low-pressure system is expected to form near the northern Bahamas. It could become a subtropical or tropical storm over parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts into early next week, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. The natural warming cycle called El Niño has disrupted Florida's typical dry season that runs from October to May, said Alejandra Garcia, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Miami. El Niño is "helping bring these low pressure systems down toward the southeastern United States, which in turn is causing these heavy precipitation events," she said. Florida mayor calls the deluge 'historically significant' In Florida, the city of Hollywood declared a state of emergency Wednesday and Mayor Josh Levy urged motorists to stay off roads and avoid unnecessary travel. Portions of the Florida Turnpike and Interstate 95 in Hollywood were closed due to high water and stalled vehicles. The city said it received more than 300 calls for service overnight. "It's a historically significant rainfall event in the city," Levy said. Some residents complained that motorists who were driving too fast caused a wake that pushed floodwaters into their homes, he said. Heavy rains caused the roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood to collapse and damaged the roof and flooded hallways at a local hospital. No injuries were reported. Rudy Taillard flew back from Texas on Tuesday night to find his apartment complex in the city flooded. "It was insane. The water kept going up," Taillard said. "If you were living on the first floor, like, you were cooked. It was pretty brutal. Thank God I'm on the top floor." The highest rainfall amount was recorded in Plantation, where resident Jade Jaime said the storm just kept going all day "and then by the time we went to sleep at night, still just pouring down like it was never going to end." In Fort Lauderdale, the 5.72 inches (14.5 centimeters) of rain that fell in a downpour ending early Wednesday broke the daily record of 1.8 inches (4.5 centimeters) set in 1959, Garcia said. Officials announced that schools will be closed Thursday in Broward and Miami-Dade counties. In northern Florida, a warning was issued for minor flooding along the St. Johns River. California is loaded with weather concerns The Los Angeles County Fire Department issued an evacuation warning through Friday morning for the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas, warning of a risk of debris flows as a storm approaches. South of San Francisco, a 47-mile (76-kilometer) segment of Highway 1 near Big Sur was closed Wednesday for the same reason. In San Francisco, which set a daily record with 2.28 inches (5.8 centimeters) of rain, areas along the Embarcadero were flooded as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm. Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties, according to the California Department of Transportation and the California Highway Patrol. Wind gusts of up to 50 mph (80 kph) were forecast for the East Bay region and up to 70 mph (113 kph) for the Altamont Pass, which connects Bay Area highways to I-5 in the Central Valley. Snow accumulations of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada. Travel issues loom ahead of Thanksgiving week The weather service issued a long-range forecast showing heavy rain is possible along the Atlantic seaboard in Georgia and South Carolina on Saturday, from North Carolina to New York's Long Island on Sunday and into New England on Sunday and Monday. Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. Associated Press writer Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco and videojournalist Daniel Kozin in Hollywood, Florida, contributed. India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.
A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.
The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.
The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.
Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.
The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.
It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.
The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.
Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.
If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.
Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.
Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.
Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.
"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.
"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably â from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.
"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)
The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.
"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.
"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.
Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".
The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.
Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.
There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.
By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.
Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.
But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.
Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.
The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.
The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.
The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.
One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.
In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.
Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.
