0706f8d9dbbc.text: By — David Rising, Associated Press David Rising, Associated Press By — Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-widens-gulf-attacks-by-targeting-u-s-air-base-in-kuwait-and-sites-in-bahrain Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iran widens Gulf attacks by targeting U.S. air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain World Nov 18, 2026 7:36 PM EST CAIRO (AP) — Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before. After about two months without such attacks, Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain in recent days. The small Persian Gulf island kingdom hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet. READ MORE: Iran fires at U.S. facility in Bahrain as Tehran resumes strikes on Arab neighbors The early morning attacks in the nearly nine-month-old war came after a U.S. fighter jet struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site Tuesday on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. strike was in retaliation for an Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain earlier Tuesday. Iran said that its recent attacks — including those on other U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday — were in response to U.S. drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers. The tit-for-tat attacks come as the commander of the U.S. military's Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, met Wednesday in Tel Aviv with Israel's military chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, and the director of Israel's intelligence agency Mossad, Roman Gofman. They also complicate negotiations for a diplomatic solution and raise the risk of resumption of all-out conflict as a conflict in Yemen between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition could drag on for months. The U.S. military didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest attacks. Blockade puts pressure on Tehran With its economy suffering under a U.S. naval blockade and American military escorts helping restore the passage of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say that the recent attacks suggest Tehran may be growing weary of the status quo. "Even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation and escalation beyond what either side originally intended," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X following the initial reports of the attack on Kuwait. U.S. President Donald Trump has sent mixed messages on his next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely, but also sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East. Though U.S. military protection has helped restore oil shipments from the Gulf, Iran has continued to attack tankers as they attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz. United Arab Emirates state-owned oil company ADNOC said Wednesday that one of its tanker crew members was missing after an attack in the strait on Tuesday, while 11 others were injured and were receiving medical care. Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel's military and intelligence services, described an "increasingly clear" pattern of attacks by Iran on shipping and U.S. facilities in the Gulf region. "Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of deliberate, calibrated escalation," he wrote in an analysis on X. "The objective is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade." He said that Washington is faced with the dilemma that a limited response may encourage Iran to push further, while a stronger response risks accelerating the escalation that the U.S. is trying to avoid. "As long as the U.S. naval blockade remains in place and no agreement is reached, further escalation will become increasingly difficult to avoid," he said. "There are two clear paths to de-escalation: a negotiated agreement or a U.S. decision to lift the blockade." Iran renews attacks on American bases After Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 to launch the war, Iran regularly fired on American facilities and interests in neighboring Gulf countries, as well as energy infrastructure and other targets. In the attack early Wednesday on the Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait, the Iranian military fired at air defense systems and drone and missile launch platforms, according to a report on Iran's state broadcaster. Kuwait's military said that its air defenses had intercepted drone attacks and didn't immediately report any damage. The Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the repeated Iranian attacks as "criminal," saying that they threatened the country's security and stability. During the war, Ali Al Salem Air Base has been struck at least 30 times by Iran, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to an analysis by The Associated Press. The AP's analysis used satellite imagery from multiple providers to help determine that Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage. AP also spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or had firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment. 13a46f7720ed.text: The Senate GOP's last-ditch effort to pass a defense-heavy, $350 billion reconciliation package is dead on arrival without accompanying spending cuts, House Republicans tell Axios. Why it matters: House Republicans have just 16 days left in session before Democrats take control in January. Many don't want to spend their final days in power adding to the national debt. "My concern is we squander these very few days we have left on something that won't get out of the House," outgoing House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios of the Senate's emerging plan. Republicans have already passed two party-line reconciliation bills this Congress: The "one big, beautiful bill" in the summer of 2025, and nearly $70 billion for immigration enforcement in the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Finding spending offsets could reopen some of the most contentious fights from the GOP's first reconciliation package. Arrington told Axios that Senate Republicans worry that finding cost savings in health care spending could open the door to amendment votes that undo Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. But Arrington, who didn't run for reelection in 2026, told Axios he doesn't believe the Senate's proposal has the votes to pass the House without offsets. State of play: Arrington said he raised his concerns with Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), and argued Republicans shouldn't let the risks deter them from pursuing additional spending cuts. "Some Republican members of the Senate might go rogue and might decide to, I don't know, repeal some of the reforms that we put in the 'big, beautiful bill.' Maybe they do it out of spite for President Trump," he said. "The midterms have passed us. We lost, but we still have this window to do what we think is right," he said. Between the lines: Senate Republicans haven't committed to moving forward with another reconciliation package. Leaving a Wednesday night meeting on reconciliation, Sen. Johnson told reporters the Senate "probably" won't move forward this week, but a reconciliation bill isn't "off the table." Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters he wants to explore working with Democrats on the funding, but that reconciliation remains an "option" Wednesday night. What they're saying: "It needs to have offsets," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, told Axios. Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), another HFC member, also expressed skepticism about the proposal and its chances of passage. "It's not that I don't want to fund the Department of Defense, but it's always, 'Hey, are we just going to add this to the debt, add this to the deficit,'" he told Axios. The intrigue : Even if the two chambers can strike a deal, House GOP leaders are struggling to get their own members to show up for votes. GOP leaders were forced to pull a procedural rule vote Wednesday after 14 Republicans failed to show up, leaving leadership without the votes needed to move forward. Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios his colleagues need to return to Washington: "I mean, they're getting paid until Jan. 3." What's next: The House departs Thursday for Thanksgiving recess.

a29e7d64fbf4.text: The left's campaign to whip up a groundswell of opposition to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) among his members failed in stunning fashion on Wednesday. Why it matters: Fewer than a dozen members voted against Jeffries' nomination for speaker. That bodes well for Jeffries' ability to manage the House going forward, his allies say. "There'll be no hostage taking," Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) told Axios. Driving the news: Jeffries won a resounding victory Wednesday morning when House Democrats met behind closed doors to vote on their nominee for speaker of the House. Out of 264 Democratic House members and non-voting delegates, 251 voted to nominate him, 11 voted against and two did not vote. It was exactly the victory Jeffries' allies had hoped for after Tuesday's announcement that he planned to request a tallied vote rather than being nominated by acclamation. Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Chris Rabb (D-Pa.) and Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) put out a statement shortly after the vote confirming they voted against Jeffries. Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III (D-Texas) also signed on to that statement, but a spokesperson said in a follow-up statement he "narrowly missed the vote" and that his "intended vote was no." Two other members-elect, Don Leonard (D-Ohio) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.), told Axios they also voted no. Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) missed the vote because he was in his district with family following the death of his father, but would have voted for Jeffries, a spokesperson told Axios. Zoom out: Many of the progressives who ultimately voted for Jeffries did so despite a torrent of phone calls and emails from constituents and grassroots activists urging them not to support him. Numerous high-profile progressives had said before the meeting they would vote for Jeffries, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Greg Casar (D-Texas). Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who was floated as a potential challenger to Jeffries, told the Boston Globe she voted for him. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) also voted for him, a spokesperson told Axios. What they're saying: Jayapal said after the vote that Jeffries had "a very strong meeting" with the Congressional Progressive Caucus on Tuesday. "A lot of the issues that matter to us ... on Medicare for All, on immigration, I felt very, very good both about the public direction he's moved in and his commitments to us," she said. "I voted for him, as I have said I was going to do, and I feel like we've been clear about how we're going to continue to need to push." The intrigue: Three "no" votes were still unaccounted for as of Wednesday night. Several progressives who were seen as potential defectors declined to say how they voted. Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pa.), when asked how she voted, told Axios: "I'll say it to Hakeem, who I will talk to first before I talk to anybody in the press." Spokespeople for Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) did not respond to requests for comment. Between the lines: This isn't the posture of a left flank emboldened to take the fight to party leadership next year, as moderates and Jeffries allies gleefully pointed out. "This has been a manufactured crisis," said Rep. Adam Gray (D-Calif.), a leader of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition. "A handful of folks wanted to amplify their voices and perspectives, and it's always been a handful. It was a handful today." What's next: The vote now goes to the House floor, where Jeffries needs 218 votes to secure the gavel when the 120th House convenes for the first time on Jan. 3. He can lose more than 30 votes from his current total — which is unlikely — and still come out on top. "They're not going to hold ... Hakeem hostage. It's gone. Move on from that," centrist Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told Axios.

fd93cd119054.text: President Trump landed in southern China after signing a trade deal and pledging increased defense cooperation with the Philippines. On Thursday, Trump will hold a historic summit with the Chinese and Russian presidents on the sidelines of a meeting of Asia-Pacific countries in Shenzhen, China. Nick Schifrin reports. Geoff Bennett: President Trump landed in Southern China today after signing a trade deal and pledging increased defense cooperation with the Philippines. Amna Nawaz: Tomorrow, Mr. Trump will hold a historic summit with the Chinese and Russian presidents on the sidelines of a meeting of Asia-Pacific countries in Shenzhen, China. And that is where Nick Schifrin joins us from tonight -- Nick. Nick Schifrin: Amna, those milestone meetings begin in just a few hours, just a few miles from here, the site of the APEC summit. There's no official agenda, but the topics will include war and peace, Iran and Ukraine, trade, and nuclear weapons. Beijing says it could have -- quote -- "groundbreaking significance," as President Trump's trip here began with an unusual show of respect. In his 14 years in power, China's most powerful leader since Mao has never done what he did today, personally greet a foreign leader at the airport. But Xi Jinping and President Trump today leaned in to their promise to stabilize the U.S.-China relationship. And next to China's communist leader, Russian President Vladimir Putin joined hands with the leader of the free world ahead of their trilateral tomorrow, the first ever formal meeting held among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States. President Donald Trump: So we're going to talk about denuclearization, tough subject. Nick Schifrin: President Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear weapons. Man: China has joined the United States, Russia, France, and Britain in the exclusive nuclear club. Nick Schifrin: For years following China's 1964 nuclear test, Beijing limited its stockpile to around 300 weapons. But, today, Beijing tests nuclear-capable missiles and its nuclear arsenal is the fastest growing in the world. The Pentagon says, by 2030, Beijing will have more than 1,000 nuclear warheads. But that's still a fraction of the U.S. and Russia's. And Xi has long refused to discuss arms control until achieving parity. But trilateral arms control has long been a Trump priority. President Donald Trump: China is, frankly -- also, we discussed the possibility of a three-way deal, instead of a two-way deal. Nick Schifrin: And ahead of the summit, a senior U.S. official admonished: "We do think it's time for China to step up to the adult table and have adult conversations about adult things. They can't just take their ball and go home." China's Foreign Ministry this week suggested the ball is in their court, and said the trilateral will have -- quote -- "groundbreaking significance." Why would Xi Jinping, why does Beijing want this trilateral meeting here? Li Cheng: Well, first of all, it makes China look good. China is the country to host these two major powers. Nick Schifrin: In Shenzhen, I sat down with Hong Kong University Professor Li Cheng, who founded the Center on Contemporary China and the World. He says Beijing sees the meeting in the context of convening the region's leaders, not as a sequel to the 1945 Yalta summit, when Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin divided up Germany and Europe. Li Cheng: China did not see Russia as, like, a three kingdom. It's a multipolar world. And the multilateralism is the emphasis. Nick Schifrin: For Putin, the meeting will allow him to play global statesman after meeting Xi today. Xi Jinping, Chinese President (through interpreter): China-Russia relations have remained as solid as a mountain, undaunted by wind and rain, providing greater stability to an increasingly complex world. Nick Schifrin: Of course, the complexity has in part been created by Putin himself. The war in Ukraine will be a topic, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's fears, as he told Amna earlier this month. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: But I hope that these big guys will not -- will not divide the world and, of course, our country. Nick Schifrin: The other war on the agenda, Iran, where today the U.S. targeted an Iranian missile site. What about Iran? Do you think that Beijing is willing to help? Li Cheng: I think the answer is yes. China wanted the strait open. China wanted to -- Iran to have a -- to not develop a nuclear weapon. But, most importantly, I help you in this area, but, as a transactional leader, you should also understand China's core interests. So, that expands China's position. Nick Schifrin: At the top of China's core interests, Taiwan, trade and technology, and President Xi and Trump tomorrow will have their third bilateral this year after the U.S. this week increased restrictions to prevent Beijing from skirting us laws to access high-end chips. Beijing has countered those export controls with their own, restricting the sale of rare earth magnets, essential for everything from electric vehicles to American fighter jets. Does Beijing feel it has leverage right now? Li Cheng: China does have leverage. And rare earth is the one of the things. This certainly makes Chinese leadership more confident that they want to demand mutual respect. Nick Schifrin: In this city of 18 million, a former fishing village whose skyline today is crammed with cranes and Xi Jinping once called a miracle of world development, it might seem natural for the government to come across as confident. But consumer spending is down, real estate is slumping, and the middle class faces economic headwinds. Jiangyuan Luo: Most people living are in really hard situations. Their salaries get less, and their workloads get more haves. Nick Schifrin: Jiangyuan Luo recently lost his job selling to overseas customers. Jiangyuan Luo: We should have cooperation, instead of conflict. Yes, people need cooperation. Otherwise, this is a lose-lose

d0ae6ef314e4.text: For perspective on President Trump’s trip to China and how foreign governments assess the president, Amna Nawaz spoke with Julia Curlee. She's a former CIA analyst and served on the National Security Council staff during the Biden and Trump administrations. She’s now a public service fellow at Lawfare, a publication that focuses on national security. Amna Nawaz: For perspective on President Trump's trip to China and how foreign governments assess the president, we turn now to Julia Curlee. She's a former CIA analyst. She served on the National Security Council staff during the Biden and Trump administrations and was Vice President Pence's main daily briefer. She's now a public service fellow at Lawfare. That's a publication that focuses on national security. Good to see you. Thanks for being here. Julia Curlee, Former CIA Analyst: Thank you. Of course. Amna Nawaz: So let's begin with Xi Jinping's decision to greet President Trump upon arrival on the tarmac, to greet him with a hug. This is not something he normally does. What does that level of warmth and some would say even deference say to you? Julia Curlee: I would say it's playing directly to what they assess as what the president most wants out of the summit, which is to play to his legacy, to be treated uniquely, to show reciprocity to the kind of treatment that he gave Xi upon his visit to Washington. This is a president deeply focused on his legacy, on his ballroom, on arches on history, how he will be remembered, and so this kind of a gift to him is deeply valuable, and they will expect a lot in return. Amna Nawaz: So, say more on this. And just the way of background, during your time at the CIA, obviously, understanding incentives, understanding the psychology of foreign leaders is part of your work. Other nations do that too. From the Chinese perspective, how would Xi Jinping be preparing for this kind of summit with President Trump? What would they hope to achieve from this meeting? Julia Curlee: Right. So they will be looking to provide the president with that which he most wants in order to extract what they most want. So, on one hand, they will be looking to feed what he wants in terms of imagery, standing astride the world, these three great leaders, him, Putin, and Xi, all showing themselves to be first among equals of world powers. That is the primary gift that he offers. In exchange, he will be looking for some much more concrete benefits from the president. Whether this is an extension of the trade truce on China's terms, whether this is to set aside any possible looming export controls, whether this is a continued extension of the suspension of arms sales to Taiwan, all of these are the concrete things that Chinese advisers will be saying to Xi might be on the table. Amna Nawaz: And what about vice versa? From the U.S. side, how would President Trump have been briefed and prepared, will be armed with going into these meetings? Julia Curlee: Well, hopefully, he has been armed. Hopefully, there has been staff work going into these. That's often been a problem. If he had been armed, he would have been told that some of the main concrete deliverables that they have wanted, like a nuclear agreement between the three powers, are probably unlikely, at least in any concrete terms. The Chinese have been very clear about this of not wanting to agree to a nuclear arms control agreement until they reach parity with the United States. Amna Nawaz: The fact that all of this is taking place in the wake of that Nvidia scandal we have spent so much time covering, how does that inform these interactions? What would you expect to be happening here? Julia Curlee: Under normal circumstances, when the president sits down across the table from a world leader who has been running a chip diversion scheme to divert some of the most important technology in the strategic competition with the United States by planting a spy at the side of his most important adviser in what is the most important technology in this strategic competition, you would think the U.S. president would be pressing the Chinese to back off of such of such efforts. But we have already seen the president in public dismiss the conclusions of the intelligence community, saying that she may or not may not have actually been a spy, and saying that the United States, of course, does things of its own, effectively taking this issue off the table. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you more about the Russian President Vladimir Putin's presence there, because we have now reported Trump is expected to meet separately with him during this trip. And we have seen those images you referenced, these three men together, Putin and Trump shaking hands, standing by Xi Jinping, and then all posing together for the larger group photo. What do you, with your intelligence background, what do you take away from these interactions and what Russia would be hoping to get from this summit? Julia Curlee: Right. So the end goal is the message that it would send to other countries, specifically countries allied with the United States in East Asia and in Europe. So, from Putin's perspective, the best outcome would be an image that looks like Yalta, that would look like the three world powers dictating terms to the other smaller powers of the world. And, in this case, it would be the United States and Russia finding a way together to settle the Ukraine issue without Zelenskyy and the Ukrainians even being at the table, and the message that would send to Europeans to NATO allies of the United States. Amna Nawaz: You have been part of the tense preparation that goes into meetings and summits like this. What does a successful outing for the U.S. president look like? Julia Curlee: Normally, it looks like concrete deliverables mostly that have been negotiated in advance. I don't see in this case what has been done to prepare the president to bring home those kind of concrete deliverables. He sees his direct relationship w

Why has Waymo pulled all its driverless cars from US freeways?
Waymo has temporarily suspended driverless rides on US freeways after California banned the service over safety concerns.
California's Department of Motor Vehicles said a series of traffic incidents, including robotaxis entering active construction zones, posed an imminent risk to public safety. Waymo has now restricted freeway operations in all other US markets while it reviews the performance of its vehicles.
Waymo currently operates in 15 US cities, though only offered driverless freeway rides in a handful of cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

36c00fa2bd76.text: In our news wrap Wednesday, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries moved a step closer today to becoming the next Speaker of the House, Democrats have secured a 56-to-44 majority in the Senate after Mary Peltola won the last outstanding race in Alaska and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new military agreement with Venezuela. Geoff Bennett: And we start today's other headlines on Capitol Hill. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries moved a step closer today to becoming the next speaker of the House, which would make him the first Black American to hold the speaker's gavel. House Democrats nominated the New York congressman for the post in a closed-door vote of 251 to 11. But Jeffries must still win a vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes in January. A group of incoming Democrats who opposed his nomination said they had secured commitments to discuss their concerns in good faith. Asked about that opposition today, Jeffries pointed to his overwhelming victory, saying the results speak for themselves. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY): We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other, to fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people. Geoff Bennett: House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark as majority leader, Pete Aguilar as majority whip, and Joe Neguse as assistant speaker. All ran unopposed. Separately, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, is taking his first steps towards investigating Trump officials and Trump family members. He's calling on Vice President Vance, Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, and President Trump's sons Donald and Eric, among others, to preserve documents related to their political and business activities. Meantime, Democrats have officially secured a 56-to-44 majority in the U.S. Senate, after winning the last outstanding race in Alaska. Democrat Mary Peltola flipped the seat, defeating two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a race called last night. In a victory speech posted on social media, Peltola focused on the rising cost of living, especially fuel prices. Mary Peltola: From Adak to Metlakatla to Utqiagvik, you have made your voices heard. And it's clear that the status quo in D.C. cannot go on any longer. We need to bring prices down. We need to lower fuel costs and build new homes. Geoff Bennett: Peltola also makes history as one of the first two Native American women elected to the U.S. Senate, alongside Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan. As Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin told the "News Hour" today, Peltola's roots helped her claim victory. Liz Ruskin: I think, for a lot of Alaskans, it's significant to see an Alaskan native person elected to the U.S. Senate. And beyond that, she was raised on the Kuskokwim River in a rural community that's off-the-road system. For some Alaskans, they see this as a homegrown win, despite the hundreds of millions of dollars that were poured into Alaska for this race. Geoff Bennett: It took nearly two weeks for Alaska's race to be called, in part because of the state's lengthy timeline for receiving mail and ballots. Alaska also uses ranked-choice voting, which requires a candidate to secure a majority of the vote to win. The FDA remains without a full-time leader after the White House pulled its nominee for the post ahead of a Senate committee vote scheduled for today. Dr. Heidi Overton, a physician and domestic policy adviser to President Trump, didn't appear to have enough support even among Republicans. She helped shape some of the administration's most controversial health policies, including efforts to scale back the number of vaccines routinely recommended for children. It's unclear whether the White House will nominate someone else before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new military agreement today with Venezuela. Venezuelan state TV showed footage of his visit to the presidential palace in Caracas, where he met with interim President Delcy Rodriguez. The Pentagon had not previously disclosed the visit. The new deal covers joint military training and intelligence sharing between the two nations. Hegseth is the latest Trump administration official to visit Venezuela since U.S. forces ousted then President Nicolas Maduro in January. In the Middle East, Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired missiles at Saudi Arabia after Saudi-led forces launched airstrikes in Yemen. In the port city of Hudaydah, well, one strike set a factory on fire. Houthi health officials say at least 15 people were killed. Another airstrike hit a shoe factory in Yemen's capital, killing at least two people. Separately, Iran says it launched a drone attack on a military base in Kuwait used by U.S. forces. Kuwait says it shot down the drone before it reached its target. The U.S. military says no U.S. service members have been injured in Iranian attacks this week. On Wall Street today, stocks ended mixed, ahead of Anthropic's public listing tomorrow. The Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 500 points. The Nasdaq managed a gain of less than half-a-percent. The S&P 500 posted its fifth straight losing session. And another of the last Pearl Harbor survivors, Gebhard Galle, has died. Galle was just 20 years old serving aboard the USS Nevada when Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. A torpedo struck his ship during the attack. Galle later helped save four fellow sailors while serving aboard another vessel. He died earlier this week on the same day as another Pearl Harbor survivor, Freeman Johnson. With their passing, fewer than a dozen Pearl Harbor survivors are known to be alive today. Gebhard Galle was 105 years old.

4bce3b8371e0.text: National security officials from the Trump administration were on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, and lawmakers had plenty of questions about the series of outages and cyber problems that have alarmed millions. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton sought to reassure Americans during their testimony. Stephanie Sy reports. Amna Nawaz: National security officials from the Trump administration were on Capitol Hill today, and lawmakers had plenty of questions about the series of outages and cyber problems that have alarmed millions. Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of homeland security, and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, sought to reassure Americans during their testimony before a House committee. Stephanie Sy has that report. Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY): Committee on Homeland Security will come to order. Stephanie Sy: On Capitol Hill today, lawmakers demanded answers from the Trump administration over a series of outages that have jolted Americans in the last couple of weeks, including the National Security Agency, Microsoft, banks, and the nationwide grounding of air travel. Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin said none of the incidents were tied to any attack. Markwayne Mullin: I have said this publicly, I'm 98 percent confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems. Stephanie Sy: Mullin was also sharply questioned by Ranking Member Bennie Thompson over a flight he took in a private plane the morning after the grounding. Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS): While Americans were stranded in airports across the country, with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game. For the secretary of homeland security to do that during a crisis was not only irresponsible, Mr. Secretary, but also incredibly tone-deaf. Markwayne Mullin: We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication, and didn't have one single incident. That in itself is a great success. And then you want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great-nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior to that, because I wanted to be a good uncle. Stephanie Sy: Mullin also said he took that flight to signal to Americans that it was safe to fly again. But the recent disruptions extend well beyond the skies to other daily life, leaving many nervous Americans with questions. Lawmakers pressed for more specifics. Rep. Michael Guest (R-MS): We have seen Microsoft services go offline, a nationwide ground stop, disruption within our major banking institutions, disruption of U.S. national security communications infrastructure. And, earlier this week, United Airlines had a nationwide system outage. Stephanie Sy: While Cabinet officials didn't provide a definitive answer on the causes, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, reassured Americans the failures were not related or coordinated. Jay Clayton: We have no indication that they have come from external threat actors or state-sponsored actors. Stephanie Sy: But Clayton did say system upgrades were being performed during some of the outages that occurred. Jay Clayton: I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions. These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. Stephanie Sy: Meanwhile, after their overwhelming election wins, Democrats also used the opportunity to grill Mullin on immigration enforcement and the role of ICE. Pablo Hernandez Rivera, Resident Commissioner of Puerto Rico: When the government enters an apartment and zip-ties children and citizens, the government is the threat. When the government opens fires on our streets, and families have to bury their dead, the government is the threat. Stephanie Sy: Mullin defended his record. Markwayne Mullin: Our policy right now is to go after the worst of the worst. But every time you go after the worst of the worst, you also have what we call collateral criminals. So, when we arrest someone that's on a warrant, most of the time, they're not by themselves. Stephanie Sy: That policy is likely to face further scrutiny by Congress next year as it ushers in new majorities. Rep. Andrew Garbarino: Without objection, this committee stands adjourned. Stephanie Sy: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

75fa20dc18bb.text: More than 30 House Republican incumbents lost their seats in the general election amid this year’s blue wave. One of those is Rep. Mike Lawler of New York. Lawler earned a reputation as a moderate, willing to buck his own party, and was rated one of the most bipartisan members of Congress during his time in office. Amna Nawaz spoke with Lawler about the midterm results and the future of the GOP. Amna Nawaz: More than 30 Republican incumbents in the House of Representatives lost their seats in the general election amidst the first time. One of those incumbents is Congressman Mike Lawler, who's represented New York's 17th Congressional District in the Lower Hudson Valley since he flipped the seat for Republicans in 2023. Lawler earned a reputation as a moderate, willing to buck his own party, and was rated one of the most bipartisan members of Congress during his time in office. To discuss the midterm elections, the future of the Republican Party, and more, Congressman Lawler joins me now. Congressman, welcome back to the show. Good to see you. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY): Thanks for having me. Amna Nawaz: So let's begin with the news. Today, we saw national security officials on Capitol Hill testifying, facing a number of questions about the series of tech outages we have seen over the last week or so, e-mail platforms, banking, the nationwide ground stop. They maintained that they were all separate service outages, not coordinated, not state-sponsored attacks. Are you satisfied with the answers that you have been getting from the administration on those outages? Rep. Mike Lawler: Listen, I'm not a conspiracy theorist, but obviously there's a lot of coincidences happening all at once. And, certainly, I think it's incumbent on the administration to give Congress a full debrief in a classified setting to really address all of the questions and concerns. Obviously, we hope there was no nefarious actions taken or any rogue states seeking to cause disruptions or cyberattacks. But it speaks to, obviously, the seriousness of cybersecurity and the seriousness of putting in place critical guardrails on AI. As AI becomes more prevalent, as we saw with a GAO study, report that just came out, AI -- in the four major AI platforms, GAO was able to have them create a terrorist manifesto, if you will. And that is something that is deeply concerning from a security standpoint. So, as we look at all of these issues, cybersecurity is real, the potential threats against our economic security, our financial institutions, our airlines, our national security. We have to take all of this very seriously. And it's why it requires an all-of-government approach, and it requires full transparency between the administration and Congress. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you about another bit of news today, which is House Democrats selecting Hakeem Jeffries as their speaker, as speaker of the House. Last week, House Republicans, as you know, chose Jim Jordan to lead them. I know you won't be in the House when he takes that role, but you did vote against him during the 2023 speaker battle. Do you still think he's the wrong choice to lead right now? Rep. Mike Lawler: No, look, I think, obviously, the conference has spoken. I have got to know Jim very well. I think he will do a great job as Republican leader and unify the conference as they head into the minority for the next two years. I think it's going to be incumbent on Leader Jeffries to show that he can actually govern and not just do the bidding of the far left of his party. Obviously, they have very large margins, but that also is going to mean that their base expects them to deliver on things the base wants. And with a Republican administration for the next two years, the question is, will a House Democrat majority and Senate Democrat majority be able to actually work with a Republican president, or will we have two years of gridlock and investigation? My hunch is, knowing Leader Jeffries as I do, we're going to have two years of gridlock and investigation and very little results. Amna Nawaz: When you look back at these midterm results, after what seemed like such a sweeping rebuke in these results, what message do you hope that your party, that Republicans take away from those midterms? Rep. Mike Lawler: Well, look, the pendulum swings in politics. Politics is cyclical. We have seen it time and again. But the pendulum keeps swinging harder and faster. As you pointed out at the beginning, I have a reputation not only of bucking my own party at times, but working across the aisle, delivering real bipartisan results. As I fundamentally believe, the party, and certainly in the next presidential election, the candidate that seeks to talk to the 60 percent of the country is going to do well. The party that finally realizes in Congress and in statehouses across the country that bipartisan cooperation is important will do well. My concern is, we're headed for two more years of gridlock, which is not going to serve the American people well. So I think, as we move forward, Republicans need to obviously rebuild, lick their wounds, but focus on the issues most acutely impacting the American people. And that obviously is economic. It's immigration. It's health care. It's housing. It's energy. It's the quality-of-life issues. Amna Nawaz: Well, before Democrats take control in this next Congress, there is still work to be done. We know government funding runs out on December 11. You see a growing number of Democrats now want to use that deadline to try to restrict funding for the Iran war. How likely, in your view, is a government shutdown right now? Rep. Mike Lawler: I think it is a disastrous endeavor by the Democrats to once again play politics with funding when it comes to national security. Remember, they shut the government down for 118 days with respect to the Department of Homeland Security. It was outrageous. And it is not something they should undertake again. They have a polic

A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies.
D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.
The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.
He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.
His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.
They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".
The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company.
"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".
Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.
On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".
A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.
He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.
He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
The arrest comes as espionage allegations roil the US tech industry, amid the news that Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
Last month, a former OpenAI employee was charged with planting a listening device in a company office. The man was later accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government.

a6f2b46fbb5d.text: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached an extraordinary milestone — traveling so far from Earth that it now takes a full day for light, or a radio signal, to reach it. Launched nearly 50 years ago, Voyager 1 is the farthest any human-made object has ever traveled, and the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Miles O’Brien puts this achievement in perspective and explains what comes next. Geoff Bennett: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling so far from Earth that it now takes a full day for light to reach it. Launched nearly 50 years ago, Voyager 1 is now roughly 16 billion miles away, the farthest any human-made object has ever traveled, and the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. It's a remarkable feat of engineering and exploration, and a testament to the enduring reach of human curiosity. Our science correspondent, Miles O'Brien, joins us now to put this achievement in perspective and explain what comes next. So, Miles, let's start with the sheer distance, a full light day away. What does that mean exactly? Miles O'Brien: Well, let's go back to grade school. Light travels at 186,000 miles per second. Nothing goes faster than that. And over the course of the day, that equates to 16 billion miles, which is where we find voyager. It happened about a little after 5:00 in the morning Eastern time, but we won't get confirmation about it from the spacecraft until tomorrow. It's a 48-round trip communication, 48 hours. Radio transmitter on board is about 23 watts. That's the power of a refrigerator bulb. It launched in 1977. It was designed to last five years, Geoff, but it's still going. And at roughly 38,000 miles per hour, it would take 75,000 more years to get to the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, although it's not headed in that direction. Geoff Bennett: Voyager is still going, as you say. It's still sending data back to Earth after all these years. What are we learning from it? Miles O'Brien: Well, it's interstellar space. It's a fascinating place. Voyager 1 went there in 2012, Voyager 2 in 2018. There were a -- a twin launch back in 1977. The sun creates an enormous bubble of charged particles, Geoff, magnetic fields. We call it the heliosphere. Voyager now is beyond that, and it's in this interstellar space, where it's examining the plasma and the magnetic fields to understand what the heliosphere does for our solar system, how it interacts with the galaxy, and how it shields us from cosmic radiation. Now, a telescope can't do this. This is the difference between looking at the ocean from the surface and diving in. Geoff Bennett: And, Miles, for people who are too young to remember Voyager's earliest missions, take us back. What did it reveal that we simply didn't know previously? Miles O'Brien: Yes. Sit down and listen, sonny. Let me tell you about what happened when I went to college. The big revelation, the outer solar system, and that is to say, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, is not a collection of frozen, dead worlds. It a lot's going on out there. They discovered active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io. Those are the first volcanoes we have seen beyond Earth. They discovered an ocean, a liquid water ocean underneath the surface of Europa, which is another Jupiter moon, astonishing complexity in Saturn's rings, established that Saturn's moon, Titan, has a methane atmosphere, definitely a no-smoking planet. And they found active nitrogen geysers on Neptune's frozen moon, Triton. This led to all kinds of follow-on missions, Galileo, Cassini, and soon the Europa Clipper, to do a deeper dive. Geoff Bennett: And Voyager 2 will eventually reach that same distance. How much longer do we expect these two spacecraft to keep sending back useful information? Miles O'Brien: Well, Voyager 2 will get to this light day milestone on November 2035. But the spacecraft may be silent by then. NASA engineers have had to shut down instruments and nonessential systems to conserve power. It's powered by decaying plutonium, and that has a limit, creates heat and thus electricity. Now, when the communications end, however, these spacecraft will keep clipping along at 38,000 miles an hour, and they each carry the famous golden records assembled under the leadership of the great late astronomer Carl Sagan. There's music on there, natural sounds, photographs. It's kind of an interesting message in a bottle for any distant civilization, should they come upon it sometime. Now, on the subject of the late great Carl Sagan, I want to take you back to June of 1990. He and the Jet Propulsion Lab team had a news conference, and they revealed perhaps one of the most famous shots of all from Voyager. Before they turned the cameras off, they got this image we call the Pale Blue Dot. Carl Sagan, Astronomer: This is -- looks like more than a dot, but it is in fact less than a pixel, a single picture element inside. In this color picture, you can see that it is slightly blue. And this is where we live, on a blue dot. That's where everyone you know and everyone you ever heard of and every human being who ever lived, lived out their lives. It's a very small stage in a great cosmic arena. Miles O'Brien: I got to say, Dr. Sagan could do poetry, couldn't he? That was 1990, Earth less than a pixel in that photograph. And as Voyager reaches this new milestone, it's kind of worth reflecting on how far we have traveled, and yet, Geoff, how small we are in the grand scheme of things. Geoff Bennett: Miles O'Brien, lyrical, as always. Always great to speak with you, friend. Miles O'Brien: You're welcome, Geoff.

c59adfa8f716.text: One of the biggest entertainment launches in history is underway with billions of dollars at stake. It’s the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest edition of the long-awaited and controversial video game. If you’re wondering what all the hype is about, Tim McPhillips has a helpful guide. Geoff Bennett: One of the biggest entertainment launches in history is under way with billions of dollars at stake. It's the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI," the latest edition of the long-awaited and controversial video game. Players jumped on for hours and livestreamed it on YouTube and Twitch starting overnight in New Zealand and Australia. Amna Nawaz: In the U.S., the game becomes available at midnight. So don't be surprised if you see a colleague or two call in sick to work tomorrow. Miami, which is the setting for the game's fictional Vice City, is fully on board, promoting it on buildings at South Beach, and all around the city. If you're wondering what all the hype is about, our own Tim McPhillips is here with a helpful guide. Tim McPhillips: Pack your bags and call out of work. We're going to Vice City. Actor: Save my city, baby. Actress: Vice City. Tim McPhillips: Here's what you need to know about what could be the biggest release in media this year. Stephen Totilo, Game File: You have a fandom eager and excited for this game. Then you have an industry that is also not just anticipating it, but arguably relying on it. Tim McPhillips: Stephen Totilo covers the gaming industry in his newsletter Game File. Stephen Totilo: Rockstar Game, which makes "Grand Theft Auto"s, has been working on "GTA VI" for four or five, six years, in earnest. Tim McPhillips: Even if you haven't cruised Vinewood Boulevard or been through Star Junction from its predecessors, Rockstar Games' upcoming release is a big deal. Stephen Totilo: They don't say how many people, but we can assume 1,000-plus have worked on it. They don't say how much. We can assume a billion dollars-plus in terms of development costs. Tim McPhillips: That would make it one of, if not the most expensive video games ever made. But to understand "GTA VI," you need to understand "GTA V." Stephen Totilo: "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the most successful video games of all time. Tim McPhillips: Released in 2013, it's estimated to have sold more than 230 million copies. Never played it? Stephen Totilo: It is up there with "Minecraft" and "Tetris" in terms of a game that is nearly ubiquitous, in terms of its cultural success. Tim McPhillips: Set in a version of Los Angeles, "GTA V" wasn't just an immersive open world game. It was a virtual city where people could just live life. Stephen Totilo: People kind of broke the rules. They said, OK, Rockstar wants us to all like commit virtual bank robberies together, but we can just hang out, the way that people might gather in real life, a country club or something like that. Tim McPhillips: For those, myself included, who have played "GTA V" for 13 years, the sheer weight has added to the buildup. Stephen Totilo: And "Call of Duty" is huge. And you get a new "Call of Duty" every year. If the "Call of Duty" fans had to wait 13 years for another "Call of Duty" they would be like crawling up the wall. Tim McPhillips: "GTA VI" returns to Vice City, a twin, if you will, of Miami, in an expanded map that represents some version of Florida. It will follow two main characters, Jason and Lucia. Stephen Totilo: They are basically kind of a Bonnie and Clyde duo. Tim McPhillips: Totilo says Rockstar has been more secretive about this game than usual. And as to the hype? Stephen Totilo: This is all the machinery of nostalgia, anticipation, marketing. What it isn't is a measure of quality yet. Tim McPhillips: While fans are cautiously hoping the hype is worth it, the gaming industry is too. Stephen Totilo: The video game industry is struggling right now. Tim McPhillips: That's despite gaming being immensely popular. Stephen Totilo: The gaming industry had a boom during COVID, when people were locked at home. Tim McPhillips: That created a flood of interest and investment. But when lockdowns eased: Stephen Totilo: The chickens kind of came home to roost for the industry, and there's been a lot of contraction since then. Tim McPhillips: Totilo says that's meant job losses, studio closures, and shrinking budgets in an industry built for big, expensive games. Yet: Stephen Totilo: People are going for, in a lot of cases, cheaper games, games they can play on their cell phones. This could be not just an exciting moment, but maybe even a turnaround moment. Tim McPhillips: Now, you're forgiven if you're surprised by all this, since Rockstar Games, especially its "Grand Theft Auto" series, has sparked controversy, even outrage over problematic depictions of women and other groups, and glorification of gratuitous violence. Stephen Totilo: They scared a nation. Rockstar was getting picketed outside of its offices in the era of "GTA IV" and "GTA V." And in the era of "GTA VI," no, they are premiering their game on Netflix. Tim McPhillips: But the games are also known for their satire-like commentary of American culture. Stephen Totilo: When I played "GTA V" in 2013, there was a lot of Obama era stuff in terms of housing crisis, in terms of -- and even stuff back to the second Bush administration, in terms of war on terror, is torture effective or not? Tim McPhillips: Which leads Totilo to wonder, for a series often ahead of America culturally, is America moving too fast for "Grand Theft Auto"? Stephen Totilo: I'm really curious as to what a Rockstar game of 2026 is going to be saying about America and if America can truly be satirized anymore. Tim McPhillips: For 810 Vice City News, I mean PBS News, I'm Tim McPhillips.

43cdbbaa4ed6.text: Best-selling author Min Jin Lee spends years meticulously researching her novels. Her latest, “American Hagwon,” examines the pressures and aspirations surrounding education in Korean culture. She joined Amna Nawaz to discuss the extensive interviewing behind her work and how she captures the immigrant experience. Amna Nawaz: Bestselling author Min Jin Lee spends years meticulously researching her novels, including "Free Food for Millionaires" and "Pachinko," which explore the Korean diaspora. Her latest novel, "American Hagwon," examines the pressures and aspirations surrounding education in Korean culture. She joined me on "Settle In" to discuss the extensive interviewing behind her work and how she captures the immigrant experience. Faith and the Christian faith community that the families are a part of also plays a big role in this book. There's so many scenes, so many pivotal scenes, and so many pivotal interactions that take place within that faith community, and also the faith that guides the morals, or doesn't in the case of some characters, through the storylines. Why make that such a big part of the book and the families? And was that a big part of your own experience? Min Jin Lee: It was definitely a big part of my experience, but I never attended a Korean church growing up. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Min Jin Lee: That said, I really wanted to focus on religious organizations and faith centers, because, for most people in the world, most people believe in God. I think that the intelligentsia very often think that religion can be regressive. And I think that could be your opinion, and I respect that very much. That said, when people of color and also immigrants and working-class people and also ruling class people believe in God and they go to their organizations, they have a whole other identity that's separate from the majority community. So for, let's say, a poor working-class immigrant, you could be working in a job that -- in which nobody respects you, you could be working in a fried fish store, for example, not owning the fried fish store, but working in it, and you could be that person who works there 60 hours a week. But then on Sunday morning, you go to church, you put on your suit, and you are somebody else to everybody in that world. And I had to look at both those things, because to not understand both parts of this character's life, we're actually missing that person, because how do you actually get through 60 hours of frying fish? Like, what sustains you? What motivates you to show up every day and to deal with the oil in your pores? When I interviewed the people who worked in fried fish stores, they always had a very good reason. Amna Nawaz: How did you report on that part of the story or research it or study it to understand it more fully? Min Jin Lee: Well, I had to look stupid a lot. (LAUGHTER) Amna Nawaz: What does that mean? And I'm asking specifically about the faith portion of this, not necessarily the fried fish portion. I want to know that too. Min Jin Lee: Well, I had to look stupid a lot because sometimes I have to be in spaces in which I'm clearly less equipped. For example, like the command of the Korean language, my comprehension is decent. My speaking is not great. So I can be with people who don't speak hardly any English at all. So in that situation, sometimes, I have translators, or if I just need to observe somebody, I will be kind of fumbling through and looking like an idiot. And -- but both of us are both willing to communicate in our limited ways. And I find that to be a very moving experience for me, because we're both trying to approach truth. Like, this person trusts me to let me enter their kitchen. This person trusts me to enter into their places of faith, where they worship, where they worship God, and they actually let me into that space. I always kind of think, well, I'm really lucky that I get to do this. Like, what do I do with this story? Amna Nawaz: You can watch that full episode and more from "Settle In" on our YouTube page or wherever you get your podcasts.

7ca32e915378.text: By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/high-school-valedictorians-to-get-custom-kicks-after-sen-elect-colom-asks-nike-to-just-do-it Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter High school valedictorians to get custom kicks after Sen.-elect Colom asks Nike to 'Just Do It' Politics Nov 18, 2026 6:07 PM EST Nike is gifting high school valedictorians across the country with a pair of custom sneakers after Mississippi's incoming senator appealed to the company on social media. Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, called on the sneaker giant to honor his historic election by giving every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of custom Air Force 1s -- his favorite style. The sneakers cost between $90 and $180 on the company's web site. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit," the Democrat suggested Monday on X, referencing Nike's famous slogan. The company accepted the challenge and took it one step further. "The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea," Oregon-based Nike responded Tuesday on X. "@scott_colom, we'll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let's go!" Nike said more details would be forthcoming, but Colom has already suggested the custom sneaker should give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippian who was the first African American to serve in Congress when he took office in 1870. WATCH: How Scott Colom won his longshot bid to flip Mississippi's Senate seat "I'm so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment. This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great," he wrote on X on Tuesday. "Please consider honoring Hiram Revels in the design." Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month's midterm elections. WATCH: Scott Colom's historic victory marks 'new moment' for Black voters, Bryan Stevenson says When he takes office in January, he'll become the state's third Black senator, following Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce, who was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate when he took office in 1875. Colom's victory marked a major shift in the Magnolia State, which has the nation's largest proportional share of Black people but for decades has largely been controlled by white conservatives. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.
Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".
A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.
Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.
This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.
The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.
She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.
Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.
When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.
Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.
"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.
"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.
That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying t

The scion of a prominent Republican donor family met with President Donald Trump in an effort to close a $5 billion deal facing fierce regulatory scrutiny.
Cintas, an $88 billion uniform and office supply behemoth, has for months been trying to secure regulatory approval to acquire smaller rival UniFirst. Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson is inclined to block the deal, Semafor earlier reported, and the FTC is preparing a âlast-ritesâ meeting, a precursor to suing to stop the merger.
Seeking to stave off a lawsuit, Cintas Executive Chairman Scott Farmer met with Trump in recent days, according to an administration official and other people familiar with the matter. Farmer urged the president to intervene and overrule Ferguson, the people said. Cintas and the family that controls it have donated to the presidentâs 2016 inauguration and helped him raise hundreds of thousands of dollars.
A spokesperson for Cintas declined to comment. Spokespeople for the FTC and the White House did not immediately provide comment.
The president has indicated that he would defer to Fergusonâs judgment, according to one person familiar with the matter.
Cintas has engaged litigation counsel and expects the FTC to sue, according to other people familiar with the situation. In an effort to appease investors souring on the deal, Cintas has indicated to some that it would seek a divestiture package to stave off a lawsuit, according to some of those people, but internally, the company has little appetite to divest, one of the people said.
Rohanâs view
Corporate America has gotten used to a light regulatory touch around deals, aided by a thriving scene of lobbyists and fixers in Trumpâs orbit. Then came the midterms, which delivered a repudiation of both AI and the perceived corporate capture of the White House and regulatory bodies.
Those in and around the administration, aware of these shifting tides, have begun to take small, cautious steps to tamp down that perception. The family that controls Cintas has long supported Trump, but their currency in this administration is significantly less valuable than it was a few weeks ago. Administration officials, chastened by the public rebuke, are no longer willing to play ball.

d73eb2790774.text: By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ap-report-bernie-sanders-unveils-how-hell-push-for-medicare-for-all-when-democrats-take-power Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP report: Bernie Sanders unveils how he'll push for Medicare for All when Democrats take power Politics Nov 18, 2026 5:38 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation's healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities. Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, is currently the ranking member on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and is expected to become its chairman when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. His agenda, first provided to The Associated Press, lays out the legislative implementation for proposals that he and progressive candidates championed on the campaign trail this cycle. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. At the center is Sanders' longstanding push for Medicare for All, a universal healthcare system that would be implemented over four years. The first year would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guarantee healthcare to children through age 18. "This is no longer a utopian vision. This is where the American people are," Sanders said in an interview with the AP. WATCH: Health care costs a major concern for voters ahead of midterms The proposals offer an early glimpse of how progressives hope to shape the Democratic Party's priorities after an election that delivered the party control of Congress but also exposed competing visions for its future. With the 2028 presidential election already looming, Sanders is seeking to push Democrats toward a populist economic agenda that he argues has gained broader support. "I think the election, in my opinion, was a crying out for fundamental change in the way the government does business and the absolute need to protect a struggling working class," Sanders said. "I think this is a time to bring about very significant changes in policies so that we can actually improve the lives of working families." Sanders keeps pushing for Medicare for All Sanders has long championed a single-payer national health insurance program that would replace most private insurance with a federally administered system providing universal coverage. His proposal for the new Congress lays out a four-year transition to that system, beginning with expanding Medicare eligibility and benefits. In the second year, the eligibility age would fall to 45, followed by 35 in the third year, before extending coverage to everyone in the fourth year. "Transforming a system which is 18% of the GDP of America, you don't do that overnight," Sanders said of the transitional period. WATCH: Trump says 'Medicare for All' doesn't work But the costs of lowering Medicare eligibility are likely to lead to massive debate between the two major political parties as the national deficit stands at $2 trillion, or 6.2% of gross domestic product. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that lowering the age of Medicare eligibility to 60 would increase federal budget deficits by $155 billion over the 2026–2031 period. Sanders' prior proposals to pay for the program shift healthcare financing away from private insurance premiums and toward payroll contributions — including a combination of employer and household premiums, higher taxes on the rich and new taxes on Wall Street and large firms. Sanders also argued that Democrats could pass the first stage of the transition through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain tax and spending legislation to advance through the 100-member Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically required to overcome a filibuster. Democrats will have a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party's largest advantage in the chamber in 16 years. Along with pushing for greater access to primary care, Sanders says Democrats will push for lower prescription drug costs. A changing political landscape Sanders has previously balanced his progressive ambitions with the realities of governing. During his first stint chairing the HELP Committee from 2023 to 2025, he worked with Republicans on legislation to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to primary care. He also chaired the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, helping advance major Democratic spending priorities. But now, just weeks after the midterms, Sanders is laying out an ambitious agenda that he argues reflects a shift not in his own positions but in voters' demands for sweeping changes to the healthcare system. WATCH: Abdul El-Sayed on Democratic leadership, health care access and inspiring a new generation He sees signs of that shift among Democratic leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has pledged to get to work "right out of the gate" to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republicans. Jeffries said Tuesday that Democrats know that simply returning to the status quo "is not acceptable" and they are preparing ways to further expand healthcare access by lowering the Medicare eligibility age, adding access to vision, hearing and dental coverage, and ensuring all kids are covered. "Jeffries basically supported the first year of Medicare for All," Sanders said. But anything that passes Congress the next two years will still need to be signed by President Don
